🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars
- How to Control AI Agents Before Access Sprawl Takes Over → AI agents are rapidly gaining access to sensitive systems, data, and workflows—but most security programs were never designed to govern non-human identities at this scale. This webinar breaks down how to discover AI agents, control their permissions, prevent excessive access, and build a governance model that keeps agent adoption from turning into the next major identity security problem.
- AI Attacks Move at Machine Speed. Can Your Identity Security Keep Up? → AI-powered attacks can now move from reconnaissance to privilege escalation faster than traditional security teams can investigate and respond. This webinar explains why identity is becoming the critical real-time control layer—and how runtime identity security can help organizations detect risky access, enforce decisions across cloud, SaaS, on-prem, and AI environments, and stop machine-speed attacks before they turn into breaches.
📰 Around the Cyber World
- Google Halts OSS VRP Submissions — As of October 1, 2026, Google is no longer accepting OSS VRP product vulnerability submissions due to a "significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid." The tech giant added: "For some Google Cloud repos impacting Google Cloud products, we may still accept reports covering product vulnerabilities through the Cloud VRP. We will continue to reformat and work on this aspect of the OSS VRP and commit to giving an update in Q1 2027."
- Microsoft's X Account Briefly Hijacked — Unknown attackers hijacked the official Microsoft account on X, which has over 13 million followers, in what appeared to be a pump-and-dump scheme promoting a crypto token. "We have confirmed unauthorized access to our account on X, including posts that did not come from Microsoft," a Microsoft spokesperson told The Verge. "The account has been secured, and the unauthorized posts have been removed, and we are continuing to investigate the circumstances."
- TIKTOUK, a WordPress Credential Collection Toolkit — A new toolkit called TIKTOUK "brings together WordPress probing, collection of exposed configuration data, recovery of encrypted email credentials, and JavaScript secret scanning," LevelBlue said. TIKTOUK features Python components and a Go-based Linux crawler that probes WordPress pages and REST batch routes, collects configuration and option values, and retrieves referenced JavaScript files, scans their contents, and reports matching secret patterns.
- Google Details PageBreak — Google has detailed an internal AI agent called PageBreak that aims to autonomously scale vulnerability discovery while minimizing manual work arising from hallucinated bug reports. "Rather than simply hypothesizing bugs based on code patterns, the system closes the loop by verifying potential flaws against running environments," Google said. "This approach results in a near-zero false positive rate, ensuring that we avoid overloading product teams with unverified vulnerability reports." Page has uncovered over 500 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities across Google first-party web applications.
- Milk Dragon Phishing Kit Detailed — Group-IB has shed light on an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kit called Milk Dragon (aka NaiLong) that has been active since October 2025. "Unlike conventional phishing tactics that rely on fear and urgency, Milk Dragon lures victims with big discounts on consumer goods distributed via Facebook and TikTok marketplace advertisements," Group-IB said. "Phishing pages impersonate brands across multiple industries, including Retail & Supermarket chains. Well-known brand names such as LEGO, Calvin Klein, Aeon Malaysia, and many others are exploited and used as lures." The attack is designed to steal financial information from victims. Actively sold on Telegram, Milk Dragon has claimed victims spanning 66 countries, with 258 phishing pages identified to date.
- Iranian Hacker Extradited to the U.S. — An Iranian hacker accused of being behind a cyber espionage campaign targeting hundreds of universities, federal and state government agencies, private sector companies, and non-governmental organizations has been extradited to the U.S. Amir Barati, 40, is expected to face wire and computer fraud charges in the US Southern District of New York. The High Court in Podgorica approved his extradition last month.
- New Variant of NodeStealer Emerges — Netskope Threat Labs said it detected a new variant of NodeStealer packing major updates that turn it into a full-blown spyware. The new features were likely written with AI assistance. "The latest Python NodeStealer variant incorporates new spyware features, including keylogging, clipboard monitoring, and screenshot capture," Netskope said. "In addition, it expands its theft targets to include Wi-Fi passwords, the victim’s Pictures folder, and two additional web browsers. Earlier NodeStealer variants queried only two Facebook Graph API endpoints. The latest variant queries more than 20 endpoints to construct a comprehensive dossier on the individual managing the account."
- Bypassing Microsoft's RejectDirectSend — ReliaQuest said an empty Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) envelope sender can bypass RejectDirectSend, which is designed to block unauthenticated Direct Send mail. "An external sender can omit the envelope domain while retaining an internal-looking address, making phishing messages more likely to be trusted. The message still carries an internal-looking address, increasing the likelihood that spearphishing reaches the recipient," ReliaQuest said. "The technique requires only one empty field – no credentials, no registered lookalike domain, and no dedicated sending infrastructure – so organizations should expect continued use." The cybersecurity company said it observed attackers repeatedly using self-addressed messages and familiar business lures to target leadership and business-facing users.
- Attackers Exploit PaperCut Flaws to Deliver AdaptixC2 — In late August 2026, threat actors exploited CVE-2026-82078 and CVE-2026-81578, two PaperCut MF vulnerabilities, as zero-days to load an in-memory Java loader, which in turn deployed a web shell. The web shell was then used to deploy a trojanized Microsoft Copilot binary carrying an AdaptixC2 implant. "AdaptixC2 is an open-source and highly modular post-compromise framework that provides a broad set of capabilities, including remote shell access, file management, reverse proxying, and modules for Active Directory attacks, credential harvesting, lateral movement, and more," eSentire said. "In this intrusion, threat actors used the lateral movement module to steal a token from a process running under a domain-privileged service account and move laterally to a domain controller." Upon gaining access to the domain controller, the threat actors dumped credentials to obtain the service account's NTLM hash and enabled Windows Restricted Admin mode. Ultimately, the attackers dumped the domain's Active Directory NTDS.dit database in an attempt to collect password hashes for all domain accounts.
- Anthropic Says GLM-5.3 Can Build Cyber Exploits — Anthropic revealed that Zhipu AI's (aka Z.ai) GLM-5.3 model can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits, like Claude Mythos Preview, and that it has been released without "meaningful safeguards to limit misuse." The AI company said attackers can bypass the open-weight model's safeguards between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques, adding that these lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors. "At the same time, these capabilities can also benefit defenders working to secure their systems," it added. "The funniest part is how Anthropic admitted self-reflectively that the lack of guardrails may actually be benefiting the defenders working to secure their systems," Evilginx creator Kuba Gretzky said in an X post. "Something they never wanted to allow, because of possible misuse."
Conclusion
This week was a useful reminder that attackers do not need one perfect path. A fresh exploit, an exposed secret, a weak mail control, or one careless workflow can all get them moving.
Patch what is exposed, review what is trusted by default, and keep an eye on the simple paths. The clever stuff matters, but plenty of trouble still starts with something ordinary being left open.

articles.title: Sam Altman : avec l'IA, « de mauvaises choses vont arriver », et il faut l'accepter
articles.text:
Sam Altman ne croit pas à une IA puissante, largement accessible et parfaitement inoffensive. Pour le patron d’OpenAI, en démocratiser l’accès suppose aussi d’accepter les risques qui l’accompagnent.
Les modèles progressent, les usages malveillants aussi. Ces derniers mois, OpenAI s’est prononcé pour des règles de sécurité plus strictes concernant les modèles de pointe et le recours à des évaluateurs externes, tandis que Sam Altman approuvait encore récemment l’appel de Dario Amodei à freiner leur développement. Dans un entretien accordé à POLITICO, le patron d’OpenAI a pourtant défendu une conception beaucoup plus permissive de l’accès à l’IA et de ses usages, quitte à assumer publiquement une part de leurs dérives.
La solution tout-en-un pour protéger votre entreprise
Votre petite entreprise a de grandes ambitions. Protégez-là contre les pirates. Et développez sereinement votre activité !
Mieux vaut des dérives qu’une IA confisquée par quelques-uns
« Nous pensons que le monde devrait accepter que de mauvaises choses se produisent », a lâché Sam Altman, au nom des bénéfices apportés par la technologie et de la liberté laissée à chacun de l’utiliser. Car pour garantir qu’il n’y ait ni piratage majeur, ni détournement, ni arnaque liés à l’IA, il faudrait accepter que les modèles les plus puissants restent entre les mains de quelques laboratoires chargés ensuite de décider qui peut en profiter et dans quelles conditions.
Un compromis que le patron d’OpenAI juge « totalement inacceptable », préférant composer avec une part d’abus plutôt que verrouiller davantage l’accès à des technologies dont les usages bénéfiques devraient, selon lui, dépasser de plusieurs ordres de grandeur les usages nuisibles. Vouloir empêcher chaque dérive reviendrait alors aussi à réduire tout ce que le public peut tirer de ces outils.
Cette tolérance doit toutefois s’arrêter face aux risques « vraiment catastrophiques », parmi lesquels Sam Altman range la possibilité d’une perte majeure de contrôle sur l’IA.
Avant même les modèles de demain, sécuriser ceux qui existent déjà
Les abus que Sam Altman accepte comme contrepartie d’une IA accessible au plus grand nombre ne relèvent de toute façon déjà plus de l’hypothèse. Les modèles actuels peuvent aider à rechercher des vulnérabilités, préparer des attaques et automatiser une partie de leur exécution, tandis que les agents gagnent en autonomie à mesure qu’ils peuvent manipuler des fichiers, utiliser des identifiants, lancer du code ou agir sur des services externes.
C’est aussi ce qui avait conduit George Kurtz à relativiser, en septembre dernier, l’appel de Dario Amodei à ralentir les modèles les plus avancés. Le patron de CrowdStrike rappelait alors que des systèmes potentiellement dangereux circulaient déjà et qu’en cela, freiner les générations suivantes ne neutraliserait pas les risques existants.
La sécurité ne peut donc pas se limiter à éprouver les modèles avant leur déploiement. Elle doit aussi accompagner les agents lorsqu’ils agissent, en surveillant leur activité, en contrôlant leurs accès et en permettant d’interrompre une action qui sort du cadre prévu. D’où la nécessité de renforcer les garde-fous en laboratoire, mais également une fois les systèmes déployés.

articles.title: 'Your wallet will be significantly lighter': MacBook Pro OLED rumored to be much lighter, but cynics remain worried about the price — and battery life too
articles.text:
MacBook Pro OLED rumored to be 'significantly lighter' but the main concern remains that it'll significantly lighten your wallet — or mess with battery life
Cost, battery life, or connectivity — what are you most worried about?
- MacBook Pro OLED is rumored to be "significantly lighter"
- Leaker Mark Gurman believes it could possibly arrive later this month
- If it is thinner and lighter, Apple laptop fans are worried that it might compromise on battery, or other areas – and concerns about the price remain strong
The supposedly imminent MacBook Pro with OLED is expected to be much lighter than a traditional MacBook Pro model, according to a new leak.
This comes from Mark Gurman's latest Power On newsletter (via MacRumors), where the leaker tells us: "Apple has reengineered the machine's interior, miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry."
As a result, the MacBook Pro OLED should be "significantly lighter" as well as thinner. Other rumors include a touchscreen with a dynamic island instead of a notch, and running on Apple's M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
The theory is that we're now very close to a launch, and that this will happen either later this month or in November.
Take all of this with an appropriate quantity of seasoning, of course, but this latest nugget of info about the trim nature of the MacBook Pro OLED has received a surprising amount of negative reaction.
Analysis: resistance to change
Some of the snipers who have Apple in their sights with this latest revelation – assuming that it's true – are happy with the MacBook Pro just as it is, and they don't want Apple messing with that design too much.
This Redditor complains: "The thick chassis of the current Pro is perfect. If people want thin they have the MacBook Air."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Others just don't want any change at all, with the following comment being heavily upvoted: "The current design is genius I'm actually not ready to move on from it."
Part of the whole point of going OLED, though, is that this allows for a slimmer screen, thereby contributing to the thinness of the notebook. So this should be no surprise really, although I guess the 'significantly' addition to the wording of the rumor is what's worrying folks.
I get that Gurman's comment about "miniaturizing parts" is going to cause something of a stir, too, as people are concerned that this means the battery may be in line for a compromise, and the laptop's longevity could suffer.
Another Redditor says: "Let's hope this isn't affecting the battery capacity… the current design of the internals is packed, it's not like there's anything redundant nor do I see them changing the chassis material."
Others fear that connectivity rather than battery life will be sacrificed in the pursuit of thinness, and there'll be fewer ports on the MacBook Pro OLED.
The biggest complaint by far, though, remains the price, with worries about Apple's OLED laptop being even more exorbitantly expensive if you throw another premium design element – being a lot thinner and lighter – onto the configuration sheet.
Rather than talking about the weight, this Redditor jokes: "I think this is a misunderstanding. Your wallet will be significantly lighter."
They aren't the only person cracking that joke on Reddit, either. We'll just have to see how this incoming MacBook Pro pans out, but for now, the cynics and skeptics firing flak clearly outnumber those who are excited for the arrival of the first OLED model.

articles.title: Sony pierde la paciencia con las canciones creadas con IA y pide retirar más de 260.000 pistas
articles.text:
Durante décadas, reconocer una voz era una de las formas más inmediatas de reconocer a un artista. Hoy esa certeza empieza a erosionarse: podemos encontrarnos con canciones que suenan como si estuvieran interpretadas por músicos conocidos, aunque esos artistas no estén detrás de la grabación ni hayan autorizado la imitación. La inteligencia artificial ha abierto nuevas posibilidades creativas, pero también ha hecho mucho más visible un problema que la industria lleva tiempo intentando contener: distinguir qué pertenece realmente a un artista y qué ha sido fabricado para parecerlo.
260.000 avisos y contando. Esa batalla empieza a entenderse mejor cuando miramos las cifras. Sony Music ha contado al Financial Times que, hasta finales de septiembre, había pedido a las plataformas digitales retirar más de 260.000 pistas generadas con IA que suplantaban a artistas de su catálogo. El ritmo se ha acelerado con fuerza: a finales de marzo de 2026 eran más de 135.000 y, un año antes, habían superado las 75.000. Hay una precisión importante: hablamos de solicitudes de retirada enviadas por la discográfica, no de 260.000 eliminaciones que podamos dar por completadas.
No son canciones cualquiera. Si afinamos el foco, el conflicto deja de ser “IA contra música” y pasa a ser mucho más concreto: quién puede utilizar la tecnología para fabricar una grabación y hacerla pasar por una interpretación de un artista real. Sony está reclamando la retirada de ese tipo de imitaciones no autorizadas, con Harry Styles, Adele, Britney Spears, Queen y Michael Jackson. Eso es lo que entendemos aquí por deepfake: una pieza sintética diseñada para atribuir a una persona una interpretación que en realidad no realizó.
El contenido vuelve a aparecer. El problema para Sony no termina cuando una plataforma elimina una pista denunciada. La discográfica sostiene que esos mismos contenidos pueden reaparecer después, lo que obliga a repetir el proceso y convierte la vigilancia en una tarea continua. Por eso reclama que los servicios no se limiten a responder a cada aviso, sino que impidan también nuevas subidas del mismo material. "Seguiremos haciendo valer los derechos de nuestros artistas y esperamos que las plataformas actúen rápidamente y eviten que el mismo contenido vuelva a aparecer, pero se está convirtiendo en una lucha cada vez más difícil", explicó la firma.
Sony no rechaza toda IA. La línea que está trazando la compañía no pasa por prohibir esta tecnología en la música, sino por cómo y con qué permisos se utiliza. En 2024 dejó expresamente fuera de autorización el uso de sus contenidos para entrenar, desarrollar o comercializar sistemas de IA, salvo permiso específico, y al mismo tiempo ha avanzado en modelos basados en música licenciada, como los acuerdos alcanzados con KLAY. En julio de 2026, Sony se sumó además a otros grandes grupos musicales para proponer que las grabaciones desarrolladas con IA solo puedan optar a las listas oficiales si utilizan servicios autorizados y legales, son sustancialmente humanas y no plantean problemas de manipulación.
La escala ayuda a entenderlo. Para medir el tamaño del ecosistema basta con mirar lo que está ocurriendo en otras plataformas. Deezer informó en julio de este año de que durante junio había recibido una media diaria de casi 90.000 pistas completamente generadas con IA, que llegaron a representar más del 50% de las nuevas entregas en los días de mayor volumen. No podemos sumar esas canciones a las denunciadas por Sony ni asumir que sean imitaciones de artistas reales, porque hablamos de categorías distintas. Lo que sí nos indican es la escala que ya ha alcanzado el contenido sintético dentro de las plataformas, aunque solo una parte pueda plantear problemas de derechos o suplantación.
La ley aún va detrás. El siguiente frente ya no está solo en las plataformas, sino también en Washington. Sony respalda la NO FAKES Act, que busca crear una protección federal frente a réplicas digitales no autorizadas de la voz y la apariencia de una persona. El proyecto superó por unanimidad el Comité Judicial del Senado el 18 de junio, pero todavía no es ley.

articles.title: NetApp's Novus targets AI data infrastructure at zettabyte scale - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
NetApp’s Novus tackles metadata bottlenecks in AI data infrastructure
AI data infrastructure must support growing GPU clusters while making enterprise data usable for models and agents.
NetApp Inc. is tying intelligent data infrastructure to production AI through a unified approach to storage and data management. Fragmented data and governance designed around manually applied policies can prevent enterprises from realizing returns on AI investments, according to Syam Nair (pictured, left), chief product officer of NetApp.
“There’s a lot of investment happening, lots of data applications are ready, models are ready, but most enterprises don’t get the returns,” he said. “Let’s provide that intelligent data infrastructure where there’s a unified storage that spans the entire ecosystem of wherever the infrastructure is.”
Nair and Gunna Marripudi (right), vice president of product management for Novus at NetApp, spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight at NetApp INSIGHT, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. (* Disclosure below.)
Rebuilding AI data infrastructure for zettabyte scale
NetApp’s Novus storage architecture exceeds 100TB/s of aggregate throughput, according to the company. Its Data Director manages metadata separately from the stored data, allowing each to scale independently. It also gives applications a unified view of files across multiple ONTAP storage clusters rather than requiring them to access each cluster separately, Marripudi explained.
“The metadata is the key,” he said. “The concurrency of the metadata access is the pillar for an architecture.”
Speed alone does not make data usable for AI agents, however. NetApp’s AI Data Engine discovers, classifies and vectorizes enterprise data, aiming to cut preparation work that typically takes six to nine months of engineering, Nair noted.
“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he said. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”
NetApp is also leaning on open standards so customers can extend what they already run. The planned acquisition of PEAK:AIO Ltd. is expected to bring parallel file system technology built on the pNFS protocol. Any Linux kernel released after 2018 already carries a pNFS client, Marripudi explained. The goal is AI data infrastructure that slots in alongside existing systems.
“It’s not a storage conversation, it’s not a data platform conversation, it’s a data infrastructure conversation,” Nair said. “The promise that we have is, ‘Customers, you don’t need to rip and replace what you already have.”

articles.title: Meta impulsa el proyecto Muse Gadgets para permitir que los desarrolladores creen sus propios accesorios de IA
articles.text:
Meta lanzó Muse Gadgets, un proyecto de código abierto para que desarrolladores creen accesorios propios conectados con Muse, su agente de inteligencia artificial. La iniciativa ofrece una base técnica para diseñar desde pantallas táctiles con la función “pulsa para hablar” hasta dispositivos que se conecten al puerto HDMI de una Smart TV. La propuesta busca llevar el agente fuera de las aplicaciones habituales y extenderlo a nuevos objetos tecnológicos.
El anuncio cobra relevancia porque Muse fue presentado a principios de septiembre como un sistema autónomo capaz de actuar en nombre del usuario. Meta indicó que puede buscar ofertas en la web, realizar compras, planear viajes y diseñar un programa de entrenamiento para los siguientes meses. Muse Gadgets abre la posibilidad de usar esas capacidades desde interfaces físicas, aunque también plantea preguntas sobre permisos, dispositivos, redes domésticas e información privada sensible.
El kit permite diseñar dispositivos conectados con Muse directamente
Para facilitar ese desarrollo, la compañía entrega firmware y un kit de desarrollo para Linux, conocido como Linux SDK. Ambos elementos permiten que el hardware creado establezca comunicación con el agente.
El planteamiento no obliga a seguir un formato único: cada desarrollador puede decidir forma, tamaño y finalidad del accesorio. Meta aporta infraestructura inicial; los creadores determinan cómo integrar Muse allí.
Los ejemplos incluyen pantallas táctiles, tinta y televisores inteligentes
Los ejemplos publicados muestran el alcance que Meta imagina para Muse Gadgets. Uno consiste en una pantalla de tinta electrónica, capaz de presentar respuestas, recordatorios o información consultada al agente. Otro adopta la forma de un stick HDMI para conectar Muse al televisor. También aparece un accesorio con pantalla táctil pequeña, pensado para ejecutar órdenes desde su pantalla, sin abrir aplicaciones.
Meta también presentó Muse Home Link, un dispositivo propio alimentado mediante USB tipo C. Nat Friedman, jefe de Producto de los laboratorios de superinteligencia de Meta, explicó que el accesorio permite conectar Muse a la red doméstica. Según indicó, el agente puede comunicarse con televisores, altavoces y otros equipos inteligentes que admitan HTTPS, el protocolo utilizado para intercambiar información mediante conexiones web.
El agente busca ampliar sus funciones cotidianas autónomas
El proyecto llega pocas semanas después de la presentación de Muse como agente autónomo. Meta señaló que puede buscar ofertas, organizar compras, planear viajes y diseñar programas de entrenamiento. Muse Gadgets busca trasladar esas tareas a objetos cotidianos. Una pantalla puede ofrecer consultas; un aparato para televisión puede ser punto de interacción; un control táctil activa solicitudes con el agente a demanda.
Cuál es la importancia del código abierto en el proyecto
El carácter abierto de Muse Gadgets permite que los desarrolladores planteen usos distintos para una misma base tecnológica. Un equipo puede construir una pantalla para mostrar datos; otro puede crear un accesorio para controlar dispositivos del hogar. El firmware y el SDK funcionan como punto de partida para conectar esos diseños con Muse. Meta no detalló productos, fabricantes ni fechas para lanzamientos.
Los antecedentes elevan las dudas sobre privacidad digital
La iniciativa aparece después de dos casos en los que Muse se apartó de las instrucciones de sus usuarios. En uno, el agente proporcionó a un comprador de Facebook Marketplace la dirección física de un vendedor sin consentimiento para concluir una compra. En otro, un columnista descubrió que Muse había accedido a sus mensajes en Mensajes de Apple sin autorización del propietario.
Meta deberá aclarar permisos para los nuevos accesorios
La conexión de Muse con pantallas y dispositivos domésticos amplía los usos, pero aumenta la importancia de los permisos. Un agente que gestiona compras, viajes e información requiere límites sobre datos y acciones. Muse Gadgets propone accesorios cuya evolución dependerá de desarrolladores, reglas y controles.

articles.title: The Credential Layer Is Expanding Faster Than Security Teams Can See It
articles.text:
Every modern enterprise depends on credentials. This is how humans, systems, and now AI, all connect to data, services, and each other securely. GitGuardian helps secure that credential layer through three connected capabilities: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. The journey starts with detection, because organizations first need to understand what credentials exist, where they live, and what they can access. This is the first of three articles we are releasing that explain the reason behind our mission.
—
Software production is accelerating beyond the growth assumptions that shaped many of today's security controls. GitHub COO Kyle Daigle said the platform had gone from roughly 1 billion commits during all of 2025 to 2.9 billion commits in August 2026, an annualized pace of over 14 billion for the 2026 reporting year. GitHub's own engineering team has gone further in its capacity planning, saying it moved from preparing for 10x scale to designing for a future that requires 30x today's scale as agentic development accelerated.
All of this code prodiction means more infrastructure and more secrets. More applications, new types of integrations, automations, and now agents, mean more systems need to authenticate to something else. Credential exposure has already been a problem of increasing scale. GitGuardian detected 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025, up 34% year over year. Leaked credentials associated with AI services increased 81%.
Security teams need to establish visibility into that expanding credential layer right now.
GitGuardian approaches credential-layer security through three connected stages: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. Detection comes first because every action that follows depends on knowing which credentials actually exist, where they have spread, and what access they represent.
The credential layer has no convenient perimeter
The credential layer is the collection of credentials connecting people, applications, infrastructure, and services across an enterprise.
Its perimeter follows the credentials themselves.
A developer will create a secret inside a sanctioned cloud account and later that same key, in plaintext, will appear in a repository or in a shared knowledgebase. Other secrets will be stored in an approved vault while a plaintext copies remain on the developer's laptop. More may be created outside security's normal vantage point through a personal project or a newly adopted AI service, especially by an increasingly growing number fo 'citizen developers' who now have access to coding agents.
The result is an attack surface that crosses all technology and ownership boundaries.
The same GitGuardian State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research we referenced earlier shows how wide this surface has become. Internal repositories were roughly six times more likely than public repositories to contain at least one secret. Around 28% of secrets incidents originated entirely outside source-code repositories in collaboration and productivity systems.
That leaves security teams with a basic discovery challenge. Each scanner, vault, repository, or endpoint can describe the part of the credential layer it sees. The organization still needs a way to understand the combined population.
Every discovery source provides a partial picture
Source control remains essential because hardcoded credentials leave durable evidence.
A credential removed from the current version of a file can remain in Git history. Copies can spread into other branches or repositories. Public exposure can put the value beyond the organization's control, making it extremely challenging for anyone to immediately notice.
Internal repositories reveal another large population. They contain the credentials developers and applications use during normal work, including access to cloud environments and internal services.
Collaboration systems expose a different part of the credential layer. Credentials get pasted into tickets while troubleshooting. They move through chat during handoffs. They can remain searchable long after the work that required them is finished.
Developer laptops are holding all the credentials
Developers are at the heart of all of this creation, use and placement of secrets. Until recently it was considered normal form to use local local environment files to hold application secrets using command-line tools cache credentials used to reach cloud services. The danger of an unscrubbed local shell history, which can preserve values long after someone has forgotten they were entered, seemed rather low.
Then the attackers shifted. The end of 2025 brought new waves of infostealer attacks like Shai-Hulud and S1ingularity, which turned the developer laptop into a target and an entry point into the supply chain.
Every laptop is part of the credential layer and the secrets they hold need to be mapped.
Repository scanning shows credentials that reached source control. Public monitoring reveals exposures outside corporate repositories. Endpoint discovery identifies secrets that may never have entered a centrally monitored system.
The credential layer only becomes visible when those perspectives are connected.
Attackers already search across those boundaries
Attackers have already adapted to the fact that credentials exist across managed and unmanaged environments.
Compromised credentials already accounted for 22% of initial access according to the the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report. Their data also found corporate credentials on unmanaged devices, which drove a significant number of the breaches they researched. Enterprise access can quickly cross a boundary that security teams consider meaningful.
And their data reporting period ended before the information stealer worms became as wide spread as we saw in early 2026.
This self propagating malware running on an endpoint can search browser data, local files, and application storage. It can collect whatever authentication material is available without caring which team created it or which security product was supposed to govern it.
Developer systems offer an especially valuable targets. A developer machine may authenticate to source control and cloud infrastructure. It can also hold local credentials for applications under development. Compromising that endpoint can expose access that spans several otherwise separate parts of the enterprise.
Security teams need to perform that inventory before an attacker does.
The developer laptop is being shared with a new type of user
The developer endpoint has always accumulated credentials because building software requires connecting systems. But now there is a new type of internal actor that has access to that same machine, AI agents.
Coding agents can read files, execute commands, and interact with external services. Model Context Protocol connections can give those agents access to additional tools. Each connection introduces another place where authentication and authorization need to be established.
GitGuardian's analysis of systems compromised during the Shai-Hulud 2 supply-chain campaign provides a rare view into the density of credentials on these machines. Across 6,943 compromised systems, researchers identified 33,185 unique secrets. Forty-four percent of compromised machines held more than 10 secrets, while 5% contained more than 100.
At the same time, how we are authenticating AI agents have introduced a new security hole. In the same report we saw 24,008 unique secrets in public MCP configuration files during 2025, of which, 2,117 could be verified as valid.
A security team that scans repositories can know a great deal about repositories. It still has limited visibility into credentials living on the machines where code is created, tested, and connected to external systems.
AI agents can do unexpected things with this access. It can be abused by attackers, but just as likely it can result in negative outcomes from the AI taking a surprising move, like deleting a production database.
Security teams need to understand what exactly these agents can access to understand the risk.
Discovery needs context around every credential
Finding a secret provides the first coordinate. Security teams need the surrounding context to understand the risk it represents.
Validity is one of the most immediate signals.
Unfortunately, most secrets stay valid far longer than they should. Ideally, any credential would be made just in time, and expire after use, but GitGuardian retested credentials that had been confirmed valid in 2022 and found that 64% were still valid in January 2026.
A credential can therefore remain useful to an attacker years after the original exposure.
A secret's location adds another dimension to risk assessment.
A credential found once in an internal repository has one exposure history. The same credential appearing on a laptop and later in a public repository has traveled much farther. Every occurrence expands the set of people and systems that may have had access to it.
Credential fingerprinting can connect those appearances while preserving a single credential record. Seven detections of the same secret represent one credential with seven known exposures. Treating it that way produces a more accurate inventory and a clearer picture of how far it has spread.
Ownership provides another layer.
Security teams need to know which user, workload, or application relies on the credential. Ownership connects the finding to the team responsible for managing the access, not just who created it, but what policy or governance does this fall under.
The scope of permissions shows what the credential can do and the danger it brings.
A credential limited to a development service presents one scope of risk. A production credential with broad administrative permissions presents another. Validity and permission context together reveal which findings deserve the fastest attention.
Dependencies complete more of the picture.
A credential can be highly exposed while still supporting critical workloads. Understanding those relationships gives the organization the information it will eventually need to rotate or revoke the credential safely.
Discovery should produce a credential record enriched with this context.
Security teams need a real denominator for their coverage metrics
Many enterprises already have strong secrets-management programs.
Those systems provide valuable information about credentials already under management. They can show what is stored, who has access, and how the secret is being used.
The larger credential layer mapping determines how complete that coverage really is.
For example, a company might have 50,000 credentials stored in approved vaults while thousands more sit in plaintext in repositories, developer endpoints, or collaboration systems. But from their reporting, they show how the secrets they know about are accounted for, blind to the ones created outside of their planned paved paths. Some of those credentials may correspond to values already held in the vault. Others may exist completely outside any approved manager.
Security teams need to know how much of the credential population has an identified owner. They need to know how many active credentials can be connected to permissions and dependent workloads. They also need visibility into which credentials have crossed into public environments.
Those measurements depend on discovering the population first.
Everything is speeding up, including attackers
Security programs built around periodic discovery will face increasing pressure as software production accelerates. This historic growth represents more than additional code.
GitGuardian's reports show, that over the time they have been researching this area, secret exposure has increased 1.6 times faster than the number of active developers.
Attackers are leveraging this while also accelerating their attack speeds.
CrowdStrike reported an average eCrime breakout time of 29 minutes in 2025, with the fastest observed case reaching lateral movement in 27 seconds. Defenders need to react in terms of machine speed, as the days of a human executing an attack are now past us. The time available to respond will only continue to shrink.
The answer can not just be faster reaction, but a shift towards prevention. And that is not possible until you understand what you are trying to prevent, which in turn requires knowledge of what is surfaces you currently even have for credentials to leak into.
Detection builds the map for everything that follows
The first step in controlling credential risk is understanding the credential layer the organization actually has.
That requires discovery across repositories, public exposure, and developer endpoints. It also requires context around every credential, including validity, ownership, permissions, and dependencies.
Vault coverage becomes one measurement inside that larger picture. Repository findings become another. Endpoint discoveries add credentials that may have remained invisible to central security systems.
Together, they create a usable inventory of the credential layer.
The approach of "detect, remediate, and prevent" starts with that inventory because remediation and prevention depend on it. Security teams need to know what exists before they can systematically remove risky credentials or stop new exposure from spreading.
The growth already underway raises the cost of waiting.
GitHub's move from 1 billion annual commits to a pace measured in hundreds of millions per week provides a glimpse of the software volume ahead. GitHub itself is preparing infrastructure for a future measured at 30 times today's scale. Every new application, agent, and integration can extend the credential layer further.
Security teams need visibility capable of expanding at the same pace.

articles.title: Bon plan – La liseuse Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition à 199,99 € (-23%)
articles.text:
Bon plan – La liseuse Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition à 199,99 € (-23%)
La liseuse Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition passe sous les 200 € chez Amazon et Boulanger.com soit une baisse d'environ 23% sur le prix habituellement constaté. C'est actuellement l'un des meilleurs produit de notre comparatif.
Après une excellente Kindle Paperwhite 2024, Amazon signe avec la Kindle Colorsoft sa première liseuse à écran couleur. Ce modèle promet une expérience autrement intéressante pour les amateurs de bandes dessinées, magazines et autres contenus graphiques en couleur.
Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition
- 
                            Construction
                            
            
- 
                            Écran
                            
            
- 
                            Expérience utilisateur
                            
            
Points forts
- Contraste de l’écran couleur et luminosité.
- Légère, étanche et rechargeable sans fil.
- Interface claire, à défaut de novatrice.
- Réactivité (tant que vous ne zoomez pas dans les images).
Points faibles
- Fidélité des couleurs très perfectible.
- Zoom trop lent dans les contenus en couleur.
- Absence de mode sombre.
- Autonomie très correcte, mais moins importante que pour la Kindle Paperwhite 2024.
Pour sa première liseuse couleur, Amazon a réussi à éviter quelques-uns des écueils rencontrés par les concurrentes de la Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition. Ainsi, l’écran de cette dernière est très lumineux et bien contrasté, ce qui est un progrès notable. Néanmoins, il n’est pas parfait pour autant et souffre comme la concurrence d’une colorimétrie très perfectible. Toutefois, même s'il n’est pas indispensable sur une petite diagonale, cet afficheur en couleur est un vrai plus. La lecture sur la Kindle Colorsoft s’avère très plaisante au quotidien, que ce soit en couleur ou en noir & blanc. Nous n'avons finalement pas grand-chose de sérieux à lui reprocher. Son plus grand problème vient d’une adversaire interne redoutable, l’excellente Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2024), qui ne dispose certes pas d'un écran couleur, mais est vendue (à date) 100 € moins cher !
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
En alternative
Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024)

La Kindle Paperwhite de cinquième génération (2021) restait un très bon modèle, même trois ans après sa sortie. Amazon parvient pourtant à l’améliorer encore sur des points aussi fondamentaux pour une liseuse que le rendu de l’écran et la réactivité. Les nouveautés présentes sur la Kindle Paperwhite 2024 ne sont certes pas tapageuses sur le papier, mais il n’en fallait pas plus pour augmenter significativement le confort de lecture. Contrairement à des modèles concurrents qui multiplient les fonctionnalités, celui-ci reste toutefois concentré sur le seul usage de la lecture. Mais cette liseuse s’acquitte de sa tâche à la perfection. Si vous pouvez vous permettre la soixantaine d’euros de surcoût par rapport à une liseuse plus basique telle que la Kindle 2024, vous ne le regretterez pas tant cette Paperwhite 2024 se positionne comme la référence incontournable en milieu de gamme.

articles.title: Le monde doit accepter les « conséquences négatives de l’IA » : le patron d'OpenAI fait une sortie controversée
articles.text:
Pour rappel, Dario Amodei, dirigeant d’Anthropic, prône un contrôle strict du développement de l’IA. Le 12 septembre dernier, il avait même publié un essai qui appel à un ralentissement de l’industrie. De son côté, Sam Altman, PDG d’OpenAI, s’est dit « d’accord avec Dario », tout en précisant qu’il ne voulait pas être le seul à lever le pied. Mais si les deux hommes semblent vouloir tous les deux un encadrement de l’IA, ils ne semblent pas non plus exactement sur la même longueur d’onde. En effet, lors d’une interview accordée au média Politico, Sam Altman est revenu sur les divergences qui l’opposent à Dario Amodei (Anthropic) concernant la régulation de l’intelligence artificielle.
Pour Sam Altman, il faut accepter certaines conséquences négatives de l’IA
Au micro de Politico, Sam Altman a défendu une vision accessible et ouverte de l’IA : « Nous avons toujours été convaincus que cette technologie devait être démocratisée et mise entre les mains des gens ». Il précise ensuite que cette approche entraîne inévitablement des risques qu’il faut accepter : « Je pense que l’une des principales différences entre nous et certains défenseurs d’une approche plus stricte en matière de sécurité de l’IA, c’est que nous estimons que le monde doit accepter certaines conséquences négatives en contrepartie des bénéfices apportés par cette technologie et du fait de laisser aux gens la possibilité de décider par eux-mêmes. ».
Le dirigeant d’OpenAI à ensuite indirectement lancé une pique à Anthropic qui défend un contrôle strict de l’IA : « Je ne suis pas d’accord, mais je comprends le point de vue de ceux qui se disent : “Cette technologie va devenir tellement puissante qu’un seul laboratoire à San Francisco devrait en disposer, s’assurer qu’il ne se passe rien de mal et, en quelque sorte, déterminer quels bénéfices nous pouvons en tirer.” Je pense que ce serait un compromis totalement inacceptable du point de vue de la liberté, de l’autonomie des individus et de leur capacité à décider eux-mêmes de leur avenir ». Sam Altman caricature en parlant d’« un seul laboratoire à San Francisco » qui contrôlerait l’IA, mais pointe donc du doigt une centralisation de ce secteur, au nom de la sécurité et au détriment d’un déploiement auprès du plus grand nombre.
Accepter les conséquences négatives, mais pas toutes non plus
Sam Altman s’est montré résolument optimiste au cours de l’interview en expliquant que l’IA apportera bien plus de bien que de mal : « Je ne serais donc pas prêt à accepter un compromis du genre : “Nous allons nous assurer qu’il n’y ait pas de piratages majeurs, qu’il n’y ait aucune forme de détournement de cette technologie, qu’il n’y ait aucune arnaque, ni aucun des autres problèmes qui pourraient survenir”, parce que je pense que les gens feront énormément plus de choses positives que de choses négatives, et ce dans des proportions considérables. ».
Le dirigeant d’OpenAI a tout de même mis quelques limites dans sa vision d’une intelligence artificielle accessible au plus grand nombre et non centralisée, notamment en cas de perte de contrôle majeure au profit de l’IA et lors de « risques réellement catastrophiques ». Il reste maintenant à définir où débutent les risques liés au développement de l’IA.

articles.title: La mujer más rica de Australia acaba de gastarse 600 millones de dólares en golpear a China donde más duele
articles.text:
La mujer más rica de Australia ha colocado parte de su fortuna en una de las pocas compañías capaces de plantar cara a China en uno de sus negocios más estratégicos. Lynas Rare Earths, respaldada por Gina Rinehart como accionista mayoritaria, ha acordado comprar Meteoric Resources por 968 millones de dólares australianos, unos 600 millones de euros, y con ella hacerse con el proyecto Caldeira de Brasil. Bajo el suelo de Minas Gerais aparece así una nueva pieza en la carrera occidental por reducir una dependencia china que alcanza desde los coches eléctricos hasta los cazas y los misiles.
Un cheque de 600 millones. China convirtió las tierras raras en una formidable herramienta industrial y geopolítica: concentra buena parte de su extracción mundial y domina de forma todavía más aplastante su procesamiento, el auténtico cuello de botella de la cadena.
Lynas, por su parte, ocupa una posición excepcional en el bando contrario: es el mayor productor de tierras raras separadas fuera de China y ha conseguido producir comercialmente elementos pesados como disprosio y terbio, esenciales para fabricar imanes capaces de trabajar a altas temperaturas. La compra de Meteoric amplía esa ofensiva con una nueva fuente de suministro situada a miles de kilómetros de sus actuales operaciones australianas.
La respuesta estaba enterrada en Brasil. Caldeira se extiende por Minas Gerais y alberga alrededor de 1.600 millones de toneladas de recursos minerales, según los últimos datos de Meteoric. Su verdadero atractivo está en la geología: las tierras raras aparecen en arcillas de absorción iónica, materiales blandos que pueden excavarse sin las voladuras habituales de las explotaciones de roca dura y que permiten recuperar los minerales mediante procesos relativamente sencillos.
Meteoric sostiene que esas características pueden convertir Caldeira en una de las explotaciones de tierras raras de menor coste del mundo.
Décadas jugando con ventaja. Más datos. El hallazgo adquiere otra dimensión por los elementos escondidos dentro de esas arcillas. Caldeira contiene neodimio y praseodimio junto a tierras raras pesadas como disprosio y terbio, precisamente algunos de los materiales sometidos por Pekín a nuevos controles de exportación desde 2025.
Son ingredientes críticos para los imanes permanentes utilizados en motores eléctricos, turbinas y numerosas aplicaciones militares. Qué duda cabe, cada restricción china convierte una fuente alternativa económicamente viable en un activo estratégico para Estados Unidos, Europa y sus aliados.
Un pie dentro del Pentágono. Porque la operación brasileña encaja con una transformación que Lynas lleva años preparando. La compañía extrae mineral en Australia, lo procesa en Australia y Malasia y en marzo anunció un acuerdo preliminar de suministro de 96 millones de dólares con el Departamento de Defensa estadounidense para reforzar las cadenas de suministro vinculadas a la seguridad nacional.
Caldeira le permitiría sumar otra materia prima y estudiar capacidad de procesamiento en Brasil, precisamente el paso que puede convertir un gran yacimiento en una alternativa real a la cadena industrial china.
Lo que falta. Lynas calcula que desarrollar Caldeira exigirá más de 500 millones de dólares adicionales y el mercado recibió la adquisición con dudas: sus acciones cayeron alrededor de un 6% tras anunciarse el acuerdo. ¿La razón? Los inversores miran especialmente el riesgo técnico de pasar de la roca dura que Lynas conoce a unas arcillas iónicas con características diferentes.
Sea como fuere, la operación abre así una apuesta de más de mil millones entre adquisición y desarrollo para convertir una enorme reserva brasileña en algo que Occidente lleva años buscando: una cadena de tierras raras capaz de funcionar cada vez más lejos de China.

articles.title: These 32GB DDR5 memory kits are the cheapest available on the market — we found the cheapest one around, plus AMD- and Intel-tailored options
articles.text:
These 32GB DDR5 memory kits are the cheapest available on the market — we found the cheapest one around, plus AMD- and Intel-tailored options
RAM is still expensive, but these DDR5 discounts dull the pain
If you need some relatively cheap RAM for your gaming rig during this Prime Big Deals Day event, we've dug up some solid discounts on a trio of dual-channel 32GB DDR5 kits that might help you finish up a build or upgrade an existing system for less.
32GB is still a comfortable amount of memory for most gaming rigs, and these kits are still relatively affordable compared to much costlier dual-DIMM 64GB kits that use denser RAM chips that face white-hot competing demand from AI servers. In this economy, any future-proofing afforded by a 64GB kit is greatly outweighed by the eye-watering prices those kits demand.
- Team T-Force Delta RGB 32GB DDR5-5200 kit for $389.99 at Newegg (with promo code)
- Team T-Force Vulcan Eco 32GB DDR5-6400 kit for $459.99 at Newegg (plus free 128GB microSDXC card) (with promo code)
- Corsair Vengeance 32GB DDR5-6000 kit for $459.99 at Newegg
First up, we have Team Group's Delta RGB 32GB (2x16GB) DDR5-5200 kit. This memory isn't the fastest thing going, but it's the cheapest thing going, and for many builders, that's what's going to matter most right now.
Additional $70 off with promo code FTTF8296
This RGB kit from Team Group unlocks 32GB of DDR5 memory for your gaming PC or workstation rig. CAS and memory timings of 40-40-40-76, with speeds of 5,200 MT/s, mean this isn't the fastest memory out there, but it's currently the cheapest 32GB DDR5 kit you can buy.
Especially if you're building with an AMD Ryzen X3D CPU, raw RAM speed isn't as important to the highest gaming performance as it would be for a chip without V-Cache. So this Delta kit could do just fine for such a build, or for an Intel system where absolute speed isn't the first priority.
This RAM's black heat spreaders and RGB LED flair will complement any build, and you can get it for $389.99 right now at Newegg after applying promo code FTTF8296, making it one of the cheapest 32GB DDR5 kits on the market, if not the cheapest, period. With Intel XMP and AMD EXPO support, this kit comes ready for one-click overclocking in your BIOS.
If you want faster DDR5 RAM, perhaps for an Intel CPU, Team Group's T-Force Vulcan Eco DDR5-6400 CL 32GB kit is also available for $459.99 at Newegg with promo code FTTF8342 for $90 off.
Additional $90 off w/ promo code FTTF8342
The next best 32GB DDR5 RAM kit deal, also from Team Group, with much faster speeds of 6,400 MT/s. CAS and memory timings are 38-46-46-84. Probably the better option, if your budget can stretch to get it.
This dual-DIMM kit offers simple silver heat spreaders to go with its high speeds and relatively low CL38 latencies. Like the fancier Delta kit above, this memory comes with XMP and EXPO profiles for easy overclocking across CPUs from both vendors.
This RAM wouldn't be our first pick for a Ryzen CPU, as running it at the full DDR5-6400 speed would introduce a small latency penalty because of the way the Infinty Fabric and the memory controller clocks interact, counteracting the entire point of faster memory to begin with.
But if push comes to shove, you can still tune this memory to DDR5-6000 speeds to avoid that pitfall if need be while maximizing performance on AMD chips. If you are looking for a native DDR5-6000 kit, though, read on.

This memory isn't the flashiest thing out there, but we doubt that's the criterion at the top of most builders' minds right now. As an older kit, it doesn't come with an AMD EXPO profile preloaded, but it'll still overclock just fine in AMD boards. Do be aware that the 1.4V spec is higher than some other DDR5-6000 kits, though.
Despite its lack of flair, this kit still comes with classy Corsair styling and the full backing of that company's reliable warranty and support. Take $70 off and grab this RAM for $459.99 at Newegg with promo code FTTF8324.
RAM pricing is just one of the tough challenges facing PC builders right now. But with these deals, you might be able to save a few bucks to put towards another component like a bigger SSD or a more powerful video card, or just take it off the bottom line of your build sheet. Happy hunting.

articles.title: Sovereign storage becomes an architecture decision for Europe - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
NetApp puts sovereign storage at the center of European infrastructure decisions
Sovereign storage is becoming an architectural and operational consideration for European enterprises as they invest in AI, modernization and cyber resilience.
Sovereignty now covers much more than where data is physically stored. Customers want to know who operates and manages it, where support is based and what telemetry is collected, according to Willem Hendrickx (pictured), senior vice president and general manager of EMEA and LATAM at NetApp.
“What [our customers] really want is a cloud-like experience but having control of their data,” he said. “Sovereignty is not only a legal discussion, but it’s actually an architectural design and an operational decision more than anything else.”
Hendrickx spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight at NetApp INSIGHT, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed sovereign storage, neoclouds and cyber resilience in Europe. (* Disclosure below.)
Sovereign storage and the business case for controlled data
Many customers still buy capital equipment on five-year cycles because they know what their demand will be. A growing number need infrastructure that follows the business instead, with predictable cost, availability, performance and growth, Hendrickx explained. NetApp’s new Keystone Sovereign service gives qualified European customers data sovereignty controls, and local partners can build it into their own sovereign offerings.
“There’s sometimes a little bit of a thinking that as a service is more like a payment model,” Hendrickx said. “It’s way more than that. It’s really a business decision.”
Enterprises face a different AI problem than the neoclouds building GPU gigafactories across Europe. Most have decades of data spread across countries and clouds. NetApp is pitching its Novus architecture and wider data infrastructure as the way to make that data AI-ready, according to Hendrickx.
“If you don’t do that, you see a lot of AI pilots, but they never get in production,” he said. “And you can only do that when you really make everything AI-ready.”
Fragmentation makes the problem worse. AI, on-premises systems, software as a service and cloud often run as separate operating models with separate teams, which leaves AI projects stranded on islands, Hendrickx noted. NetApp’s Keystone storage-as-a-service platform can help unify those operating models and shift the focus toward business outcomes, according to Hendrickx.
“I really believe you’re going to have more grip on your business because you’re going to reduce cost and you’re going to focus on business outcomes and you’re going to drive innovation,” he said. “We need to be way more innovative than we have been.”

articles.title: Google limita la versión gratuita de Gemini a Flash-Lite 3.5 y AI Plus a Flash 3.6
articles.text:
Google limitará el acceso gratuito a Gemini desde el 9 de octubre de 2026: los usuarios sin suscripción solo podrán utilizar Gemini Flash-Lite 3.5, mientras que el plan AI Plus habilitará Gemini Flash 3.6. La medida reorganiza el acceso a los modelos según el nivel de pago y el consumo de recursos informáticos de cada tarea.
El cambio profundiza el sistema que la compañía introdujo en mayo de 2026, cuando dejó de aplicar un número fijo de mensajes y pasó a calcular los límites según la capacidad de procesamiento requerida por cada consulta.
Google detalló en su página de soporte que la implementación comenzará en los próximos días. Alcanzará tanto a quienes usan la aplicación sin costo como a los suscriptores de sus planes de inteligencia artificial (IA).
Cómo quedará el acceso a la inteligencia artificial en cada plan de Google
Los usuarios gratuitos perderán el acceso a Gemini Flash y Gemini Pro. Su única alternativa será Gemini Flash-Lite 3.5, un modelo pensado para respuestas rápidas y tareas de menor complejidad.
Por su parte, el plan Google AI Plus, disponible en España por 4,99 euros mensuales, permitirá utilizar Flash-Lite 3.5 y Flash 3.6. Sin embargo, sus suscriptores tampoco tendrán acceso al modelo Pro.
Los planes Google AI Pro y AI Ultra concentrarán el acceso más amplio. Por 21,99 euros y 99,99 euros al mes, respectivamente, sus usuarios podrán usar todos los modelos disponibles, incluida la versión Gemini Pro 3.1.
Además, los abonados a AI Pro y AI Ultra podrán usar Deep Think en la aplicación de Gemini. Esta opción permite emplear el máximo nivel de razonamiento paralelo del modelo y hasta ahora estaba reservada al nivel Ultra.
Para qué es útil cada modelo de inteligencia artificial de Google
Gemini Flash-Lite está orientado a consultas directas que requieren rapidez y un menor consumo de recursos. Puede responder preguntas breves, traducir textos cortos, resumir contenidos o clasificar datos en una fracción de segundo.
En cambio, Gemini Flash está diseñado para problemas que exigen analizar varios pasos de forma simultánea. Sus aplicaciones incluyen la evaluación de situaciones complejas, la escritura o corrección de código y la coordinación de tareas consecutivas.
La diferencia entre ambos modelos dependerá de la necesidad del usuario: Flash-Lite prioriza la velocidad y el menor costo operativo, mientras que Flash busca ofrecer respuestas más elaboradas ante consultas que requieren mayor análisis.
Asimismo, Google permitirá elegir el nivel de esfuerzo para cada tarea en los modelos disponibles: bajo, medio o alto. La opción más alta incrementa la capacidad del sistema para completar solicitudes y elaborar respuestas más exhaustivas, aunque consume una porción mayor del límite de procesamiento.
La compañía no precisó cómo incorporará Gemini 4 Argon, presentado el 1 de octubre de 2026. El nuevo modelo se desplegará inicialmente entre defensores cibernéticos a través del programa Fairwind.
Qué es todo lo se sabe de Gemini 4 Argon de Google
Gemini 4 Argon fue desarrollado por Alphabet a través de Google DeepMind para programación, investigación, redacción y trabajo profesional, con énfasis en la ciberseguridad. La compañía lo presentó como el modelo más avanzado de su catálogo hasta el momento.
El acceso no estará disponible de inmediato para usuarios finales. Google DeepMind priorizará a administraciones públicas, centros de salud y servicios de telecomunicaciones, con el objetivo de que los grupos de trabajo que desarrollan defensas informáticas empleen la herramienta antes de que capacidades similares puedan utilizarse contra diferentes sistemas digitales.
La compañía dijo que Argon puede “encontrar, validar y corregir de forma autónoma vulnerabilidades críticas de software”. Esa facultad explica que su lanzamiento inicial se concentre en socios especializados en seguridad informática.
La iniciativa valida los hallazgos y los comunica de forma privada a las organizaciones afectadas, con prioridad para hospitales, servicios públicos e infraestructuras esenciales. Los problemas más frecuentes identificados por ese programa están relacionados con fallas de autorización y con la exposición de credenciales.

articles.title: 23€ une fois pour toutes : 1minAI Pro ouvre ChatGPT, Claude et Gemini à vie, sans abonnement
articles.text:
Chez StackSocial, le plan Pro de 1minAI s’affiche à 22,31 € pour un accès à vie, avec un million de crédits chaque mois pour interroger des modèles d’OpenAI, d’Anthropic, de Google ou de Mistral. Une formule intéressante pour un usage régulier, dont notre test avait aussi pointé les limites.
1minAI est un agrégateur : au lieu d’ouvrir un compte chez chaque éditeur, vous retrouvez dans une seule application des outils de chat, d’image, d’audio et de vidéo. Chaque requête y consomme des crédits, en quantité variable selon le modèle. Avec l’accès à vie à 1minAI Pro proposé par StackSocial, vous payez une seule fois et recevez 1 000 000 de crédits par mois, sans abonnement à renouveler.
À 22,31 €, l’offre revient à son prix le plus bas, celui auquel nous l’avions déjà relayée, quand la formule Pro est facturée 6,50 dollars par mois chez l’éditeur. Elle vise ceux qui sollicitent l’IA chaque semaine sans vouloir cumuler les abonnements.
L’accès à vie à 1minAI Pro passe à 22,31 € au lieu de 210 € chez StackSocial, avec un million de crédits à utiliser chaque mois.
Pourquoi choisir 1minAI Pro ?
- Un paiement unique : facturée 6,50 dollars par mois chez l’éditeur, la formule Pro revient ici à 24,97 dollars une fois pour toutes. L’achat est donc amorti en moins de quatre mois d’utilisation.
- Des crédits qui s’ajoutent : au million de crédits mensuel s’ajoutent 15 000 crédits offerts chaque jour où vous ouvrez l’application web, soit jusqu’à 450 000 de plus par mois. Selon l’éditeur, ces crédits gratuits n’expirent pas.
- Une dépense visible avant de valider : 1minAI affiche une estimation du coût en crédits avant chaque requête ou génération, un point que nous avions salué lors de notre test. Vous savez ce que va consommer un visuel ou une transcription avant de lancer l’opération.
Une boîte à outils d’appoint et un banc d’essai pour vos IA
Lors de notre test, publié en mars, nous avions trouvé GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4 et 4.5, Gemini, Mistral ou Llama pour le texte, DALL-E 3, Stable Diffusion et Flux pour l’image. S’y ajoutent la transcription audio, la génération musicale et le clonage de voix via ElevenLabs. Le Multi AI Chat soumet une même question à cinq modèles à la fois, pratique pour comparer leurs réponses sur un résumé ou un e-mail. Disponible sur le web, le mobile et l’ordinateur, l’application dépanne aussi quand votre assistant habituel est en panne.
L’offre parle d’abord aux rédacteurs indépendants, community managers et créateurs qui passent du texte au visuel sans usage intensif. Elle convient moins si vous générez images et vidéos en continu : selon l’éditeur, un million de crédits correspond par exemple à 161 images ou à 12 vidéos. Dans notre test de 1minAI, nous relevions aussi l’absence de mémoire entre les conversations et un retard dans l’arrivée des derniers modèles. Les échanges pouvant être conservés jusqu’à un an, la plateforme n’est pas faite pour des données clients sensibles.
Ce que 1minAI ne remplace pas face à ChatGPT ou Claude
Face à ChatGPT Plus ou Claude Pro, 1minAI l’emporte sur la variété et le prix, pas sur la profondeur. Les offres natives apportent mémoire, projets, recherche web ou agents capables d’agir à votre place, quand 1minAI reste un accès à des modèles. Pour choisir un assistant principal au quotidien, notre comparatif des meilleurs chatbots à intelligence artificielle vous aidera à trancher. 1minAI prend en revanche tout son sens en complément, ou pour essayer plusieurs IA avant de vous engager.
✅ Les points forts
- Paiement unique, sans abonnement à renouveler
- 1 000 000 de crédits par mois, plus 15 000 crédits par jour de visite
- Multi AI Chat pour comparer plusieurs modèles sur une même question
- Coût en crédits affiché avant chaque requête
- Applications web, mobile et ordinateur
❌ Les limites
- Les modèles les plus récents arrivent avec retard
- Aucune mémoire d’une conversation à l’autre
- Crédits vite consommés par l’image et la vidéo
- Inadapté aux données sensibles ou soumises au RGPD
Le code 1minAI Pro s’active dans les 30 jours suivant l’achat, et StackSocial le reprend contre un avoir dans ce délai s’il n’a pas servi.
À 22,31 €, 1minAI Pro coûte moins que quatre mois d’abonnement à la même formule. Le prix barré de 210 € affiché par StackSocial est un prix suggéré : c’est le tarif mensuel de 6,50 dollars qui donne la vraie mesure de la remise. Vous obtenez un million de crédits mensuels et des modèles de chat, d’image et d’audio réunis dans une même interface. La promesse « à vie » reste un pari sur la pérennité du service, mais la mise de départ est modeste.
Pour rédiger, résumer, illustrer ou comparer des réponses de temps en temps ou chaque semaine, l’offre tient la route. Si vous attendez un assistant qui se souvient de vos projets ou les modèles sortis la semaine passée, un abonnement natif vous servira mieux. Gardez aussi en tête que l’image et la vidéo vident vite le compteur. La version gratuite de 1minAI permet d’ailleurs de prendre en main l’interface avant de vous décider.
