articles.title: PhysicsWallah retreats from direct student lending as FinZ loan book heads to Auxilo
articles.text:
PhysicsWallah retreats from direct student lending as FinZ loan book heads to Auxilo
PhysicsWallah’s sale of Rs 95.79 crore of loans marks a rethink of its May push to scale FinZ, with the company shifting to third-party lenders amid questions over capital allocation, credit risk and strategic focus.
Edtech firm PhysicsWallah (PW) has moved decisively to reduce its exposure to direct student lending, with its wholly-owned subsidiary FinZ Finance agreeing to sell a Rs 95.79 crore loan portfolio to Auxilo Finserve, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on education finance.
The deal covers a substantial or major part of FinZ’s loan book and is expected to result in a partial closure of its lending operations, PW said, adding the transition of the loans and borrowers should be completed within 60 days.
The significance of this move lies in the speed of the reversal.
In its October 4 filing, PW said “the closure of substantial/major part of the total loan portfolio of FinZ Finance forms part of a broader strategic realignment,” aimed at focusing on the core business, optimising capital allocation and reducing balance-sheet and credit risks.
Going forward, lending will be facilitated through regulated third-party NBFCs instead of being carried directly through FinZ, the Noida-based firm noted.
On May 27, PW’s Audit Committee approved an investment of approximately Rs 120 crore in FinZ through a rights issue to fund working capital and expand the business. FinZ had received its RBI licence in September 2025 and had only recently begun operations.
In the May 27 earnings call, management said the model was built on an earlier partnership with an external NBFC that had disbursed nearly Rs 200 crore over about two years, with less than 1% NPA, or non-performing assets, and around 70% of loans going to PW students. Asked whether new loans would sit on PW’s balance sheet, management replied, “Yes, so we got NBFC license from RBI and yes, we will be giving loans through that NBFC only.”
The market reaction then provided a signal as after the Rs 120 crore investment announcement, PW shares fell nearly 18% over five sessions. On June 4, after PW announced that it would instead work with regulated third-party NBFCs, the stock surged as much as 17.75% on the BSE.
That does not establish that investors alone triggered the change, and PW has not said that they did. But the sequence strongly suggests that capital allocation and financial-risk concerns had become important considerations. Earlier, PW had also shifted its K-12 strategy towards an asset-light model after investor questions around capital-intensive expansion.
Recently, The CapTable wrote about how the edtech firm is finding that revenue and profit are not enough. Investors are rewarding restraint, and they want to know exactly where the next leg of growth will come from.
The listed company’s explanation for the lending reversal was explicit.
Co-founder Prateek Maheshwari had said, “Our lending business is best left to regulated third-party NBFCs who have created robust underwriting capabilities.” He also added that the company had received feedback from partners and that it had a fiduciary responsibility to revisit the earlier decision in the interests of capital allocation and shareholders.
The June-quarter financial notes subsequently recorded that Rs 120 crore had been invested in FinZ, so the reversal did not simply cancel the capital injection.
The wider lending environment also favours regulated intermediaries. RBI’s Digital Lending Directions, 2025 strengthened requirements for platforms working with multiple lenders, including clearer presentation of loan offers, interest costs and tenures, while its framework keeps regulated entities responsible for their lending arrangements.
Education finance itself remains a growing market, with Crisil expecting NBFC education-loan assets to rise 20% in FY27, although that forecast largely concerns higher education and is not directly comparable with PW’s short-duration course financing.
Byju’s provides the cautionary backdrop. Its India CFO had said in January 2024 that 25-30% of the company’s business had come through customer loans, but NBFCs had stopped lending to its customers after audit delays, disrupting the earlier model and affecting collections. Byju’s subsequent collapse involved much broader financial, governance and lender disputes. Its insolvency battle followed a major dispute with lenders and a series of other setbacks.
The FinZ loan sale looks less like a retreat from student financing itself than a decision to separate education distribution from credit risk as PW can continue connecting students with lenders, while regulated financial institutions carry the lending exposure.

articles.title: JSE wants to turn 10 SMEs into investor-ready businesses
articles.text:
The Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), Africa’s largest stock exchange, has teamed up with the Technology Innovation Agency (TIA), a government agency that supports technology commercialisation, to help 10 South African tech SMEs become investment-ready and connect with new markets and sources of capital.
The 16-week pilot gives the companies access to capital-market expertise, investor networks and commercial opportunities, as the JSE tests whether it can play a bigger role earlier in the startup funding pipeline.
Launched on September 30, the programme will support SMEs in the health, agriculture and fintech sectors with investment readiness, market access and connections to potential sources of capital.
The 10 companies were selected based on their existing products or services, operating maturity and commercial potential, according to a statement. Participants will receive support on investment readiness and pitch development, while gaining access to JSE networks through a market access day and sector-specific engagements.
At the end of the programme, the JSE and TIA aim to produce SMEs with funding-ready pitch packs, market linkages and a pipeline of potential capital engagements. Some participants could also become eligible for AltX screening, the JSE’s process for assessing companies for potential listing on its alternative market for smaller and growing businesses.
That does not mean the companies will be listed or funded as a result of the programme. Instead, the initiative is designed to move them closer to the point where they can engage investors and potentially access formal capital markets.
For TIA, the partnership addresses a persistent problem in South Africa’s innovation ecosystem: getting technologies that have been developed locally into the market.
“One of the key challenges in the innovation value chain is ensuring that new technologies and innovations are commercialised and access the markets,” said Patrick Krappie, executive for innovation enabling at TIA, in a statement.
He said the partnership between TIA and JSE Rise, the local bourse’s SME investment-readiness programme, aligns with the agency’s role as a “connector and facilitator” for the commercialisation of locally developed innovations. The agency wants the programme to support businesses addressing national priorities while helping them move from developing technologies to finding markets, customers and capital.
The JSE said the initiative expands its SME Rise, the JSE’s SME growth support programme, into technology sectors it considers important to economic growth. SMEs account for 91% of formal businesses, provide 60% of jobs and contribute up to 34% of GDP, according to Deputy Finance Minister Ashor Sarupen.
“We are pleased to expand our suite of SME Rise development solutions to support sectors that are critical to driving economic growth,” said Vuyo Lee, chief marketing and corporate affairs officer at the JSE.
Through the partnership, Lee said the JSE is seeking to equip South African technology SMEs with the capabilities and opportunities to compete regionally and globally. The move also gives the exchange an earlier role in the lifecycle of high-growth businesses.
Traditionally, capital markets sit further down the growth journey, after a company has developed a product, found customers, built revenue and established the governance and financial systems investors require. Optasia, a global fintech platform that provides mobile financial services, listed on the JSE’s Main Board in November 2025 at an implied market capitalisation of R23.5 billion ($1.4 billion). Technology group 4Sight also moved from AltX to the JSE Main Board in January 2025.
The JSE and TIA are now testing whether bringing some of that capital-market preparation forward can improve the chances of innovative businesses reaching that stage.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Una pedanía de Huesca rechaza el centro de datos de Amazon en Walqa en la primera consulta vecinal celebrada en Aragón
articles.text:
Una pedanía de 144 vecinos con derecho a voto no quiere un centro de datos a pocos metros de sus casas. Y el no ha sido casi unánime. Es la primera consulta popular de este tipo en una comunidad que, irónicamente, ha convertido los centros de datos en su gran apuesta industrial. Hablamos de Cuarte, en Huesca.
Contexto. Cuando el Gobierno de Aragón puso en marcha el Parque Tecnológico Walqa en 2002, la idea era crear un polo de innovación a las afueras de Huesca. Se levantó en el antiguo municipio de Cuarte, hoy incorporado a la capital, sobre unas 53 hectáreas y con un presupuesto inicial de unos 10 millones de euros.
Nació como centro de I+D y campo de experimentación para empresas, sobre todo de TIC, biotecnología y energías renovables: hoy tiene 14 edificios y en torno a 90 organizaciones. Veinticuatro años después, el nombre de Walqa suena por una parcela contigua al parque donde Amazon construye un centro de datos de casi 70 hectáreas. Los vecinos de Cuarte no lo quieren.
Un "no" casi unánime. La consulta, organizada por la Asociación de Vecinos de Cuarte, movilizó a 117 de las 144 personas llamadas a votar. Esto es algo más de un 81% de participación. Se plantearon cuatro preguntas. Las dos primeras eran si los vecinos sentían vulnerados sus derechos por la información recibida y si la declaración del proyecto como PIGA (Proyecto de Interés General de Aragón) demostraba que los beneficios superaban a los costes ambientales, energéticos y sociales.
La tercera era si era acertada la política del Gobierno de Aragón de impulsar 34 centros de datos. La cuarta, si estaban de acuerdo con el de Walqa. El 96% contestó que sí se sentían vulnerados, el 95% dijo que el PIGA no estaba justificado, el 100% rechazó la política autonómica y el 99,1% votó en contra del centro de datos.
¿Sirve de algo? A medias. La consulta es no vinculante. Sus promotores llevarán los resultados al Ayuntamiento de Huesca y al Gobierno de Aragón, y preparan una recogida de firmas en la capital. Un 99,1% no obliga a nadie a nada, pero es bastante contundente y complicado de ignorar.
En construcción. El nuevo centro, denominado Walqa 2 (el primero ya opera en la Plhus, la Plataforma Logística de Huesca), ocupará casi 70 hectáreas y tiene prevista una inversión de 714,6 millones de euros, sobre antiguas granjas avícolas. Es uno de los cinco nuevos centros de datos que AWS levantará en Aragón, que se suman a los tres que ya tenía. En total, Amazon planea ocupar 354 hectáreas en la comunidad. Para que nos hagamos una idea, hablamos de una “Región AWS” entera (127.887,89 metros cuadrados construidos) repartida entre Huesca y Zaragoza.
UN VISTAZO A...
Cuarte no se amedrenta. El conflicto viene de lejos. De hecho, a comienzos de 2025 los vecinos recibieron cartas que les avisaban de una expropiación de terrenos junto a Walqa, y les preocupaba una línea de alta tensión que atravesaba el pueblo. Consiguieron que Amazon desviara parte del trazado y que financiara infraestructuras de agua para Cuarte y otras poblaciones. Es decir, ya sabían que protestar funciona. Ahora quieren saber hasta dónde llega.
Agua, luz y empleo. Las dudas de los vecinos apuntan siempre a los mismos tres sitios. Se estima que los centros de datos aragoneses consumirán más de 755.000 metros cúbicos de agua al año para refrigerar equipos, y la propia Amazon reconoció que necesitaba un 48% más de agua de la prevista por culpa del calor. En electricidad, se estima que estas instalaciones se llevarán una parte descomunal de la que consume la región. Definamos descomunal: al menos 2.270 gigavatios-hora (GWh) anuales, "una cuarta parte de toda la electricidad que absorbe la comunidad autónoma".
Y en empleo, el representante de la asociación, Carlos Oliván, resume que habrá trabajo mientras duren las obras, pero después mucho menos que en otros sectores productivos. Según documentos que obtuvo El País, en 2021 cada uno de los tres centros ya existentes no pasaba de la veintena de empleados directos. Muchas hectáreas, vatios y muchos litros, pero pocas nóminas.
Placas tectónicas. Cuarte no está sola, claro. El domingo 27 de septiembre, más de mil personas marcharon en Zaragoza contra el centro de datos de Microsoft proyectado junto a los Pinares de Venecia, con consignas que iban más allá del pinar: la plataforma rechaza los centros de datos "ni aquí, ni en ningún sitio". Ya había presentado 349 alegaciones y reclama una moratoria. El proyecto ya había generado polémica por expropiar suelo a 2 euros el metro.
Y el malestar también es institucional. El Burgo de Ebro y Villanueva de Gállego se quejan de que AWS paga el Impuesto sobre Actividades Económicas en Madrid y no donde están instaladas sus naves. Si Aragón pone el suelo, el agua y el sol, algo no encaja.
Pero ya lo contábamos hace unos meses: Amazon pagó 1,5 millones de euros para tender el cable que alimentará este mismo centro, y avisamos de que convertirse en paraíso de los centros de datos no es tan buena noticia como parece. Entonces el debate giraba en torno a transformadores y pozos. Ahora llega a las urnas, aunque sean las de una asociación de vecinos. Que esto frene algo es otra cuestión. El centro de Walqa sigue en construcción.

articles.title: À seulement 27 ans, elle achète un vieux bus scolaire à 5 000 € et le transforme en maison pour ne "plus payer de loyer à un propriétaire"
articles.text:
À seulement 27 ans, elle achète un vieux bus scolaire à 5 000 € et le transforme en maison pour ne "plus payer de loyer à un propriétaire"
De plus en plus de Français s’intéressent à la van life et au lieu d’investir dans un véhicule neuf, en retapent un à moindre frais. À seulement 27 ans, c’est ce que Danielle, qui vit outre-Atlantique, a décidé de faire en rachetant un ancien bus scolaire Chevrolet Express pour environ 5 000 €. Elle vit désormais dans une maison sur roues de 10,4 m² équipée de tout le nécessaire pour vivre.
C’est en septembre 2021 que Danielle repère le Chevrolet Express sur la Marketplace de Facebook pour 5 500 $, soit environ 5 000 €, le tout avec 320 000 kilomètres au compteur. La jeune femme de 27 ans était à ce moment à la recherche d’un véhicule avec bien plus d’espace qu’un fourgon, mais surtout une idée précise en tête : choisir elle-même chaque élément de son futur logement sur roues.
Elle transforme un bus scolaire en petit cocon
Au final, le projet lui a coûté 30 000 $, soit environ 27 600 €. Lorsque l’on retire le prix du bus, c’est 21 800 € de facture pour les travaux et le matériel. Dans le détail, les panneaux solaires ont coûté 2 000 $ à Danielle. Pour l’isolation, ce fut environ 900 $ et 400 $ pour la plomberie.
Près de 85 % du chantier a été réalisé par Danielle elle-même pour réduire les coûts, et ce alors qu’elle n’avait jamais utilisé d’outils électriques de sa vie. Bref, une vraie détermination pour arriver au bout de ce projet colossal en solitaire. Et bien évidemment, l’intérieur n’a plus rien à voir avec un véhicule qui transportait des élèves avec ses rangées de sièges.
Danielle a installé un lit double, une cuisine avec deux plaques à induction, une douche, un réfrigérateur, des toilettes sèches et une ouverture vers le toit. Il lui aura donc fallu trois ans pour fabriquer son véritable cocon. Mais tout ne fut pas simple et Danielle raconte qu’après une journée à fixer seule de grands panneaux de contreplaqué au plafond dans le froid, elle a craqué. "Je crois que j’ai pleuré ce jour-là", confie Danielle.
Le coût du logement aux États-Unis l’a aussi poussée dans sa décision alors qu’elle rêvait d’une vie de nomade depuis l’enfance. "Je ne voulais pas de ça pour moi", explique-t-elle. Puisque pour elle, l’objectif est de ne pas de travailler uniquement pour payer un loyer.
Évidemment, ne pas payer de loyer à un propriétaire ne signifie pas vivre gratuitement. Danielle paie l’essence, l’assurance, l’entretien et parfois un emplacement. Pour l’eau propre et la vidange, il faut également qu’elle s’organise. Mais en retour, elle profite d'un énorme privilège : se déplacer n’importe où dans son cocon sur roues et ne pas à payer un loyer à un propriétaire. La liberté, en somme, pour beaucoup qui rêvent aussi de ce genre de vie.
Peut-on vivre dans un bus aménagé en France ?
Et en France, ce genre de projet est-il possible ? Bien sûr, puisque d’anciens véhicules de transport scolaire sont régulièrement proposés sur le marché, comme des Renault Trafic de 12 mètres², entre 5 500 et 10 000 €, selon l’âge et le kilométrage. On trouve aussi des Renault Trafic ou Master plus petits avec des prix entre 1 900 et 2 500 €. Le choix dépend surtout de l’espace recherché, du poids du véhicule.
Et il y a des familles connues pour ça. Par exemple, la famille française Roadcats Family voyage dans un ancien autobus avec tout le nécessaire pour vivre avec des enfants. Il y a également une autre famille française qui a transformé un ancien bus scolaire utilisé entre le Calvados et la Vendée en logement de 30 mètres² pour six personnes, comme le rapporte La Maison Écologique qui a visité le lieu de vie de Stéphanie, Arnaud et leurs quatre enfants.
En revanche, c’est bien plus lourd administrativement qu’aux États-Unis. Pour circuler comme logement, un ancien bus passe par une validation appelée réception à titre isolé. C’est la Direction régionale de l’environnement, de l’aménagement et du logement qui examine le dossier.
Le ministère prévoit une procédure pour retirer le véhicule de la catégorie transport en commun, puis une autre pour le classer en VASP caravane, soit la catégorie administrative des camping-cars. Le permis dépend ensuite du poids. Jusqu’à 3,5 tonnes et avec neuf places maximum, le permis B suffit. Entre 3,5 et 7,5 tonnes, c’est le permis C1 qui s’impose. Au-dessus de 7,5 tonnes, il faut un permis C.

articles.title: Windows 11 Celebrates 5th Birthday with Over One Billion Users Worldwide
articles.text:
Monday, October 5th 2026
Windows 11 Celebrates 5th Birthday with Over One Billion Users Worldwide
Five years ago today, on October 5, 2021, Microsoft released its Windows 11 operating system, marking the beginning of a new era. With its fresh design, Windows 11 quickly became a hot topic among gamers, enthusiasts, and tech observers worldwide, especially as Microsoft gradually phased out updates for its previous Windows 10 operating system. When Microsoft reported its earnings for the fourth quarter of 2025, ending December 31, the company highlighted that Windows 11 was achieving its goals faster than its predecessor, Windows 10. As of today, Windows 11 has officially reached over one billion global users. It took just 1,576 days for the new Windows OS to reach this milestone, compared to the 1,706 days it took Windows 10.
Windows 11 has been on the market since October 5, 2021. In the tech world, that is a long time for any software product. Over the years, it has evolved from a slight reskin of Windows 10 into a completely different user experience with more modern layouts and a modernized interface. However, it has also faced a range of issues. As Microsoft attempted to integrate everything into a singular OS, problems became common with updates, leading to random bugs and system crashes. Nowadays, it is popular to criticize Windows 11, but despite its buggy nature, its success and market penetration speak for themselves. Microsoft plans to keep Windows 11 as a long-running version, so it might be a while before we see a Windows 12 or anything similar.Microsoft saw a massive influx of new Windows 11 users after the end of life for Windows 10. On October 14, 2025, Microsoft officially ended support for an operating system that had powered billions of desktops since 2015. After 10 years, Windows 10 was phased out, and Windows 11 is now running the show, with over one billion users. We can expect to see many more Windows 11 updates, whether good or bad, but it continues to be a central topic for millions of enthusiasts worldwide.

articles.title: Mass quarantine issued in Russia after unexplained death of plague researcher
articles.text:
Roughly 200 people are under medical observation, several hospitals are under quarantine, and dozens are in isolation in Russia following the unexplained death of an infectious disease researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, according to early reports of the situation on Sunday and Monday.
Researcher Darya Shipilova reportedly died last week from pneumonia of “unknown” cause, according to Rospotrebnadzor, a Russian public health agency.
Unconfirmed information regarding her death has swirled. Some reports have claimed she accidentally broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen, Yersinia pestis, on September 25. She subsequently fell ill, was admitted to a hospital September 29 with severe pneumonia and died overnight between October 1 and October 2. The head of the Russian region that neighbors Irkutsk, Alexey Tsydenov, initially reported that she had died of plague but later altered his statement to say she “possibly” died of the disease.
Y. pestis can cause several forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic—the latter of which can be aggressive and quickly fatal. However, the pathogen is generally easily treated by antibiotics. In the US, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that anyone exposed to the pathogen should undergo an immediate seven-day post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis treatment. Additionally, though pneumonic plague is spread via respiratory particles from coughing, it is not considered highly infectious; it requires direct, close contact for the bacteria to be transmitted.

articles.title: ChatGPT empezará a marcar sus textos con una señal invisible en España y otros países
articles.text:
OpenAI confirmó que añadirá una marca de agua en los textos que se generen en ChatGPT y Codex. Siguiendo los pasos de Anthropic, la compañía de inteligencia artificial reveló que implementará un sistema similar que ayudará a diferenciar el contenido de IA frente a los textos que escriben las personas. La medida debutará pronto en España y el resto de la Unión Europea, ya que la empresa debe cumplir con la legislación vigente.
Los textos generados por ChatGPT se han convertido en una constante que circula a diario en redes sociales, medios y bandejas de entrada sin que nadie sepa que provienen de una IA. A diferencia de las marcas de agua en las imágenes de Gemini o Grok, el contenido escrito no cuenta con un distintivo, por lo que garantizar que está hecho con ChatGPT es una tarea difícil. Debido a ello, la Comisión Europea promulgó una ley que obliga a los proveedores a dejar una huella reconocible por máquinas para este tipo de contenido.
En una publicación en su blog, OpenAI dijo que comenzará a incluir una marca de agua invisible en los textos que generen ChatGPT y Codex. La empresa no confirmó la fecha específica, solo se limitó a decir que se aplicará en las próximas semanas dentro de la UE. Las marcas de agua se activarán por defecto en los países del Espacio Económico Europeo debido al Reglamento de la IA, mientras que el resto de países tendrá que esperar.
Así es como OpenAI marcará tus textos de ChatGPT y Codex
De acuerdo con la explicación, la técnica que usará OpenAI se llama textGrain y será invisible al ojo humano. Los usuarios no verán cambios en el texto, ya que ese sistema añade una señal estadística a las palabras que el modelo elige al escribir. Esta señal se valida a través de un detector, que buscará ese patrón para estimar si un fragmento lleva la firma de OpenAI.
Esto es parecido a lo que vimos con Anthropic, que se basa en la técnica de lista verde y lista roja que divide todo el vocabulario del modelo en dos grupos antes de que se genere cada palabra. Cuando la IA redacta el texto, el modelo aumenta ligeramente la probabilidad de elegir palabras del primer grupo, pero lo hace de forma imperceptible y sin afectar la coherencia del texto final. Para detectar la marca, basta con analizar qué proporción de palabras pertenece a ese primer grupo y eso determinará si fue generado con una IA.
OpenAI dijo que su herramienta solo dirá si encuentra la marca en el texto. La compañía no compartirá datos del usuario ni el prompt que utilizó en ChatGPT. Otro detalle que podría decepcionar a muchos es que el detector no estará disponible para el público en general. OpenAI solo aceptará solicitudes de investigadores y organizaciones expertas.
En el caso de los desarrolladores, el trato será distinto. Actualmente, los usuarios de la API pueden activar el marcado en modelos seleccionados, ya que viene deshabilitado por defecto. OpenAI señaló que cada empresa decide cómo y cuándo lo activa para encajar con sus obligaciones de transparencia. La compañía dijo que está trabajando con sus socios de nube para ofrecer la marca de agua durante las próximas semanas.
¿Qué tan fiable es la marca de agua de ChatGPT?
OpenAI admitió que textGrain iguala o supera a otros métodos que probó, incluido SynthID, pero no es infalible. El detector encontró la marca en 80% de los textos de 200 tokens y en alrededor del 95% de los de 400 en contenidos de psicología. En textos de matemáticas y otros en los que hay menor libertad para elegir palabras, los porcentajes de éxito bajaron considerablemente.
El detector de OpenAI tampoco funciona bien con textos editados. En una prueba en la que se cambió el 10% de las palabras por sinónimos, el porcentaje de detección pasó de 92% a 66%, y al sustituir un 25% de las palabras, el porcentaje se cayó hasta el 17%.
La compañía mencionó que su tecnología no mide cuánto trabajo humano hay en un texto, no identifica a la persona que lo generó y no confirma que lo escrito sea cierto. Si no aparece la marca de agua, no necesariamente quiere decir que tenga origen humano, ya que puede estar editado o traducido. También podría provenir de modelos anteriores que no aplican el distintivo.
En resumen, los usuarios de ChatGPT no tendrían que preocuparse mucho. La marca de agua se implementará por un requisito regulatorio, pero no podrás usar el detector y tampoco habrá modo de asegurarse de que el contenido viene de una IA.
Con la implementación, es probable que veas una oleada de estafadores ofreciéndote herramientas para verificar si tu contenido es de ChatGPT o Codex y ofrecerte la opción de "humanizarlo". Ni OpenAI ni Anthropic pueden determinar con total certeza si un texto fue generado por una IA, por lo que resulta difícil confiar en que herramientas de terceros puedan hacerlo mejor.

articles.title: At 19, founder raises $11M for Ghost, maker of a $3,499 computer for personal AI | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For much of his life, Zain Javaid, 19, wanted to be a quant who uses math and data to guide his investment decisions. And for a while, he was one. But he got bored. Then, in 2022, ChatGPT was released, and he told TechCrunch, “I felt fundamentally excited in a way that I never had been before.”
He became interested in personal AI, and that interest led him to start Ghost, which announced Monday that it has emerged from stealth after a year of building, along with an $11 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Other investors in the round include Abstract, Audacious Ventures, SV Angel, and Nova. His founding team includes Nicholas Chua, 19, Yifei Chen, 24, and Gautam Sharda, 23.
Ghost’s first product is Core, a personal computer designed specifically for AI agents that can take actions on a person’s behalf. According to Javaid, the idea is to centralize a person’s data, from what’s on their desktop to apps to smart home devices, into one piece of hardware designed to continuously run AI agents that can act as an assistant, perform tasks, and understand a person’s life. “You can run models on existing hardware, but it’s a terrible experience on many levels,” said Javaid, who is also Core’s CEO.
Core includes an Nvidia RTX Pro 4000 SFF Blackwell GPU (a type of chip commonly used to run AI models), said Javaid, adding that the GPU is bundled into the device’s price, so customers don’t need to buy one separately. He said it also has its own software layer, browser, and filing system and can continuously process information and tasks without constant prompting. Core costs $3,499. Preorders for the first batch open Monday, and shipping is scheduled for the last week of October.
Javaid described Core as a “brain in a box” without a screen, which users access through a phone or app. Voice mode is also available, but users must speak into the Core app rather than the box itself. Core comes with three models preinstalled: Qwen-3.8-Next, Qwen-3.8-27B, and Gemma-4-31B.
Javaid said users can also install other models from Hugging Face, where developers share AI models, or load their own trained models. Asked how Core differs from a Mac Mini, Apple’s small desktop computer that some people set up to run AI tools, Javaid said Core’s hardware and software were built specifically for running AI agents, with models already installed, while the Mac Mini is a general-purpose computer that can be configured for AI.
“As new models or improvements to existing models come out, we can push out over-the-air updates, similar to how Tesla works,” Javaid said of Core, adding that if a new generation of models comes out, the company asks users whether they want to switch. “Users can also turn on auto-updates so they’re always running the latest generation of a given model.”
The team currently builds the units at its San Francisco facility. Javaid said the goal is to sell a fully functioning computer that doesn’t require complex setup or configuration. He said the models and personal memory run locally, and that all personal information is encrypted so that no cloud provider or third party, including Ghost, can meaningfully access it. He also said users can control how much autonomy they give their Core agents, and that the device is programmed to keep working if Ghost shuts down.
“All of the source code, logic, and model weights live on the device, not the services,” he said. “We build this device to not be dependent on having an outside entity maintaining the service.”
He said the team is also building a firewall to limit how the agent can use its credentials, such as logins and passwords. The firewall “monitors every outgoing network request on the computer and if it sees the agent performing a sanctioned action or exfiltrating data it shouldn’t, it rejects the request and flags it for user review.”
“The user owns all of it,” he said of the device, memory, and data. “Once you buy the hardware, everything is stored, run, and processed on the device.”
He said he is not too worried about the competition, including from established tech companies. “People sometimes give incumbents credit for having already built the product because they have the ingredients,” he said. He credited Apple with good hardware and disruption, but said much of what Core is aiming to tackle is software: “The model reasons over your life, how it remembers, how it takes action, how it knows when to reach out,” he continued.
Javaid offered an example of how Core is meant to work: “Core proactively sends you a notification that you might be getting sick because it sees your resting heart rate is elevated, sees from computer history that you were up late working on a project, and has seasonal context that it is flu season in San Francisco.”
The company’s main focus is building a product people love, he said. “If we can’t do that, Apple isn’t the reason we failed,” he said.
Above, Core’s founding team (L-R): Gautam Sharda, 23; Yifei Chen, 24; Zain Javaid, 19; and Nicholas Chua, 19.

articles.title: Cyber resilience now depends on governing AI agent data use - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Storage admins get automated guardrails as agents outrun human-in-the-loop review
Enterprises pushing AI agents into production are finding that cyber resilience now depends as much on governing what autonomous software does with data as on keeping attackers out. Much of the risk doesn’t come from malicious intent at all; it comes from agents doing unexpected things at machine speed.
That shift is pushing storage providers to build intelligent data infrastructure that can judge how data is being used. NetApp Inc. is moving access controls away from simple yes-or-no permissions and toward policies based on behavior, according to Russell Fishman (pictured), senior director of global AI solutions and field activation of NetApp.
“We’re starting to get away from thinking about everything through a human lens,” Fishman said. “This is an agent. Agents don’t think the same way. They’re not acting the same way.”
Fishman spoke with theCUBE’s Christophe Bertrand and Rebecca Knight at NetApp INSIGHT, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed a week of NetApp announcements, including Novus, a new storage architecture for AI factories and neoclouds, and the growing importance of cyber resilience as the market matures. (* Disclosure below.)
Cyber resilience moves into the data layer
NetApp’s traditional protection tools still carry weight as threats speed up. Its autonomous ransomware protection service uses AI to detect and block attacks, and a newly announced integration feeds those signals into recovery workflows from Commvault Systems Inc., Fishman explained. NetApp has built similar links with Microsoft Corp.’s Sentinel and Cisco Systems Inc.’s Splunk, he added.
“We become an indicator of compromise,” he said. “We can actually detect things and tell Commvault, ‘hey, there’s a problem,’ and vice versa.”
AI agents raise a different problem. Most organizations Fishman talks with worry less about bad actors than about agents causing unintended consequences while they try to finish an assigned task. New features in NetApp’s AI Data Engine, which prepares and governs enterprise data for AI, include a behavior-based policy engine that flags unusual patterns of data use, he noted.
“I would expect you to look at maybe one customer’s account, not all of the customers’ accounts,” he said. “That seems a bit weird to me.”
Responding at the speed of AI means organizations can’t always keep a human in the loop, so automation has to carry more of the load, Fishman explained. For NetApp customers who want stronger cyber resilience now, AI Data Engine can be deployed against any existing NetApp system, and the company announced a free six-month offer at the event, according to Fishman.
“If I was an ONTAP admin — if I was a NetApp customer — that’s the first thing I’d be doing,” Fishman said. “I want to lock this down now. The risk of not doing so, not just from a lack of innovation, but the risk of misuse of data, the lack of control, it’s too great.”

articles.title: Infrastructure modernization with NetApp ONTAP native in OCI - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
NetApp puts ONTAP inside Oracle’s cloud, betting native beats bolted-on
Infrastructure modernization often stalls at the storage layer, where moving mission-critical applications to the cloud can mean redesigning them from scratch. Now, AI is raising the stakes as enterprises push decades-old data estates into production AI.
NetApp Inc. and Oracle Corp. are tackling that problem with an inbound, fully managed storage service that runs NetApp’s ONTAP data management software natively inside Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The co-engineered offering is built to behave like any other OCI service rather than a third-party add-on, according to Pravjit Tiwana (pictured, left), senior vice president and general manager of cloud storage and services at NetApp.
“As far as our partnership, this is a co-engineered and co-developed product of ours,” Tiwana said. “It’s not like we have taken it and bolted it in OCI, but both [Oracle] and our organizations have worked very closely to have a deep integration into [the] control plane, data plane, as well as to the OCI’s native billing infrastructure, to provisioning, to console, to API.”
Tiwana and Konstantinos Papamiltiadis (right), senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Christophe Bertrand at NetApp INSIGHT, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed native ONTAP integration in OCI, migration for existing NetApp workloads and plans to bring AI closer to enterprise data. (* Disclosure below.)
Native integration as a path to infrastructure modernization
Oracle has long built its own storage products, but customers wanted a way to bring mission-critical deployments from their data centers into the cloud. Many already run ONTAP on-premises, so matching that experience was a design priority, Papamiltiadis explained.
“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” Papamiltiadis said. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”
The native approach also matters for migration, where many cloud projects get bogged down. The two companies plan to co-sell the service, drawing on NetApp’s experience with other hyperscalers, according to Tiwana.
“The one important thing is nobody wants to redo the application redesign and all,” Tiwana said. “If you have applications or systems running on-prem, you bring it to OCI with ONTAP, you don’t have to do anything. It works as seamlessly as it was working on-prem.”
AI adds another layer to infrastructure modernization. NetApp’s decades of work on data protection, compliance and lineage let it prepare enterprise data for agentic workflows and inferencing, not just store it, Tiwana explained.
“Both the companies do plan to work together to bring Oracle’s great AI efforts into our ONTAP so customers don’t have to move data somewhere else,” Tiwana said. “They can run the AI right where the data lives.”

articles.title: Nouveau Siri : la douche froide que les utilisateurs d’iPhone redoutaient tant
articles.text:
Les utilisateurs européens du flambant neuf iPhone 18 Pro devront encore s’armer de patience. Alors que la firme de Cupertino déploie progressivement Siri AI, son nouvel assistant dopé à l’intelligence artificielle à travers le globe, le Vieux Continent reste une nouvelle fois sur le banc de touche. En cause : le bras de fer réglementaire permanent entre la marque à la pomme et Bruxelles autour du Digital Markets Act (DMA).
Apple justifie officiellement ce blocage par les exigences d’interopérabilité imposées par le texte européen, affirmant qu’elles mettraient en péril la sécurité et la confidentialité des données privées de ses clients. Mais derrière cette prudence technique affichée se cache un calcul stratégique bien plus agressif.
Une attente de plus de 5 mois est possible
Interrogé sur le calendrier d’une sortie sur notre territoire, le journaliste de Bloomberg Mark Gurman, très bien informé en la matière, affirme :
« Ne vous attendez pas à ce que Siri AI arrive de sitôt dans l’Union européenne. Apple se sert de l’absence de l’IA Siri sur iOS dans la région pour faire pression sur la Commission européenne, dans l’espoir que les clients frustrés s’opposent à l’approche réglementaire de l’UE. L’IA Siri en elle-même n’est pas suffisamment convaincante pour susciter un tel élan, mais ce retard frustre clairement les utilisateurs européens — à en juger par le flot constant de messages que je reçois à ce sujet. Le meilleur précédent est celui d’Apple Intelligence. Ces fonctionnalités ont été lancées ailleurs en octobre 2024, mais ne sont arrivées dans l’UE qu’à la fin du mois de mars 2025, soit un décalage d’environ cinq mois. Je considérerais un retard similaire pour Siri AI comme le meilleur scénario possible cette fois-ci — et je ne serais pas surpris que les utilisateurs européens doivent attendre bien plus longtemps encore. »
En répétant la méthode déjà employée lors des premiers pas d’Apple Intelligence, l’entreprise espère probablement transformer le mécontentement de ses clients en levier politique face aux régulateurs. Pour se faire l’avocat du diable, ajoutons qu’il est vrai qu’Apple a mis en place des procédés de protection des données très avancées qui rendent l’interopérabilité plus compliquée à mettre en place. Mais si la firme à la pomme a fini par y parvenir concernant l’App Store, il n’y pas vraiment de raison pour un tel blocage sur d’autres sujets.
De son côté, la Commission européenne refuse pour l’instant d’assouplir ses exigences de concurrence. Résultat le bras de fer s’installe dans la durée, laissant les possesseurs d’iPhone en Europe privés du nouveau Siri pour un bon moment. On peut également citer les nouveautés de watchOS, pour la plupart matinées d’IA, qui devront prendre quelques mois avant d’être déployées. Un sujet qui commence à devenir une habitude chez la firme à la pomme depuis le lancement d’Apple Intelligence.

articles.title: Pourquoi plusieurs F1 ont perdu leur puissance au départ du Grand Prix de Malaisie
articles.text:
Au départ du Grand Prix de Bahreïn, couru hier 4 octobre sur le circuit malaisien de Sepang, plusieurs monoplaces ont perdu leur puissance en plein tour de formation. La FIA a reconnu un bug dans le logiciel commun aux moteurs de 2026, jamais testé sous la pluie à des vitesses aussi faibles.
Annulé en avril, ce Grand Prix de Bahreïn a été déplacé en Malaisie par la F1. Et si vous étiez au rendez-vous ce dimanche, alors vous avez assisté à de drôles de ballets de bolides. Sous des pluies torrentielles, la direction de course a d’abord repoussé le départ de quarante minutes, puis lancé le peloton derrière la voiture de sécurité. À mi-tour, Max Verstappen, en tête, a brusquement ralenti avant de reprendre de la vitesse, tandis que Lewis Hamilton s’est immobilisé juste avant le dernier virage. D’autres voitures, notamment à moteur Ferrari, ont roulé au pas ou se sont arrêtées en piste et ont poussé la FIA à brandir le drapeau rouge et abandonner la procédure de départ. Le feu vert a finalement été donné avec plus de 45 minutes de retard. Cette pagaille est d’origine logicielle, et ni la FIA ni les écuries n’avaient repéré le défaut lors des essais.
Un mode de sécurité piégé par les très basses vitesses
Depuis cette saison, la puissance des monoplaces est partagée presque à parts égales entre le moteur thermique et la partie électrique, et les écuries jouent une bonne partie de leur course sur la gestion de cette énergie. Au freinage, l’électricité est récupérée par un moteur-générateur, le MGU-K, puis restituée à l’accélération. Jusqu’en 2025, la pression du turbo était maintenue à bas régime par un second générateur, le MGU-H, supprimé par le nouveau règlement.
Sous la pluie, les équipes doivent passer sur un mode moteur obligatoire limité à 250 kW, contre 350 kW sur le sec. Pour des raisons de sécurité, la puissance électrique est aussi plafonnée dans certains secteurs, dont le virage 9 de Sepang. Dans cette zone, le MGU-K peut être coupé d’un coup, sans réduction progressive.
Derrière la voiture de sécurité, certaines monoplaces roulaient presque à l’arrêt, avec un effet d’accordéon dans le peloton. Leur pression de suralimentation a diminué sans la moindre assistance électrique dans ce virage, et à cause d'un bug, ces voitures sont alors passées en mode de bridage continu. La FIA impose depuis cette année ce blocage d’urgence de 60 secondes pour empêcher les écuries de couper volontairement le MGU-K. Pendant ce délai, le moteur thermique peut aussi être privé d’alimentation. En avril, la fédération avait d’ailleurs interdit à Mercedes et Red Bull de couper le MGU-K en fin de tour de qualification. Leur astuce avait été repérée après des arrêts moteur en essais libres à Suzuka.
« Ce bug a empêché la réalimentation électrique et le redémarrage des voitures », a expliqué Nikolas Tombazis, directeur des monoplaces à la FIA. Avant ce Grand Prix, les F1 de 2026 n’avaient roulé sur le mouillé que lors d’essais de pneus Pirelli, à Suzuka pour Red Bull et Racing Bulls, puis en avril pour Ferrari, sur une piste de Fiorano arrosée artificiellement. Lors de ces séances, les voitures n'avaient jamais roulé aussi lentement. « Je pense qu’avec davantage de tests, nous aurions probablement pu le détecter à temps », a admis le dirigeant.
Un correctif écrit en urgence, des pilotes excédés
Pendant l’interruption, le département technique de la FIA a écrit en urgence une mise à jour pour lever la limite d’énergie dans les secteurs concernés, puis l’a envoyée à toutes les écuries. Il a fallu entre 20 et 25 minutes pour faire installer ce correctif sur chaque voiture et en vérifier la présence. Nikolas Tombazis admet un « travail bâclé », mais pour lui, la priorité était de relancer la course au plus vite. Ce code commun est développé par la FIA avec le fournisseur du calculateur standard, Motion Applied, ainsi qu’avec les écuries et les motoristes. « Il s’agit clairement d’un problème logiciel de la FIA. Nous avons évidemment une part de responsabilité », a reconnu le directeur des monoplaces.
Dans le paddock, plusieurs pilotes n’ont pas digéré l’épisode. Pour Lando Norris, ce tour de formation était « horrible », et la preuve que la F1 ne devrait rien avoir « de tout ça côté électronique ». Carlos Sainz a dénoncé des règles extrêmement compliquées pour tout le monde. « Si c’était un V8 atmosphérique, cela ne serait jamais arrivé », a lancé le pilote Williams. Contraint à l’abandon en fin de course, George Russell a estimé de son côté que « plus on complique les choses, plus il y a de choses qui peuvent mal tourner ».
La FIA va passer l’incident au crible avec les écuries et les motoristes. « Puis-je garantir que cela ne se reproduira plus jamais ? Ce problème précis ? Oui. Un problème ? Non », a prévenu Nikolas Tombazis.

articles.title: Quand les bornes de recharge ultra-rapides de BYD sont détournées en balançoires par des enfants
articles.text:
Les bornes de recharge les plus puissantes de BYD ont trouvé un usage que le constructeur n’avait pas prévu. Une vidéo tournée le 2 octobre à Nanning, dans la région autonome du Guangxi, montre deux jeunes enfants accrochés aux pistolets d’une station Megawatt Flash Charging du géant automobile chinois. Ils se balancent, les pieds dans le vide, pendant que des adultes filment. La séquence a fait le tour des réseaux sociaux chinois pendant les congés de la fête nationale, rapporte CarNewsChina ce lundi 5 octobre.
Dans une réponse relayée par le site chinois IT Home, le service client de BYD a rappelé dimanche 4 octobre qu’il est strictement interdit de jouer avec les équipements de recharge. Le constructeur a envoyé des techniciens inspecter la station et promet de renforcer la surveillance et les contrôles sur place.
Pour mémoire, BYD a présenté une première version de ces bornes en mars 2025. Elles délivrent jusqu’à 1 000 kW de puissance et permettent de passer de 10 à 70 % de batterie en cinq minutes avec les modèles compatibles. Depuis le début de leur déploiement au mois de février.
Une forme de borne parfaite… pour jouer
Pour faire passer une telle puissance, ces câbles refroidis par liquide sont imposants, lourds et difficiles à manipuler. BYD a donc suspendu l’ensemble à un rail en forme de T installé en hauteur, avec un enrouleur à ressort. Le rail porte le poids du câble, alors que le pistolet reste à hauteur de poitrine afin que rien ne traîne dans la boue ou les flaques. C’est là tout le problème : un pistolet de 3 à 5 kilos pendu à un rail devient un pendule dès qu’un enfant s’y accroche.
Le risque d’électrocution immédiate reste naturellement limité. Les normes imposent que les contacteurs de la borne restent ouverts tant que le pistolet est rangé. La haute tension n’arrive qu’une fois le connecteur branché et verrouillé sur la prise d’une voiture, après une série de vérifications d’isolement entre la borne et le véhicule.
Finalement, le danger est surtout mécanique. Les enrouleurs, les passe-câbles et les renforts à la base du connecteur sont dimensionnés pour les gestes d’un conducteur qui branche sa voiture, pas pour des balancements répétés.
Sous leur gaine, ces câbles contiennent des conducteurs en cuivre, des fils de communication et des canaux de liquide de refroidissement. Plier et tirer le câble encore et encore peut abîmer ces éléments, ou le fil de terre, par l’intérieur, sans laisser de trace visible à l’extérieur. Le conducteur suivant brancherait alors sa voiture avec un câble endommagé, traversé par des courants très élevés.
Il ne faudrait pas que ce genre de comportement devienne une pratique courante, car BYD vise 20 000 stations Flash Charging en Chine d’ici la fin de l’année 2026. Ça en ferait des bornes à surveiller. À l’international, ces bornes ultra-rapides seront progressivement déployées, notamment en Europe où l’on devrait en compter 3 000 à l’horizon 2027.

articles.title: Bhavish Aggarwal pledges 4.32% stake to back Ola Electric’s Rs 1,000 Cr rights issue
articles.text:
Bhavish Aggarwal pledges 4.32% stake to back Ola Electric’s Rs 1,000 Cr rights issue
Ola Electric Chairman Bhavish Aggarwal has pledged a 4.32% stake in the company to raise funds for its upcoming Rs 1,000 Cr rights issue.
Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal has stepped up to back the company’s upcoming Rs 1,000 crore rights issue, pledging a 4.32% stake in the EV maker to fund his participation.
The move comes days after Ola Electric’s board greenlit the plan to raise fresh capital through partly paid-up shares and appointed Deepa Bansal as its new compliance chief to bolster governance.
According to stock exchange filings on Sunday, Aggarwal pledged 20 crore shares against non-convertible debentures issued by Krutrim Data Centre Private Limited—a non-operative promoter entity owned by Aggarwal—to CTL Trusteeship Limited. The company clarified that no shares are being sold, no other pledges exist on his holdings, and Aggarwal will subscribe to the issue on the same terms as all other shareholders.
Unlike many tech founders whose ownership dilutes quickly after going public, Aggarwal and his promoter group still hold about a third of Ola Electric. By subscribing to his share of the rights issue, Aggarwal ensures his ownership stake stays intact once the new shares hit the market.
The fresh cash push arrives at a high-stakes moment for the Bengaluru-based EV manufacturer. Sharper competition from legacy brands like TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, and Hero MotoCorp, along with rival Ather Energy, recently dragged Ola Electric down to fifth place in monthly vehicle registrations. In Q1 FY27, revenue fell to Rs 455 crore from Rs 828 crore a year earlier, though losses narrowed to Rs 336 crore.
Having raised Rs 780 crore through a qualified institutional placement in June, the Rs 1,000 crore rights issue gives Ola Electric another balance-sheet cushion as it works to defend its market position.
(Disclaimer: Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory, is an independent director at Ola Electric.)

articles.title: El ingenioso truco que usa ‘Gears of War: E-Day’ para funcionar mejor en Xbox Series S
articles.text:
Gears of War: E-Day está a pocas horas de su lanzamiento oficial, pautado para mañana, martes 6 de octubre. El nuevo juego de The Coalition, que ha logrado muy buenas críticas tanto de la prensa especializada como de quienes tuvieron acceso temprano, aspira a ser uno de los grandes bombazos de 2026. Y sus responsables han revelado un curioso truco del que echaron mano para lograr que funcione de la mejor forma posible en la Xbox Series S.
Desde el estudio le revelaron a Digital Foundry una muy ingeniosa solución para lidiar con las limitaciones de hardware que tiene la Xbox Series S en comparación con la Series X, su hermana mayor. Puntualmente, para afrontar la disponibilidad de una menor cantidad de memoria RAM. Tengamos en cuenta que el modelo de entrada tiene 10 GB, mientras que la variante mayor cuenta con 16 GB.
Al ser Gears of War: E-Day un juego que presenta escenarios opulentos y muy densos, en The Coalition tuvieron que ponerse creativos para evitar que la experiencia gráfica y jugable se degradara (en demasía al menos) en la Xbox Series S. Para ello, desarrollaron un sistema que utiliza una porción del almacenamiento interno de la consola como si fuese RAM.
Kate Rayner, directora técnica de la compañía, explicó que la tecnología en cuestión les permite generar alrededor de 1 GB de "RAM" a partir de "un par de GB" de almacenamiento SSD. Claro que esto es bastante más complejo que simplemente asignar una porción del espacio interno para convertirlo en memoria del sistema.
Gears of War: E-Day usa parte del SSD de la Xbox Series S como memoria RAM
Según The Coalition, han desarrollado un método que detecta cuáles son los datos de uso más frecuente al jugar Gears of War: E-Day. Así, pueden determinar cuáles deben utilizar la RAM real y cuáles de acceso menos habitual pueden residir en la memoria generada a partir del SSD. El estudio ha logrado que la transferencia de esa información desde el disco de estado sólido hacia la RAM sea lo suficientemente veloz como para que los jugadores no noten nada extraño al accederla.
De esta manera, Gears of War: E-Day se puede ejecutar en la Xbox Series S con una calidad de gráficos y de jugabilidad muy buena. The Coalition incluso ha logrado que el título corra a una tasa regular de 60 fotogramas por segundo. Aunque eso no se ha conseguido solamente al transformar parte del almacenamiento en memoria de sistema. Desde la compañía reconocen que han tenido que eliminar los reflejos de Lumen, una característica de iluminación de Unreal Engine 5.
Si bien Rayner menciona que depender en exceso de esta característica puede afectar negativamente el desempeño de un juego, también puede ayudar a simplificar la adaptación al hardware de la Xbox Series S. Recordemos que Microsoft exige que todos los juegos que se lanzan en Series X también tienen que estar disponibles en su hermana menor. Esto ha llevado a retrasos en el debut de ciertos juegos y a la eliminación de características importantes.
Pero el trabajo realizado en Gears of War: E-Day podría abrir el camino a nuevas soluciones. De acuerdo con The Coalition, otros estudios ya están interesados en conocer más sobre esta técnica para aplicarla sobre sus propios desarrollos.

articles.title: Jordan Bardella peut-il demander à Meta un historique de ses conversations ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Depuis la présentation par Mediapart des coulisses de son enquête sur Jordan Bardella, on redécouvre le droit d’accès à ses données prévu par le RGPD (règlement général sur la protection des données) dans l’Union européenne.
Il est en effet possible de demander l’intégralité de son historique de conversation sur Facebook Messenger à Meta. C’est ce qu’a utilisé la source de Mediapart pour exporter ses conversations avec un compte intitulé « Jordan Bardella » ayant tenu des propos antisémites entre 2013 et 2015. Le média d’investigation a par la suite associé ce compte Facebook à Jordan Bardella, en recoupant ces conversations avec des événements de la vie du président du Rassemblement national. L’intéressé conteste formellement les révélations de Mediapart.
Plusieurs hypothèses s’opposent
Ce lundi 5 octobre, Pascal Praud a suggéré sur CNews que Jordan Bardella fasse à son tour valoir ses droits au titre du RGPD en demandant une archive de ses conversations sur Facebook Messenger. Selon lui, Jordan Bardella pourrait ainsi prouver très simplement son innocence.
Pourquoi il n’extrait pas lui-même toutes les conversations ? Si tu fais sortir toutes les conversations […], t’arrives et tu dis bah voilà ! C’est facile à prouver !
Alors, est-ce que Jordan Bardella peut vraiment faire cette démarche ?
Première hypothèse, le compte a été supprimé depuis. La conversation récupérée par la source de Mediapart ne prouve pas le contraire. Quand un compte Facebook est supprimé, les messages qu’il a envoyés restent dans la boîte de réception de ses correspondants, et donc dans leur archive. Son titulaire, lui, ne peut plus télécharger ses données 90 jours après la suppression du compte.
Deuxième hypothèse, le compte est seulement inactif ou suspendu. Son titulaire doit alors réussir à s’y reconnecter pour demander l’archive à Meta.
Encore faudrait-il que ce compte soit bien celui de Jordan Bardella, ce qu’il conteste.
Selon Mediapart, Jordan Bardella a créé dès 2013 un second compte Facebook, tourné vers sa communication politique, en parallèle de celui où il aurait tenu ces propos. S’il demande l’archive de ce compte à Meta, elle ne contiendra pas les conversations du premier. Sur le plateau de CNews, le député RN Philippe Ballard admet lui-même, à propos des comptes Facebook de Jordan Bardella : « je crois même qu’il en a eu plusieurs. »
Une archive insuffisante
Jordan Bardella pourrait donc demander l’archive d’un compte qu’il utilisait à l’époque et n’y trouver aucune des conversations en cause. Cela ne prouverait pas son innocence, puisqu’il pourrait avoir tenu ces propos depuis un autre compte.
C’est pour ces raisons que si Jordan Bardella pourrait bien demander à Meta une archive de ses activités, cela ne pourrait pas suffire à totalement démontrer son innocence.
Le Rassemblement national défend de toute façon la thèse d’un faux compte. Dans cette hypothèse, Jordan Bardella ne peut pas demander l’archive d’un compte qui n’est pas le sien.

articles.title: Rejetto HFS servers now actively scanned for critical RCE flaw
articles.text:
Hackers are actively scanning for a Rejetto HFS weak signing key vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-61500, that allows session forgery, account takeover, and remote code execution (RCE).
VulnCheck VP of Security Research Caitlin Condon posted on LinkedIn over the weekend that the company's Canary Intelligence honeypots had observed probes targeting CVE-2026-61500.
Condon said the observed activity appears to be small-scale reconnaissance from a single China Telecom IP address probing deployments in Japan and the United States.
Rejetto HFS (HTTP File Server) is a free and open-source file-sharing server tool used for self-hosted file sharing on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
CVE-2026-61500, first published on July 13, 2026, is a session-cookie signing weakness and leakage issue fixed in Rejetto HFS version 3.2.1.
"Rejetto HFS 3.0.0 through 3.2.0 derives its session-cookie signing key from the non-cryptographic Math.random() generator and discloses outputs of the same generator to unauthenticated clients during login," reads the flaw description on the NIST NVD.
"A remote attacker can collect a small number of login responses, reconstruct the generator's state, recover the signing key, and forge a valid administrator session cookie, leading to full administrative access and remote code execution via the server_code configuration feature."
Horizon3 researchers discovered the flaw using Anthropic's Mythos model, which identified both the weak signing-key generation and the leak that enabled key recovery.
Horizon3 published more details about the flaw and a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit in a write-up on September 30, 2026.
"Mythos didn't just flag the insecure PRNG in isolation – it simultaneously identified that the application leaked raw Math.random() outputs through a separate code path, recognized those two facts as a chain, and determined the leak produced exactly the observations needed to make state recovery feasible," explained Horizon3.
The researchers' exploit demonstrates the chain to abuse HFS's built-in ability to execute custom server-side JavaScript to achieve remote code execution.
The release of these technical details may have prompted the probing activity targeting CVE-2026-61500.
Possible attack scenarios include accessing, stealing, or deleting HFS files, installing malware on the server, or using the compromised host to access internal systems.
However, VulnCheck has not shared details on successful exploitation or any post-exploitation activity.
Users of Rejetto HFS are recommended to upgrade to version 3.2.1 or, ideally, the latest stable release, 3.3.4, as soon as possible.

articles.title: Why VOA spends six months inside startups before investing
articles.text:
Most investors decide whether to back a startup after a pitch, a handful of meetings and several weeks of due diligence. Victoria Olayide Adesanya, founder of VOA Venture Partners, an Africa-focused venture capital firm, demands something more before writing a cheque: she wants to spend six months working inside the business.
VOA backs startups building the financial infrastructure that moves money into and out of Africa, with a focus on founders from the African diaspora. Adesanya said she bets on the parts of fintech most people never see, pushing back on the idea that African fintech is crowded.
She calls the market young and says financial infrastructure, mostly business-to-business, is full of gaps. Two of VOA’s portfolio companies show what she means. Blockradar lets fintechs offer stablecoin wallets through an API without hiring blockchain engineers. REasy helps small businesses in Francophone Africa pay suppliers in China and Dubai and handle the shipping.
Before starting the firm, Adesanya spent over a decade in finance, including roles at Barclays and Credit Suisse and advisory work for investment banks such as Morgan Stanley. Adesanya spends six months inside a company through VOA Build, a programme the firm has been piloting with a handful of companies this year. VOA works with a startup as an extra go-to-market strategist, with no investment, and the only goal is to grow revenue.
In return, VOA earns a share of the revenue it helps create and a small equity stake that vests over the engagement. Whether VOA’s fund later invests is a separate decision. Adesanya built the programme for a market where early-stage startup funding is hard to find. According to Africa: The Big Deal, the number of African startups raising between $100,000 and $1 million fell 44% in the first half of 2026.
In this conversation, Adesanya explains why she started VOA, how VOA Build works and what founders give up to join it; what six months alongside a team shows that due diligence misses; and why she tells pre-seed founders not to make fundraising their North Star.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You worked at Barclays and Credit Suisse, then ran a startup advisory. Why start VOA, and why this thesis?
When I was at Barclays, I ran an events programme called the Africa Forum. Once a quarter, we brought in about 200 people, some Barclays employees and some clients, to learn about what was happening on the continent. We would pick a topic, such as healthcare or how technology was helping countries leapfrog. This was the early 2010s, when mobile money was just rising, and everyone was saying Africa is the future.
Roughly 15 years later, we are still saying the same things, and it feels like not much has changed.
When we started the fund, we thought about the kinds of startups we wanted to back. But the real question was this: how do we make sure Africa becomes a key player in the global economy? If Africa is where growth will be, how do we speed that up, and how do we keep a piece of that pie?
Most African businesses are small, and most can only sell to customers in their local area. Their counterparts in the West can transact globally. We want to change that, and we want more global businesses to set up on the continent. For both, the most basic thing needed is financial infrastructure.
We looked at the core barriers to capital moving into and out of Africa, and that became our thesis. We use a five-pillar framework: market fragmentation, regulatory and compliance challenges, technology and infrastructure gaps, financial inclusion and the informal economy, and cybersecurity and fraud risk. We invest in financial infrastructure and solutions that make that movement possible.
People on the continent talk a lot about closing the financing gap for small businesses. If we truly want to close it, those businesses need the same opportunities as their global counterparts. Then they can build sustainable companies that stand their ground in the long term, with or without financing.
There is a personal side too. My grandmother was a trader in the 1970s and 1980s. She bought goods in London and Hong Kong and sold them in Nigeria, and the way that kind of business works has not changed much since. We also kept meeting amazing founders who lacked capital. African and African diaspora founders receive less than 2% of global venture funding. It is ridiculous.
Fintech is already the biggest sector in African tech. What do you think about it?
First, a caveat. The African market is young. The biggest companies you can name are 10 to 15 years old, and ventures have been around much longer in the West. Compared with what we see globally, we are scratching the surface.
Second, fintech is a big word. People picture a consumer remittance app and think that is all there is. Financial infrastructure is mostly a B2B play. It covers the things that happen in the background, which many people never think about, and there are many gaps there.
One big example is cybersecurity and fraud risk, one of our pillars. There are not many companies there to begin with, and many of the ones we have seen are consultancies that turned into startups. We are still looking for a big, successful company in that space, and fraud risk keeps increasing.
Everything we look at is a necessity. The internet has made the world global. You can use WhatsApp anywhere, and that should filter into every area of our lives, including how money moves.
Investors also need the best startups to return money to their own backers. How do you plan to stand out to startups?
Capital is scarce for everyone right now, investors and founders alike. Many investors are mostly doing follow-on rounds, and new pre-seed companies are finding it hard to raise. Some people see the continent as risky, and some think fintech is saturated. I do not agree with that, but we wanted a way to get assurance for ourselves and for our investors.
That is why we created a programme called VOA Build. We work hand in hand with a company for about six months. Think of it as having an extra go-to-market strategist on your team. There is no investment during those six months, and the only focus is building sustainable revenue. There are some economics involved, such as revenue partnerships and a small equity stake.
We get to see how the startup really operates, and we help it scale. After six months, if the founders decide they do not need outside funding and want to keep bootstrapping, that is fine with us. We have helped build a sustainable business. If they do want to raise, we can do that too, and now in a de-risked way.
Exits are not really happening, so investors are much more selective about where they put capital. This gives early-stage startups a way to build a relationship with an investor who then backs them for their business. We have piloted it with a few companies, and it has shown us things we would not have seen as a traditional fund basing everything on due diligence.
How many companies have gone through the pilot so far, and how did you choose them?
We have worked with a handful of carefully chosen companies this year. We tend to choose businesses we could see ourselves investing in through the fund.
The company needs to be post-revenue, with real, paying customers, and there needs to be a clear opportunity for our involvement to add value. We also look for founders who are willing to engage openly, share information and put decisions into practice.
How do the economics work for a founder?
The economics reflect the scope of each engagement. Broadly, they combine revenue participation linked to specific commercial opportunities we help create or advance and a small equity stake that vests over the engagement period. Any investment from VOA’s fund is a separate decision.
You said Build showed you things you would have missed in due diligence. What has it taught you?
Three lessons keep coming up.
First, execution matters. A strong product or an attractive market does not mean a team can execute consistently.
Second, behaviour is data, and traditional due diligence gives you little visibility into it. A founding team’s responsiveness, follow-through, priorities and decision-making tell you a great deal about how a business operates. Working alongside founders shows you how they take feedback, make hard choices and turn those choices into action. That gives us a stronger basis for judging whether they can scale.
Third, commercial outcomes matter. A busy pipeline or a list of partnerships can look impressive, but we want to know whether those relationships turn into revenue, usage or other real milestones. Working with founders over a long period gives us a clearer view of that.
Some founders may be wary of giving up equity before any investment comes in. What would you say to them?
That is a fair concern. Founders should think carefully about dilution and should not give up equity without understanding what they get in return.
In our case, the equity vests over the engagement period. We also choose companies carefully, and founders will already have seen how we think through their business and the feedback we give before they decide to work with us.
In the end, founders should weigh that trade-off for themselves.
What happens if another investor wants to back a company while it is still in the programme?
We welcome that. Companies can raise money while they are in VOA Build and keep working with us through the programme. Our purpose is to help founders build sustainable companies, and investment that supports their growth is a good outcome.
That speaks to the wider purpose of VOA Build. Working closely with founders gives us first-hand insight into how they execute, make decisions and respond to problems. By focusing on execution, VOA Build helps a founder’s operating record carry more weight in funding conversations. That can reduce the reliance on trusted networks, which often leave capable founders, particularly African, diaspora and Black founders, outside those conversations.
When there is very little data to go on, which signals matter most to you?
First, I look at the founder’s motivation and the decisions they have made so far. Why this problem? What have they done with the resources available? I am looking for evidence of resilience and sound judgement, especially when things have not gone to plan.
Second, there needs to be real traction. I want evidence that customers value the product. A business whose whole plan for winning customers depends on raising money does not give me that.
Third, I look for depth of understanding: the customer, the market, the product and the alternatives already out there. A founder should be able to explain why customers would choose their product and where competitors are stronger. That tells you a lot about how seriously they have engaged with the problem.
How do Blockradar and REasy, two of your portfolio companies, show what you look for?
They are good examples for the argument that fintech is saturated, because they do such different things.
Blockradar’s angle is that blockchain and stablecoins are becoming necessary to make payments efficient. You can settle in real time with stablecoins, without waiting ages for correspondent banking. But for a fintech or a financial institution to use this technology, it usually has to hire blockchain engineers, and that is expensive. Blockradar removes that complexity. A business can plug into its APIs and get stablecoin wallets and all the features it needs without hiring a blockchain engineer. Everything becomes faster and more affordable.
REasy is very impressive. For now, it focuses mostly on the Francophone African market. It makes payments and logistics simpler for small businesses that trade globally, with China or Dubai, for example. A lot happens behind the scenes in those trades, and if a small business does not get its money on time, the impact is huge. Today’s infrastructure does not really work for very small businesses, so they sort out payments and logistics informally, through a black market that sometimes works and sometimes does not, with delays and inefficiency. REasy brings everything into one digital place, so it is transparent and more affordable. Over time, as more businesses transact on the platform, REasy can use that data to help them get credit or financing.
Both sit in the fintech bucket, and neither solves the problem you would expect a normal fintech to solve. One serves small businesses, starting in Francophone Africa, with plans to cover most of Africa and other emerging markets. The other helps fintechs avoid the complexity of blockchain. They are completely different businesses in the same sector. My point is that there is so much opportunity. I challenge everyone to think more deeply about fintech, and financial infrastructure in particular, because there are so many inefficiencies.
You called cybersecurity and fraud a big white space. What would a company you would back there look like?
We are still looking, but we have a clear sense of what we want to see: deep domain expertise, a strong understanding of fraud risk and cybersecurity across several African markets, and the local knowledge and networks to support that.
The challenge is that the problem is so broad that startups in this space can end up offering many different products and custom services. That can push a business towards a consultancy model and make it harder to scale. Still, we are hopeful that AI can help companies build more focused products that scale.
What data or experience shaped your thesis?
Our thesis is not based on any one book or report. We spent one to two years researching the core barriers to capital moving into and out of Africa. The data is fragmented and spread across many places. We narrowed it down to the five pillars.
Our Bridging Borders with Africa series, on our website, takes each pillar and explains what the problem is and why it matters. Each article draws on 20 to 30 data points. The problem is complex and systemic. When we work on regulatory solutions or cybersecurity, that is not technically a fintech issue. We are looking at the whole system.
What advice would you give a pre-seed fintech founder who is raising right now?
The name of the game is staying in the game. Do not make raising money your north star. Focus on understanding your market and customers deeply, building something they value, and finding creative ways to make progress with the resources you have. That work can strengthen your case for funding even if the money arrives later than expected, and the experience will always be valuable. For fintech in particular, that foundation also means understanding your regulatory requirements, how you manage risk and the economics of serving your customers. You should be able to explain these clearly to investors, alongside your growth.
Also, build genuine relationships with investors instead of only reaching out when you need funding. We can tell. Where an investor offers thoughtful feedback, consider it, act where it makes sense, and keep them posted on your progress and what you have learned. A regular investor update is a simple way to keep that relationship going and help them see how your business is developing.
And remember that venture capital is one path among several, which may sound unusual coming from a VC. Depending on the business, grants or suitable debt may be a better fit. We keep relationships across those sources because our wider goal is to help build sustainable businesses and ecosystems.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution.
