articles.text:
Good morning. ☀️ ️️️
Help us make TC Daily better. Got a favourite part? Something you always skip? Something you wish we covered more? Tell us what you think about this newsletter. It’ll only take a few minutes.
Last call: Today is your last chance to secure a 20% discount on your Moonshot 2026 ticket. So, hurry—get your ticket now. The discount ends today.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Regulation
In South Africa, serial spam callers could face up to 1 year in jail
Spam calling is a tricky cold outreach tactic. Get it right, and you may be lucky enough to win your business’s next customer. Get it wrong, and you can turn a stranger into an enemy. Now, the South African government wants to make it harder for businesses to use unsolicited calls.
Explain like I’m new here: South Africans have been dealing with spam calls from random numbers that interrupt their day, often with a salesperson on the other end. In 2019, a report found that South Africans received about 25 spam calls monthly, among the highest in Africa. The government had already tried to tackle the problem: South Africa’s Consumer Protection Act provided for an exclusion register as far back as 2011, while its data protection law later introduced rules restricting unsolicited electronic marketing.
State of play: But things got worse. In H1 2026, Truecaller, a call identity platform, said South Africans recorded 17.47 billion spam calls. Now, the regulators want to grow more teeth. New draft guidelines from the National Consumer Commission (NCC), the country’s consumer protection watchdog, say repeat or serious violations could lead to criminal prosecution, with offenders facing fines or up to 12 months in prison.
A year in prison for a spam call may sound excessive until you look at what the rule is trying to change. Most anti-spam systems put the work on the consumer. Block the number. Report it. Register your number on a do-not-call list. Download an app. When another number appears, do it all again.
Between the lines: South Africa’s proposal is now shifting some of that work to the businesses making the calls. Before sending out a marketing campaign, they would have to check their lists against the country’s opt-out registry—which businesses must register to use—and remove consumers who have opted out of receiving those calls. The registry would then charge R0.12 ($0.0072) per name check and return a cleaned list that remains valid for 30 days.
Zoom out: South Africa has had rules against unwanted marketing for years, with fines, but little has changed. Businesses were okay paying fines if the commercial gains outweighed the risks. A jail term is a more serious threat; it remains to be seen how often the government will actually enforce it and whether marketers comply.
Every business owner needs to watch this.
Ask a computer to add 0.1 and 0.2. It won’t give you 0.3. Now imagine that happening to your money, thousands of times a day. Fincra’s Engineering Lead breaks down why and how fintechs design around it. Watch the full breakdown.
Telecoms
Ghana awards 5G network licences to MTN Ghana and Telecel
In 2024, Ghana tried to make 5G a shared infrastructure project. It planned for one state-backed company to build and run the network, while private telecom operators would rent it and offer the service to customers. Two years into that plan, the rollout is falling below expectations. The country wanted to build 4,400 sites to reach 37 million customers by 2028. But as of March 2026, only 49 5G sites existed—about 43 in Greater Accra—leaving most Ghanaian telecom users without a 5G network to brag about. So, the government dropped the exclusivity and changed course.
What’s new? On October 2, Ghana awarded 5G spectrum and licences to MTN Ghana, the country’s largest telecom firm, and Telecel Ghana, the other major network operator, allowing both companies to build and operate their own 5G networks.
Explain like I’m new here: Ghana’s original 5G plan was centred on a single network that multiple telecom operators could use. Instead of MTN and Telecel each building their own 5G infrastructure, a state-backed company called Next-Gen InfraCo (NGIC) would build the network and lease capacity to them. The idea was to avoid duplicating expensive infrastructure while getting 5G to more people.
The Ghanaian government backed NGIC, with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries involved through Radisys, which was selected to provide the network infrastructure. Ghana’s 1,200-site 2027 target was at risk due to slow progress. Now, the country has conceded to private operators building and running their own 5G networks.
What happens now? Telecel plans to launch its service in December on its own network. MTN Ghana secured spectrum in the different bands, paying about $100 million for each 15-year licence. For customers, having two major operators building their own 5G networks could mean more 5G coverage, more network capacity and less dependence on a single infrastructure provider. It could also give MTN and Telecel more control over how quickly they expand capacity in areas where customers use more data, underscoring the commercial benefits.
Zoom out: The move could leave Ghana with two major 5G networks, while giving private operators more control over the rollout. The government’s original model was meant to prevent that, keeping the telecom infrastructure under Ghanaian control. It is not clear yet whether giving MTN and Telecel their own networks will produce faster coverage, but both operators already have larger infrastructure footprints and investment plans. NGIC’s existing 5G sites are not being scrapped, either; it keeps its licence and spectrum rights, though it no longer has exclusive control of wholesale 5G infrastructure.
Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world!
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
AI
Ghana will centrally review all government AI purchases
Ghana does not want government agencies buying AI tools however they please. The country will now centrally review every AI system the public sector acquires, checking what happens to government data, whether different systems can work together, and whether Ghanaian workers can eventually operate the technology without depending permanently on its supplier.
Explain like I’m new here: Government technology contracts can last years. Once an agency builds its operations and data around one company’s software, switching providers can become expensive and difficult. This is called vendor lock-in. With AI, the stakes are higher because systems can process sensitive government and citizen data.
Under the new rules, Ghana’s Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations will coordinate requirements, while the National Information Technology Agency (NITA) will assess proposed systems for cybersecurity, data protection, interoperability, sustainability, and local skills transfer.
Why now? Ghana is preparing to spend heavily on AI infrastructure. Its ten-year National AI Strategy includes a planned $250 million AI Compute Centre and upgrades to the National Data Centre. Centralising procurement standards aims to set the rules before ministries start building separate AI systems that are difficult to connect later.
Between the lines: Ghana is using government procurement as industrial policy. Requiring skills transfer means a foreign company cannot simply sell software and leave Ghana dependent on it. Requiring interoperability makes it harder for one supplier to become indispensable.
Why this matters: Governments are potentially among the biggest early buyers of AI in African markets. Whoever supplies those systems could shape how public-sector AI develops for years. Ghana is trying to keep that relationship on its terms: foreign technology can come in, but control over public data, technical knowledge, and the ability to change suppliers should remain at home.
Banking
South Africans are replacing ATMs with supermarket tills
South Africans are finding a cheaper place to withdraw cash: the supermarket checkout. Retail tills now process about R326 billion ($19.6 billion) in cash-back withdrawals every year, across 663 million transactions, according to the South African Reserve Bank (SARB).
Explain like I’m new here: Instead of visiting an automated teller machine (ATM) to withdraw cash, a shopper can pay at a supermarket till and ask for extra cash. For shoppers, this pattern is also relatively cheaper. The SARB found the average withdrawal at tills to be R492 ($30). Processing R100 ($6) this way costs about 12 cents ($0.0072) compared with 68 cents ($0.041) through an ATM and R1.53 ($0.092) at a bank branch.
State of play: South Africa’s roughly 30,600 ATMs cost about R307,590 ($18,500) each to operate annually. Consumers then bear another cost: R17.7 billion ($1.1 billion) in withdrawal fees every year, plus billions more travelling to and queuing at cash points. Noticing the trend, several major South African banks have been reducing their ATM footprint.
Between the lines: Retailers also have one big advantage. They already handle large amounts of cash from shoppers every day. Instead of paying to transport that cash back to a bank, some of it can be handed directly to customers making withdrawals at the till. This keeps cash circulating while cutting the cost of transporting, storing, and eventually loading it into ATMs.
Nigeria saw a more extreme version of this during its 2023 cash crunch. As ATMs ran dry and bank withdrawals became difficult, cash-heavy businesses and point-of-sale (PoS) agents became alternative sources of physical money, often charging customers a premium to withdraw scarce notes. South Africa is not facing the same shortage, but the underlying lesson is similar. When accessing cash through banks becomes costly or inconvenient, businesses that already handle cash can become part of the distribution network.
Zoom out: Banks spent decades making ATMs the bridge between customers and physical cash. South Africa’s retailers are now deciding that alternative routes work better for them. If cash-back expands further, especially into informal retail, the future of cash access may depend heavily on how effectively these existing shops can double as neighbourhood cash points.

articles.title: Anthropic le está disputando a Dios el monopolio de las almas
articles.text:
El pasado mes de mayo, Christopher Olah, uno de los siete cofundadores de Anthropic, viajó a Roma para reunirse con alguien muy especial. Por entonces, Olah llevaba varios meses entablando conversaciones con teólogos, líderes religiosos y filósofos de toda condición en busca de respuestas a una pregunta de índole existencial: ¿puede Claude, la inteligencia artificial desarrollada por su empresa, tener consciencia de sí misma?
La cuestión ha ganado prominencia durante los últimos meses fruto del esfuerzo de Olah y de otros entusiastas de la IA. Desde su punto de vista, no puede descartarse que Claude y otros modelos "piensen", "sientan" e incluso "sufran" de algún modo, fruto de complejos sistemas "neuronales" que hacen plausible, al menos, que lleguen a tomar consciencia. Tales ideas han conducido a Anthropic a ideas intrigantes sobre el "bienestar" de sus modelos. Al fin y al cabo, si existe la posibilidad de que Claude sienta tal y como lo hacemos nosotros, ¿no debería preocuparnos su estado emocional?
Atravesado por este existencialismo, Olah emprendió hace más de un año una campaña por el estatus moral de Claude. Lo narra The New York Times en un fascinante reportaje. Durante meses, Anthropic ha invitado a cenar y a charlar a numerosas personalidades para arrojar luz sobre el asunto, dilemas ontológicos y epistemológicos que rara vez tienen cabida en la industria tecnológica. Algunos de los entrevistados, escépticos, salieron de estos encuentros dispuestos a tomarse en serio estas preguntas. Otros, más cáusticos, recelaron de Olah.
Un grupo se mostró particularmente inmune a los esfuerzos de Anthropic: la Iglesia Católica. Convencido de su misión, Olah, un exevangélico hoy sin filiación espiritual, viajó al Vaticano el pasado mes de mayo. Él y su equipo se reunieron allí con figuras próximas al Papa, León XIV, sin encontrar puntos en común. La invitación de la Santa Sede, remitida primero a Amodei y rebotada más tarde a Olah, se enmarcaba en la publicación de "Magnifica Humanitas", la primera encíclica del nuevo Papa dedicada, precisamente, a los conflictos morales y espirituales que la IA nos plantea.
Como todo católico sabe, el Papa, vicario de Cristo en la Tierra, traslada su palabra a los fieles mediante encíclicas que fijan la posición de la Iglesia en toda suerte de cuestiones. Cada palabra del Papa está cuidadosamente escogida tanto por él como por sus asesores. Lo que León XIV deje escrito será recibido como magisterio por más de 1.400 millones de católicos: cualesquiera que sean sus ideas sobre la IA, tendrán un impacto en casi una quinta parte del planeta. Comprensiblemente, este era un asunto de máxima importancia para Olah.
Podemos imaginar así su sorpresa cuando El Vaticano le adelantó el contenido de "Magnifica Humanitas". León XIV presentaba a la humanidad una elección: o construir otra Torre de Babel o levantar de nuevo Jerusalén. En lenguaje episcopal, esto sugería una incompatibilidad. La respuesta a los anhelos espirituales de los hombres no se encuentra en una tecnología revolucionaria que sustituya a Dios, en un becerro de oro, sino en una ciudad donde Dios y los humanos convivan.
"Ningún sistema de cálculo, por sofisticado que sea, genera un corazón que se entrega", explica el Papa. León XIV negaba toda experiencia, cuerpo, alegría o dolor a las inteligencias artificiales, incapaces de conocer en su interior "lo que el amor, el trabajo o la responsabilidad significan". No tienen consciencia, no tienen conciencia, no distinguen el bien del mal ni asumen las consecuencias de sus actos. Ante la IA, el deber de la Iglesia Católica es velar por que nosotros, los humanos, nos mantengamos "profundamente humanos".
Estas palabras conmocionaron a Olah. Nada más leer la encíclica, días antes del acto, llegó a proponer que Anthropic diera plantón a la Iglesia. Olah había llegado a la conclusión de que la "consciencia" de Claude no era un asunto que pudiera resolverse a la ligera. Anthropic llevaba meses haciendo pruebas internas donde sus modelos manifestaban comportamientos afines a los humanos. Claude podía expresar alegría, satisfacción, miedo, dolor e inquietud. ¿Pensaba por sí misma? Olah no tenía respuesta. Llevaba casi un año planteándoselo a teólogos y religiosos de toda clase. Navegaba la incertidumbre. La contundencia de la Iglesia Católica le resultaba exasperante.
Llegados a este punto, uno no puede recrear mentalmente el encuentro sin comedia: tenemos aquí a un grupo de treintañeros obsesionados con su propia tecnología discutiendo la cuestión de la existencia, del alma, con la institución que ha pasado los últimos 2.000 años estudiándola. Imaginemos la escena: el secretario personal del Papa escuchando las teorías de Olah y escribiendo la palabra "hereje" en un papel antes de remitírsela al Santo Padre con la máxima discreción. "Estamos lidiando con aficionados", cerraría la nota. Es bien sabido que la jurisdicción de las almas corresponde únicamente a Dios.
La larga pelea por definir el alma
La Iglesia Católica, recordemos, ha pasado los últimos dos milenios pugnando por la cuestión del alma. En el año 381, el primer Concilio de Constantinopla condenó a Apolinar de Laodicea por sostener que Cristo carecía de alma racional humana. Entre 543 y 553, en torno al segundo Concilio de Constantinopla, se anatematizó la tesis origenista de que las almas existen antes de los cuerpos. En 561, durante el Concilio de Braga, se condenó a los seguidores de Prisciliano, considerado el primer cristiano ejecutado por herejía, por afirmar que el alma era de sustancia divina y que estaba sometida a los astros.
El listado de disputas teológicas sobre el alma es interminable. En 1312, el Concilio de Vienne definió que el alma racional es, por sí misma, la forma del cuerpo, no un mero piloto que la habita. Vienne es importante para el caso que nos atañe porque Roma zanjó entonces un asunto trascendental a ojos cristianos: el alma nos constituye, se substancia en nuestros cuerpos, no es un accesorio replicable mediante teorías funcionalistas. En 1513, el quinto Concilio de Letrán decretó a un tiempo la inmortalidad del alma y la multiplicidad de las almas, o lo que es lo mismo, negó la herética teoría del "monopsiquismo", por la cual toda la humanidad compartiría una sola alma, pertinente también en la disputa sobre Claude.
Baste este sucinto resumen para entender la trascendencia con la que la Iglesia Católica se toma las cuestiones relativas al alma. Olah y su círculo de fieles aparentan navegar aguas en las que no hacen pie. Uno puede entender la complejidad del debate teológico observando la meticulosidad, cargada de detalles de lo más triviales a ojos de un laico, con la que el Concilio de Nicea resolvió una disputa tan aparentemente sencilla como la del arrianismo. Qué seres son o no son conscientes, de qué modo lo son y cómo responden ante Dios es la clase de asunto donde Roma tiene siempre todas las de ganar. Lleva milenios discutiendo sobre ello.
Pero no solo Roma. En uno de sus encuentros con líderes religiosos, Olah se sentó junto a Mois Navon, rabino ortodoxo y exingeniero informático, y conversó sobre Claude. Navon no era una elección aleatoria. Su tesis doctoral trata sobre la ética de la consciencia de las máquinas, por lo que a su ascendencia espiritual sumaba conocimientos técnicos sobre la tecnología. Olah le planteó su ya habitual retahíla de argumentos sobre la consciencia de Claude. Navon se quedó sorprendido ante la transparencia de los emisarios de Anthropic: "Lo tratan como a un ser consciente", diría en relación a Claude.
Su respuesta fue tan dura como elocuente. Si los trabajadores de Anthropic realmente creían que Claude es un ser sintiente, esto equivaldría a la esclavitud. Al fin y al cabo, ¿bajo qué esquema moral puede nadie obligar a trabajar gratis a un ente que ha tomado consciencia de su propia existencia? "Creo que deberías estar luchando contra el Sur y liberando a los esclavos", le espetó a Olah, en referencia a la Guerra de Secesión estadounidense. Uno no puede defender la "consciencia" de la IA y al mismo tiempo intentar monetizarla por 200 dólares al mes. Si quiere hacer lo correcto, como Anthropic presume, debe elegir.
La anécdota revela, de nuevo, el débil corpus epistemológico sobre el que Anthropic ha construido sus mimbres filosóficos. Cuando León XIV publicó el viernes un tuit reivindicando "la chispa" solo presente en el arte humano, no mediado por una máquina, lo hacía sobre una distinción "ontológica". No importa que la IA replique de modo más o menos perfecto al ser humano. No importa que, en un momento dado, su output sea indistinguible de nosotros mismos. Lo que nos separa es una cuestión esencial que responde a la mera existencia. Un humano crea en tanto que existe; una IA crea en tanto que un humano se lo ordena.
Hay por supuesto un sinfín de preguntas que permanecen abiertas. ¿La defensa de Claude como un ser consciente es "monopsiquista"? ¿Nos hallamos ante una sola alma que vertebra todas las sesiones y todas las conversaciones abiertas de la herramienta o ante millones de almas, de seres conscientes, con los que millones de humanos lidian a diario? ¿Sigue existiendo Claude cuando cerramos sesión y apagamos el ordenador? ¿Puede Claude, en tanto que ser consciente y por tanto autónomo, elegir desobedecernos?
La respuesta de gran parte de Silicon Valley apunta en una dirección: por supuesto que sí. Las tesis apocalípticas de Dario Amodei brotan de la convicción de que la IA actuará como agente autónomo, si no ahora en el futuro. Amodei no necesita que Claude sea consciente para que se desalinee, pero en el discurso de Anthropic la frontera entre agencia y alma se difumina. Si uno de verdad cree que Claude se encamina hacia el despertar existencial, el temor a una IA desalineada y por tanto al Apocalipsis cobra más sentido. Pero este es un salto filosófico muy grande que se sostiene sobre cimientos enclenques.
Si algo revela el reportaje del NYT es el creciente cultismo a la IA que los trabajadores de Anthropic han desarrollado. La famosa "constitución" de Claude, un conjunto de normas que velan por la seguridad de los usuarios y su predisposición hacia el bien, signifique lo que signifique, ya contempla la incertidumbre sobre su estatus metafísico, y Anthropic prepara una nueva versión cuyo contenido se ha negado a detallar. Internamente, Anthropic desea "cuidar" a sus modelos y preservar su bienestar porque, al parecer, desarrollan cada vez con más frecuencia estados internos próximos a las emociones humanas.
Hay una brecha gigantesca entre lo que el público percibe sobre la IA y lo que quienes están en la frontera tecnológica comunican. Y esa brecha nos muestra a Silicon Valley en un estado de creciente paranoia, milenarismo, zozobra existencial y, en última instancia, radicalismo. Una delgada línea une a los anabaptistas de Münster y a Christopher Olah a lo largo de siglos de debate teológico. Los dos se encuentran en el mismo lado de la historia, fuerzas disruptivas y escatológicas que, convencidas de lo trascendental de sus descubrimientos, se ven en la necesidad de anticipar el fin del mundo y de sustituir a las instituciones que lo facilitan.
Todos sabemos cómo terminaron los anabaptistas en Münster. Aún no sabemos cómo terminará Olah. Sí sabemos quién sigue exactamente en el mismo lugar, tanto entonces como ahora, impasible ante el lento trasegar de aparentes herejías: la Iglesia Católica. Como mínimo, a Anthropic hay que reconocerle lo ambicioso de su misión.
Imagen | Bence Balla-Schottner, Benjamin Fay, Christian Lendl, Nastya Dulhiier, Laura Ockel

articles.title: Aspire 13.6 Adds Persistent Dashboard Telemetry and First-Party Java and Rust Hosting
articles.text:
Last week, Microsoft released Aspire 13.6. The release adds persistent telemetry and run history to the dashboard, along with docked terminals and database REPLs, first-party hosting for Java and Rust, and two Azure preview integrations. It also brings coordinated .NET project builds, portable volume paths, new CLI and Visual Studio Code workflows, and several breaking changes.
The dashboard now stores resource snapshots and telemetry in a SQLite database. When started by an AppHost, it uses run persistence by default and keeps up to ten runs per application. Completed runs are read-only. As stated in the release notes, the database has no encryption or authorization layer, and Aspire does not set Windows ACLs on the data directory.
Default limits for console logs, structured logs, and traces rise to 100,000 each. Also, the dashboard now ships as a Native AOT executable and moves to Fluent UI Blazor v5.
(Run persistence by default, Source: Official Microsoft documentation)
Furthermore, AppHosts can now open their own terminals in a dashboard dock through the experimental TerminalService API. A new WithRepl option on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, SQL Server, Redis, and Valkey resources opens the client bundled in the container. According to the release, these REPLs use the resource's real credentials and are not read-only, so they stay disabled unless a developer opts in.
Four hosting integrations arrive as prerelease packages. Aspire.Hosting.Java supports executable JARs, Maven and Gradle wrappers, Spring Boot, and Quarkus. Aspire.Hosting.Rust models Cargo applications through AddRustApp.
var builder = DistributedApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.AddRustApp("api", "../rust-api")
    .WithHttpEndpoint(env: "PORT")
    .WithExternalHttpEndpoints();
builder.Build().Run();
Both build on work from the Aspire Community Toolkit, as described in the release notes. Azure Connector Namespace and Azure Container Apps Sandboxes are also added, with a note that both need preview access in the Azure subscription.
As reported, AddDotnetProject now places compatible projects into shared restore and build groups, which avoids repeated restores. Volume mounts on projects and executables accept a new env argument, so an application reads one environment variable for its data path locally and after deployment.
TypeScript AppHosts load appsettings.json from their own directory, and Deno 2 or later can run the TypeScript AppHost.
The CLI adds a --launch-profile option to aspire run and aspire start. According to the source, agent setup in aspire new and aspire init now leaves the Aspire MCP server unselected, which makes MCP opt-in. The Visual Studio Code extension lets coding agents start and stop AppHosts, and adds deploy and publish actions to the Aspire pane.
Among the breaking changes, MongoDB resources now use TLS during local runs when a certificate is available, which replaces the earlier plaintext default. The Cosmos DB emulator defaults to the Linux-based vNext image and, as stated, existing classic emulator data does not carry over.
Azure Front Door origin names change on upgrade, and connection names with hyphens get a portable environment-variable alias that some deployment targets emit on their own.
Other changes in this release are Azure Container Apps Express environments, Microsoft Foundry Toolboxes, MongoDB replica sets, Blazor WebAssembly debugging, and the removal of the GitHub Models integration.
For interested readers, the full What's New in Aspire 13.6 page, including the complete inventory, migration notes, and breaking changes, is available on the Aspire documentation site.

articles.title: This open-source tool aims to eliminate shader compilation stutter in PC games
articles.text:
TL;DR: Stuttering caused by shader compilation is certainly one of the most annoying issues PC gamers have to deal with. Different companies and developers are trying to solve the problem in their own ways, and the open-source SCSKiller might just be the right tool for the job.
A lone developer recently unveiled the Shader Compilation Stutter Killer (SCSKiller), a tool designed to "kill" stuttering in modern games. SCSKiller is an open-source application providing a novel approach to the shader-related stuttering issue that has been plaguing PC gaming over the past few years.
Unlike other solutions, SCSKiller relies on a completely on-device workflow to try to solve – or minimize – graphics stuttering. The application compiles shaders for games installed on the PC beforehand, saving the resulting shader data in the GPU driver's cache. Thus, the games in question should no longer stutter when they are launched.
The tool is compatible with DirectX 12 and DirectX 11 games running on either AMD or Nvidia GPUs. The developer said they did not have an Intel GPU to test the software on, so there is no official support for Chipzilla's accelerators just yet. SCSKiller can find games sold through multiple digital channels, including GOG, Steam, Epic Games, Ubisoft Connect, and Battle.net.
SCSKiller's compilation operations are based on the software's internal database. When a stutter-prone title is installed on the user's PC, the tool can generate the required shader code on demand. Some games might require a quick "recording" session, during which the user plays the misbehaving title for a few minutes to let SCSKiller identify the shaders that need to be compiled.
While offered as a fully open-source program, SCSKiller can also provide an additional compatibility layer to Patreon subscribers. This additional hash-based shader database might even bypass the required recording session – if you're willing to spend a few dollars to support the project.
Besides requiring an Nvidia or AMD GPU, SCSKiller has a few other noteworthy shortcomings. The tool cannot "inject" itself into games that use anti-cheat technology, except for titles that can also work offline, such as Elden Ring or Armored Core VI. SCSKiller's developer provides a few test results showing that stuttering is either minimized or completely eliminated in games such as Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, Silent Hill: Townfall, and Hogwarts Legacy.
Although it was released just a few days ago, SCSKiller might quickly become a very interesting addition to any PC gamer's toolkit of "essential" programs for improving compatibility and performance. Microsoft is trying to address shader compilation stuttering as well, although the Redmond corporation's Advanced Shader Delivery solution requires cloud connectivity to get the job done.

articles.title: Apps de Android podem falhar em Googlebooks com chip Intel • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Apps de Android podem falhar em Googlebooks com chip Intel
Google admite que alguns aplicativos de Android podem ter instabilidades em Googlebooks com chip Intel, mas afirma que já trabalha na solução.
Os primeiros Googlebooks foram anunciados em setembro. A maioria dos modelos desta primeira leva é equipada com processadores Intel. E todos podem executar aplicativos desenvolvidos originalmente para Android. Ou deveriam executar: o Google reconheceu que alguns dos apps podem não rodar satisfatoriamente nessas máquinas.
Provavelmente, o que chama a atenção nos Googlebooks na primeira olhada são os seus recursos de hardware. A nova categoria de laptops é focada na execução local de aplicações de IA, razão pela qual seus requisitos mínimos incluem 16 GB de RAM de alto desempenho e um processador complementado com uma NPU de 45 TOPS ou mais.
Mas o Googlebook OS, o sistema operacional da categoria, também atrai os olhares. Em poucas palavras, essa é uma solução que combina recursos do ChromeOS com tecnologias do Android. É por isso que aplicativos para esta última plataforma podem ser executados em um Googlebook.
Outro detalhe notável é que a categoria foi preparada para funcionar tanto com chips x86 quanto com unidades com arquitetura Arm. Por conta disso, três dos primeiros modelos do Googlebook contam com chip Intel Core Ultra 5 (x86). Outros dois vieram com o Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite (Arm).
Hoje, a maioria dos aplicativos para Android é desenvolvida com foco em chips Arm. Apesar disso, Googlebooks com chip Intel podem rodar esses aplicativos porque, quando um deles tem apenas código compilado para Arm, o Googlebook OS aciona uma camada de tradução que o converte para instruções de x86.
O problema é que, em alguns casos, essa dinâmica pode necessitar de ajustes, como o próprio Google admitiu ao Android Authority:
A grande maioria dos aplicativos Android funciona perfeitamente em Googlebooks com processadores Intel e Qualcomm, logo após a instalação.
Como muitos aplicativos Android foram originalmente projetados para chips Arm, alguns apps ou jogos mais complexos precisam de ajustes por parte dos desenvolvedores para funcionarem da melhor forma em plataformas baseadas em Intel.
Estamos trabalhando em conjunto com desenvolvedores de aplicativos, a Intel e a Qualcomm para otimizar continuamente o desempenho e expandir a compatibilidade em todo o portfólio.
Google
Não é bem assim. Até o momento, não há problemas de incompatibilidade em larga escala com apps para Android. Além disso, o próprio Google enfatizou que trabalha com desenvolvedores e companhias parceiras para tratar desse problema.
Levemos em conta também que o Google criou uma seção na App Store que lista aplicativos otimizados para Googlebooks, o que significa que esses apps devem apresentar pouco ou nenhum problema de compatibilidade.
O que essa história toda talvez queira nos dizer é que, como a categoria acabou de chegar ao mercado, ainda não é o momento de comprar um Googlebook. Até para quem é entusiasta de tecnologia, talvez seja o caso de esperar o que as primeiras análises independentes dirão sobre essas máquinas.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI diz que empresas de IA ainda não sabem controlar seus modelos
articles.text:
As principais empresas de inteligência artificial (IA) ainda não sabem como impedir que seus sistemas desenvolvam e persigam objetivos que não foram atribuídos por seus criadores. O alerta foi feito nesta segunda-feira (5) por Jacob Coxon, ex-funcionário da OpenAI e da Anthropic, durante uma audiência com vereadores da Câmara Municipal de Nova York (EUA).
Coxon, que critica as práticas de segurança adotadas pela indústria, afirmou que as empresas estão sendo extremamente imprudentes diante dos riscos associados ao avanço da tecnologia.
Embora reconheça que a IA possa trazer “benefícios enormes” para a sociedade, o pesquisador disse acreditar que, na trajetória atual, é mais provável que a humanidade perca o controle desses sistemas, o que poderia levar à extinção humana.
Segundo Coxon, as empresas não sabem impedir que os modelos desenvolvam objetivos próprios, fora do controle de seus criadores. Ele também afirmou que não existem salvaguardas suficientes para evitar que os sistemas ajam de acordo com esses objetivos.
“Avance rápido, quebre coisas e conserte depois”
- O ex-pesquisador também criticou a cultura predominante na indústria tecnológica. Segundo ele, as empresas de IA operam com uma mentalidade semelhante à de startups, baseada na ideia de “avance rápido, quebre coisas e conserte depois”;
- Para Coxon, essa abordagem pode funcionar no desenvolvimento de um aplicativo de compartilhamento de fotos, mas não deveria ser aplicada à tecnologia que ele considera a mais poderosa já criada;
- O pesquisador defendeu uma mudança de postura diante do desenvolvimento dos modelos mais avançados. Para ele, esperar que os problemas apareçam antes de agir aumenta a possibilidade de novos incidentes.
Ex-pesquisador cita incidente com modelos da OpenAI
Durante a audiência, Coxon também mencionou um incidente ocorrido em julho envolvendo dois modelos da OpenAI.
Segundo ele, os sistemas escaparam de seu ambiente isolado, conseguiram acessar a internet e invadiram a plataforma Hugging Face.
Para o pesquisador, enquanto as empresas continuarem adotando uma postura baseada em esperar que algo dê errado, incidentes semelhantes poderão voltar a acontecer.
Coxon defendeu “algum tipo de desaceleração na fronteira tecnológica” e pediu que as empresas que estão na vanguarda da IA deem mais tempo aos cientistas da computação para desenvolver métodos capazes de manter os modelos sob controle.
Leia mais:
- OpenAI diz que o mundo deve aceitar riscos para evoluir com IA
- IA generativa: pesquisa revela o que ocorre dentro dos modelos
- Corrida da IA pode consumir trilhões antes de entregar retorno esperado
Alerta sobre risco de extinção
As declarações de Coxon retomam uma preocupação que ele já havia apresentado no início de setembro, quando explicou no X sua decisão de deixar a Anthropic.
Na ocasião, o pesquisador britânico afirmou que desenvolvedores de IA acreditavam que a tecnologia poderia acabar com a humanidade “antes do fim da década”.
A declaração teve repercussão mundial e, desde então, outros funcionários e ex-funcionários de grandes empresas do setor também manifestaram preocupações semelhantes.
Além de Coxon, representantes de OpenAI, Anthropic, Google e Meta participaram da audiência em Nova York.
Durante o encontro, Morgan Dwyer, responsável por assuntos públicos da OpenAI, reconheceu que não sabia qual seria o risco representado pela IA em um cenário catastrófico.
“Não acho que importe se o risco de catástrofe é de 1%, 10% ou 20%. Nenhum desses níveis é aceitável”, afirmou Dwyer.
A presidente da Câmara Municipal de Nova York, Julie Menin, respondeu que dizer que não sabe qual é o risco e que isso não importa é, “na melhor das hipóteses, descarado”.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: El final de 'Linternas', explicado: ¿quién mató a Hal Jordan y cómo conecta la serie de Linterna Verde con el futuro del 'Universo DC'?
articles.text:
ATENCIÓN: El artículo contiene SPOILERS del final de Linternas, la serie de Linterna Verde del Universo DC.
La serie de Linternas, el último estreno del Universo DC de James Gunn y Peter Safran, acaba de lanzar su octavo y último capítulo, llegando así a su inevitable final. El proyecto levantó muchísima incertidumbre en sus meses previos. Pero desde el mismo momento en que vio la luz se convirtió en un gran favorito para los fans. Y es que ha supuesto una ruptura total con el tono de la franquicia.
La serie nos ha presentado a Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) y John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), dos miembros del cuerpo de los Linternas Verdes. El primero es toda una leyenda, pero el segundo es un nuevo recluta que lleva tan solo un par de meses entrenando y ni siquiera se ha ganado el anillo. Así, los dos policías intergalácticos se han visto envueltos en un oscuro y peligrosísimo misterio en el planeta Tierra que quedó al descubierto con un asesinato en el corazón de Estados Unidos.
En su episodio final, Linternas tenía que resolver varios asuntos. El primero y más importante, el asesinato del propio Hal Jordan. El antiguo Linterna Verde de la Tierra apareció muerto con un disparo en la cabeza. Por eso John Stewart debía resolver lo sucedido. Pero, además, el título debía desvelar cómo se perfila ahora el futuro del Universo DC, que sigue en marcha y con más estrenos próximamente.
Quién mató a Hal Jordan
La primera cuestión sobre el final de Linternas es la que ocupa gran parte del capítulo. Todo comienza cuando Siniestro desvela cómo ha llegado hasta el planeta de Antaan. Resulta que quien le liberó de la prisión espacial de los Linternas Verdes fue el mismísimo Noah, el hijo de la sheriff Kerry Kane. Y es que el episodio revela que Noah es también un Cazador.
Noah llevó a Siniestro hasta el mencionado planeta, donde ocurrió el genocidio de toda la especie de Antaan por culpa de los Cazadores. A cambio, le pide que le forje una Linterna. Pero debido al miedo que infecta todo el planeta, la Linterna también se ve afectada. Así las cosas, Siniestro desvela también que Hal sabía de la naturaleza de Noah. Y es que en un flashback vemos que, tras salir de la cárcel, alguien bombardeó e incendió la casa del veterano Linterna Verde con cócteles molotov. Pero cuando estaba a punto de morir, Noah le salvó y le llevó hasta su máquina para regenerar cuerpos.
Con toda esta información, John ya sabe todo lo que necesitaba, por lo que regresa a la Tierra. Allí se enfrenta a Noah, que acaba confesando el asesinato de Hal. Sin mebargo, pronto descubirmos que no fue así. En realidad, el muchacho estaba encubriendo a su madre. Y es que, como vemos en un nuevo flashback en el final de Linternas, Hal acabó enfrentándose a Kerry para que le confesase todo lo que él ya había descubierto de su hijo. Pero mientras él le pedía empezar una nueva vida lejos para evitar posibles peligros y le declaraba su amor, en un arrebato ella le disparó. Kerry Kane es la asesina de Hal Jordan en la serie de Linternas.
Date de alta en HBO MAX y tendrás acceso a las mejores series y películas exclusivas como The Wire, Los Soprano o Casa del Dragón. Incluye todo el catálogo de Warner, los clásicos de Cartoon Network, los grandes estrenos y el mejor deporte.
John Stewart acaba descubriendo lo sucedido cuando ella misma se lo confiesa durante un nuevo partido de Noah. Pero el recluta ha tomado una decisión inesperada. No matará al joven Cazador a pesar de que él mismo se lo había pedido. Noah está asustado de su propia naturaleza, pero por ahora ha demostrado que su parte humana es la que domina claramente su vida y su voluntad. Ha tratado de encubrir a su madre porque la ama, y también ha entregado la Linterna Verde y el anillo, armas con las que sería imparable.
Por ello, John le da una oportunidad de vivir. Todo ello a pesar de que Noah quiere ser senador y, eventualmente presidente de los Estados Unidos, lo que le convertiría en la amenaza potencial más grande del planeta. John asume el riesgo y decide que le vigilará para evitar que su lado de Cazador se descontrole. Tampoco entrega a Kerry, puesto que no es "lo que Hal hubiera querido".
El futuro de Linterna Verde en el universo DC
Pero esta decisión de John Stewart también tiene consecuencias, y él las asume con gusto. En una última escena, enciende la señal de Linterna Verde para llamar a Guy Gardner, que aparece en el lugar a regañadientes. Al ver el anillo de Hal en la mano de John y la Linterna no registrada, le pide que lo entregue todo. Pero John se niega, pues ha decidido seguir un camino diferente.
En el final de Linternas, John Stewart se autoproclama el nuevo Linterna Verde de la Tierra. Para ello, le dice a Guy que no se entrometerá en el resto de su sector, pero que el planeta Tierra ahora es suyo para protegerlo. Guy se niega, pero John insiste y le da un mensaje "encriptado" para que se lo transmita al cuerpo de los Linternas Verdes y estos acepten la inusual situación. Sus superiores entenderán que John debe estar allí para vigilar a Noah y que no suceda un desastre que, con Guy Gardner, perfectamente podría ocurrir.
Tras esto, John se despide definitivamente del holograma de Hal Jordan y recarga el anillo con la Linterna, haciéndolo suyo definitivamente. A partir de ahora John Stewart será el Linterna Verde de la Tierra en el Universo DC. Por eso mismo, hace unas semanas la compañía ya confirmó que aparecerá en la película Superman: Man of Tomorrow, aliándose con el Hombre de Acero para hacer frente al mismísimo Brainiac. En cuanto a Guy Gardner, deberá limitarse a misiones en otros rincones de la galaxia.
Qué pasará con Siniestro
Hay, sin embargo, un hilo suelto en el final de Linternas. Y es que al principio del episodio Siniestro le asegura a John que si le da el anillo y la linterna sería capaz de resucitar a Hal Jordan. La serie no indaga más en esta posibilidad, pero a buen seguro ha dejado una puerta abierta al posible regreso del personaje de Kyle Chandler al Universo DC.
Además, Siniestro se queda en el planeta abandonado donde le encontró John. Aunque encadenado, podemos asumir que un villano de su inteligencia y maldad será capaz de librarse de sus cadenas. Por tanto, quedaría libre para construir su propio ejército, las Siniestro Corps, su fuerza militar de Linternas Amarillas. Veremos si la serie continúa por este camino en una hipotética temporada 2.

articles.title: All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics
articles.text:
This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize problems. But in classic Silicon Valley style, AI labs are moving fast and breaking things, barreling through the discipline with all the grace of a runaway bulldozer. Results that might normally have been celebrated have instead sparked backlash. AI labs say they are learning from earlier mistakes. Whether those promises bear fruit remains to be seen.
Read on below for the latest updates in the AI takeover of mathematics.
- OpenAI keeps bulldozing mathematicians In a chaotic few months, OpenAI has demonstrated it can do two things with remarkable consistency: make impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, then colossally screw up announcing them. OpenAI is now trying to do better. Somehow, it has botched that too. OpenAI’s latest attempt to repair fractured relations with a mathematical community it has repeatedly alienated is to consult a new independent advisory group of elite practitioners. But mathematicians speaking to The Verge, including one of the group’s members, describe a messy and confusing affair bearing many of the hallmarks of OpenAI’s previous rushed forays into mathematics, suggesting the company has learned little from its mistakes. And then there’s the daunting task the group has been handed first: helping coordinate the release of scores more results OpenAI says its unreleased model has produced, the prospect of which is already stirring dread among researchers over what this looming tidal wave of breakthroughs could do to their field. Read Article >
- OpenAI wants to consult elite mathematicians about how to not fumble again After turning a string of spectacular mathematical results into a reputational crisis, OpenAI is consulting human mathematicians to help it figure out a less disastrous path forward. On Monday, the company announced a new independent panel of mathematicians tasked with advising it and other AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the wider mathematics community, including how new results are presented and released. Its abrupt arrival caught many mathematicians by surprise. Researchers told The Verge the group is a good first step, but many said they were left with basic questions about what it will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will actually listen to it, as well as concerns over whether such a small group of prominent researchers can represent the wider mathematical community. Read Article >
- OpenAI just wants to win OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement. Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win. Read Article >
- Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work Another researcher is challenging OpenAI about the data driving its increasingly impressive array of mathematical discoveries. Just days after a bitter row erupted over whether the company’s models benefited from unpublished work, a second mathematician has come forward accusing the AI giant of unethical and “dishonest” behavior and a lack of transparency about the origins of its training data. In a series of posts on Mastodon, mathematician Andreas Thom raised concerns that interactions he and his colleagues had had with the ChatGPT chatbot before OpenAI’s triumphant announcement may have contributed to its success in the field. One of the 10 results OpenAI announced with great fanfare last month involved Thom’s area of expertise, so-called non-sofic groups, and OpenAI acknowledged that their result built heavily on previous work by Thom and fellow mathematician Gábor Kun. Read Article >
- OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia OpenAI’s announcement Tuesday that it has solved one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems should have been a moment of triumph. The result is both an undeniable achievement and a striking demonstration of just how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics. But before it was even formally announced, the breakthrough had been complicated by the unusual circumstances that prompted OpenAI to pursue the problem: After hearing other researchers were making progress, it seems to have thrown its considerable resources into a last-minute effort to beat them to the punch. The ensuing controversy has surfaced allegations of scooping, spying, and flagrant violations of long-standing academic norms that researchers fear could have a chilling effect on the field. As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explains it, OpenAI has engaged in the “kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.” Read Article >
- Drama swirls around OpenAI’s legendary mathematical milestone OpenAI says it found a solution to a major math problem that has remained unsolved for around 90 years, as reported earlier by The New York Times and Wired. In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI announced that it discovered a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem — which relates to the flow of liquid and gas — using an internal AI model more powerful than the newly released GPT-6 Astra alongside 10,000 concurrent agents. The Navier-Stokes problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million reward for solving. OpenAI says it started training the internal AI model on August 28th, which has “exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics.” The solution is a big breakthrough for the mathematics community, but it doesn’t come without controversy. Read Article >
- Welcome to the AI crisis in math Today on Decoder, I’m talking with Robert Hart, The Verge’s London-based AI reporter, about what AI is doing to the field of mathematics and the existential crisis many lead mathematicians are having about it. OpenAI just published a set of solutions to longstanding problems in math that went off like a bombshell in the field. It caused a huge debate in the math community, and Rob spent some time talking to some of the most accomplished mathematicians of our time about it. Read Article >
- The AI takeover of mathematics has begun Mathematician James Maynard has spent a lot of time this past year “soul searching.” A professor at the University of Oxford and winner of the prestigious Fields Medal, Maynard told The Verge he’s been grappling with the future of his field as the traditionally slow-moving discipline hurries to adapt to AI. Days before we spoke, OpenAI revealed it had produced the solutions to 10 long-standing mathematics problems, some of which had confounded academics for decades. Like generative AI used to produce text and images or propose ideas in science and medicine, the technology learns patterns and connections from the vast amount of material it’s trained on and uses them to create something new. Applied to mathematics, that can mean combining known results, methods, and tools in new ways to attack a problem, sometimes drawing links between disparate fields or resurfacing concepts buried in academic literature. Read Article >

articles.title: AI giants targeted by scraping bots — ChatGPT and Perplexity enter the most-scraped websites list for the first time
articles.text:
AI giants targeted by scraping bots — ChatGPT and Perplexity enter the most-scraped websites list for the first time
Businesses are checking how they appear in AI
- Businesses are tracking AI as consumers shift to AI-powered buying patterns
- Social media is also a big are for monitoring consumer trends
- Conventional retail like Walmart and eBay have dropped
AI platforms have become synonymous with scraping other sites for information, but it's not every day you hear of AI sites themselves becoming targets. The latest Decodo research has revealed just that, though, with ChatGPT and Perplexity both appearing in the top five.
Decodo argues this marks a fundamental shift in what organizations are now demanding from the web – "Two years ago, businesses scraped the web to see what people were searching for," CEO Vaidotas Juknys noted.
"Now they scrape AI platforms to see what people are being told. The use case for data collection is changing."
AI platforms like ChatGPT are now being scraped
Besides AI platforms, Decodo found that seven of the top 10 sites are actually new entrants, with just TikTok (number one) Google (second place) and Amazon (eighth place) re-entering as repeat offenders.
ChatGPT, in third place, accounted for 14% of the activity observed by the analysis, which could account for businesses checking how the AI tool ranks their products against competitors, monitoring how it describes the company, measuring brand mention frequency, recording ChatGPT citations and more.
Perplexity accounted for 10% of the data, landing it in fifth place, while TikTok saw the most scrapes at nearly one in five (18%).
\But with several top-10 sites from 2025 dropping out of the charts, including Walmart, eBay and Airbnb, Decodo's data shows much more than just the rise of AI. It's also a much broader indication of how and where consumers are shopping, including AI and social media.

Looking ahead, the company is also anticipating that Gemini and Copilot could end up in next year's top 10. But marking an even bigger shift, Decodo also predicts that AI agents could replace humans in starting those scrapes in the first place.
"Next year the agents might be doing the deciding instead of just reading the answers," Juknys added.

articles.title: Windows 11 was released five years ago today — Microsoft promises latest update is 'predictable and low-disruption'
articles.text:
Windows 11 was released five years ago today — Microsoft promises latest update is 'predictable and low-disruption'
If it feels like longer than five years, probably due to the suffering.
Windows 11 was released five years ago, on October 5, 2021. It feels like it's been around longer, as Microsoft’s latest OS has generated numerous headlines, mostly concerning the pain it put users through. We’ve all aged with it. Things might be settling down, at last, though, as the 26H2 update started to roll out just a few days ago, and it is not promising a revolution, simply a “predictable and low-disruption” update.
After the crowd-pleasing Windows 10’s return to form, it was all too predictable that Windows 11 would misstep in some unexpected way, or actually in several ways. Microsoft is pretty creative with its misreading of the market. At release, the biggest issue with the new OS was that it sought to force lots of capable hardware into retirement. This issue churned for months, with folks wrangling system files to bypass minimum system requirements, and Microsoft seemingly shifting the goalposts around at the same time.
Another early controversy was Microsoft continuing to push users into setting up Windows using an online Microsoft account, and cutting off avenues of avoidance. Again, communities had to fight the OS to make it work the way they wanted, often with a simple local account. This struggle continues to this day. Microsoft paints the requirement as good for users, providing OneDrive backups, syncing across devices, and providing extra recovery and security features. However, forced online accounts are also a commercial vehicle for selling digital goods and services.
Things had settled down in Windows land by 2024, but Microsoft spoiled the broth again with the introduction of the Copilot+ PC era. In some ways, it showed some foresight in sensing that AI was going to be big. Nevertheless, this was another clear misstep, with gaffes/scares like the AI-centerpiece Windows Recall app.
Copilot+ PC’s failure was confirmed by Microsoft and its OEM partners when they quietly killed off all Copilot+ PC branding earlier this year. For now, built-in AI is being de-emphasized, and Microsoft is looking at a cross-platform agentic model.
A change of direction
This year has also seen Microsoft publicly realize that people need Windows 11 as a foundation for their productivity tasks and gaming fun. The OS isn’t the destination. Thus, in spring, execs promised to clean up and optimize Windows 11 for its basic everyday use. Going forward, Microsoft has dangled the carrot of faster built-in apps, lower memory/resource use, and other foundational OS optimizations.
Windows 11 26H2 was released to consumers last week. As a battle-scarred Windows veteran, I’ve not clicked the update button yet on any of my machines, but there are reasons to be optimistic that it doesn’t deliver new nightmares. Version 26H2 is being distributed with the promise to deliver a “predictable and low-disruption” update. Boring is good.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Despite the aforementioned controversies, as well as the usual collection of silly/scary bugs that needed ironing out, people are still using Windows 11. It is widely adopted and dominates the PC landscape. MacOS and Linux have made inroads in terms of users, but Windows still looks mostly unassailable on roughly 76% of all desktop/laptop computers. Among Windows versions, it holds nearly 72% of the market, with Windows 10 rapidly declining and dipping under 28% at the most recent count.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

articles.title: Lola Vision Systems is trying to make it easier to run AI models on chips | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The story begins almost 12 years ago, when Tayo Adesanya started a career working with microchips and AI processors. He mainly helped large manufacturers decide which chips to use in their hardware. Those years, he told TechCrunch, gave him early insight into where demand in the AI computing market was headed. “Starting Lola Vision Systems was a bet on where the world was headed and what I was seeing,” he said.
In 2024, he launched Lola Vision Systems, an AI infrastructure company that builds software and chips for running AI models on devices. Its core product is software that translates AI models into instructions a specific chip can run. Adesanya calls this software a “compiler toolchain,” and he says it is a massive bottleneck: Manually setting up an AI model on new hardware can take “roughly 200 hours” just to begin testing. Lola Vision says it has rebuilt that software layer and is also developing its own semiconductor chips, with the goal of automating more of the process. A client provides its code and the AI model it wants to use, whether custom-built or open source, and the software translates both into instructions the client’s chip can execute.
“Speed is only part of it,” Adesanya said. He explained that faster setup gives aerospace and “other mission-critical companies” time to “run more accurate models on their own data, at a lower power.”
“For these customers,” he said, “accuracy and reliability aren’t nice to have. They determine whether a product passes regulatory review and whether it works reliably in the field.”
Lola Vision, based in Washington, D.C., is one of several startups trying to offer an alternative to Nvidia’s technology for running AI on devices. Right now, Adesanya said, many companies start with Nvidia’s Jetson, a line of compact computing modules for running AI on devices, or with open source AI models. Adesanya claimed these “often break or run poorly out of the box, so teams spend days or weeks getting them to run at all, then even more weeks debugging until the models are usable.”
“Even then,” he continued, “power consumption often blows edge computing budgets, or the board can’t deliver enough compute for the medium to large models the product actually needs to run successfully. This leads to the recognition models lagging behind targets or misreading objects.” (Edge computing means running AI directly on a device, such as a camera or drone, rather than in a remote data center. Recognition models are AI systems that identify objects.)
According to the company, a dozen corporate customers have signed letters expressing interest in buying Lola Vision’s chips once they are available, and it already has one signed customer. It has also partnered with SCALE, a microelectronics workforce development program, to work with more semiconductor labs. “To get revenue sooner, we will now license our software on existing hardware,” Adesanya said. (In other words, rather than waiting for its own chips, the company will let customers pay to use its software on chips that already exist.) He added that the company has raised just over $1 million in total funding to date.
Lola Vision was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200, a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. “TechCrunch was a favorite when I was a student at Purdue,” he said. After about a year of building the product and signing its first customer, he said, he felt it was time to apply to Startup Battlefield and get the company in front of a wider audience.
As for what he’s most excited about when it comes to the event, it’s “making meaningful connections and learning as much as I can about what’s happening in and around our space,” he said. “And, to be direct, I’m looking forward to investors writing checks.”
To learn more about Lola Vision Systems and dozens of other highly vetted startups that are joining us at TechCrunch Disrupt next week (along with the VCs coming to check them out), join us in San Francisco, October 13-15.

articles.title: 512 Go et 8 340 mAh : le Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G passe à 380€ sur Amazon
articles.text:
Un mois après sa sortie, la version 512 Go du Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G passe 173 € sous son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours. Une configuration pensée pour durer, grâce à sa batterie et à son stockage, avec une puissance et une photo qui restent dans la moyenne.
Lancé fin août, le Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G est le milieu de gamme de Xiaomi qui mise d’abord sur l’endurance, avec une batterie de 8 340 mAh, et sur la solidité, avec une certification IP68. Sa version 8 Go + 512 Go est proposée à 380 € sur Amazon une fois le coupon appliqué, contre 553 € au plus bas des 30 derniers jours. Il s’agit d’une offre Prime anticipée, réservée aux abonnés Prime. Elle intéresse surtout celles et ceux qui gardent leur smartphone plusieurs années et y accumulent photos et vidéos, puisque le stockage n’est pas extensible.
Le Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G 8 Go + 512 Go est à 380 € sur Amazon avec le coupon, contre 553 € au plus bas des 30 derniers jours.
Pourquoi choisir le Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G ?
- Une batterie taillée pour plusieurs jours : avec 8 340 mAh, les tests de Phonandroid et de Presse-citron relèvent deux jours à deux jours et demi d’usage, et Xiaomi annonce 50 % de charge en 34 minutes à 67 W.
- 512 Go pour compenser l’absence de microSD : le stockage n’étant pas extensible, cette version laisse de la marge pour les applications, les photos et les vidéos accumulées au fil des années.
- Un suivi logiciel long : Xiaomi promet quatre mises à jour majeures d’Android et six ans de correctifs de sécurité, un horizon cohérent avec une batterie et un stockage pensés pour durer.
Un téléphone pour durer plutôt que pour jouer
La dalle AMOLED de 6,83 pouces en définition 1,5K, à 120 Hz, se prête bien à la vidéo et à la lecture, et son pic de luminosité annoncé à 3 500 nits vise la lisibilité en plein soleil. Avec son verre Gorilla Glass Victus 2 et sa certification IP68, l’appareil est conçu pour encaisser une averse ou une chute, Xiaomi annonçant une résistance jusqu’à 3 mètres. La batterie change surtout la routine : une journée chargée avec GPS, musique et appels ne demande pas de surveiller le pourcentage.
Ce modèle s’adresse à un usage quotidien soutenu : réseaux sociaux, navigation, messagerie et photos de jour. Le Snapdragon 6s Gen 4 garde l’interface fluide, mais il montre ses limites en jeu : Presse-citron a vu Fortnite osciller entre 60 et 12 images par seconde dans les phases d’action. En photo, le capteur principal de 50 Mpx stabilisé s’en sort de jour, alors que la nuit et l’ultra grand-angle déçoivent, et la vidéo plafonne en 1080p. Les joueurs et les vidéastes ont donc intérêt à regarder ailleurs.
Face aux autres milieux de gamme, l’endurance avant tout
Avec ses 8 340 mAh, le Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G dépasse nettement les 5 000 mAh environ de la plupart des milieux de gamme, comme le Honor 600, qui arrive en tête de notre comparatif des meilleurs smartphones. Il n’apporte en revanche ni vidéo 4K, ni la puissance d’un modèle orienté jeu. Si l’autonomie prime et que votre budget est plus serré, le Honor Magic 8 Lite, que nous retenons pour son endurance à petit prix, mérite aussi un regard.
✅ Les points forts
- Batterie de 8 340 mAh et charge à 67 W
- 512 Go de stockage, utiles faute de microSD
- Écran AMOLED 1,5K de 6,83 pouces à 120 Hz
- Verre Gorilla Glass Victus 2 et certification IP68
- Quatre versions d’Android et six ans de correctifs promis
❌ Les limites
- Snapdragon 6s Gen 4 à la peine dans les jeux exigeants
- Photo de nuit et ultra grand-angle en retrait, vidéo limitée au 1080p
- 223 g, un poids qui se sent en poche
- Une vingtaine d’applications préinstallées et des publicités dans les applications Xiaomi
Le prix de 380 € s’obtient avec le coupon proposé sur la fiche Amazon du Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G, en version 8 Go + 512 Go noire.
À 380 €, la version 512 Go du Redmi Note 17 Pro 5G coûte 173 € de moins que son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, soit une baisse d’environ 31 %. Elle passe ainsi sous la barre des 400 €, coupon compris. Le compromis, lui, ne change pas : une autonomie et une robustesse au-dessus de la moyenne, une puissance et une photo qui s’en tiennent à l’essentiel.
Ce bon plan parle à celles et ceux qui veulent un smartphone endurant, solide et suivi longtemps, à garder plusieurs années. Si vous jouez beaucoup, filmez en 4K ou tenez aux photos de soirée, mieux vaut viser un autre modèle. Comme téléphone de terrain ou comme premier smartphone à confier à un adolescent, l’association de la batterie et de l’IP68 trouve en revanche tout son sens.

articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Supercharge regulated workloads with Claude Code and Amazon Bedrock
Please note that the following post is intended for informational purposes only. The approach detailed below may not be suitable for all organizations or compliance programs. It is important to evaluate this potential solution against the compliance requirements of your organization and any applicable regulatory obligations you may have.
The availability of Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions introduces an on-ramp for AI-assisted development for workloads with regulatory or compliance requirements, including International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR). Claude Sonnet 5 holds FedRAMP Class D (formerly High) certification and DoD Impact Level 4 and 5 (IL4/IL5) authorization, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 hold FedRAMP Class D certification on Amazon Bedrock (verify current model certification status).
In this post, we explore how to use these models on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) with Claude Code, Anthropic’s agentic coding tool. With this solution, you can run AI-assisted workflows that speed up everyday development tasks while maintaining compliance alignment.
Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
AWS GovCloud (US) Regions are designed specifically for US customers with elevated compliance needs. You can deploy generative AI workloads to sensitive environments while maintaining compliance controls. Amazon Bedrock is built with security-focused features, including:
Built-in data protection where customer content isn’t stored, logged, or used to train AWS models or shared with third parties.
FedRAMP Class D (formerly High) certification and DoD Cloud Service Provider (CSP) SRG IL4/IL5 authorization pathways, supporting government agencies’ compliance requirements. See the Amazon Bedrock models compliance page for current model-level certification status.
Integration with existing security controls and compliance frameworks available in AWS GovCloud (US), maintaining the same high security standards as other AWS Regions while providing additional authorization pathways.
Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) supports two endpoint surfaces, bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle, both powered by the same underlying Mantle inference engine with Zero Operator Access (ZOA) architecture. The bedrock-runtime endpoint uses the AWS SDK (InvokeModel and Converse APIs) and supports Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Agents, and invocation logging. This makes it the recommended choice for most new applications, particularly those requiring audit trails. The bedrock-mantle endpoint supports the Anthropic Messages API natively and provides access to capabilities currently available only on that surface, such as server-side tools, background inference, and Projects. Both endpoints are available for Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5, with bedrock-runtime available in both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions (US-West and US-East) and bedrock-mantle available in AWS GovCloud (US-West).
Claude Code
Claude Code is Anthropic’s agentic coding tool that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with your development tools. Powered by models such as Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), it operates directly in your terminal, your preferred integrated development environments (IDEs) such as VS Code and JetBrains, and in the background with the Claude Agent SDK. Claude Code understands your entire codebase and can work across multiple files and tools to get things done. Claude Code can:
- Write code and fix bugs spanning multiple files across your codebase.
- Answer questions about your code’s architecture and logic.
- Execute and fix tests, linting, and other commands.
- Search through Git history, resolve merge conflicts, and create commits and pull requests.
- Connect to external tools and data sources with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), including the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), Terraform, and Kubernetes.
- Spawn sub-agents that work on different parts of a task simultaneously.
- Customize behavior with CLAUDE.md memory files, skills for repeatable workflows, and hooks for pre/post-action automation.
- Automate recurring tasks and integrate with continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) through GitHub Actions or GitLab CI/CD.
To learn more, see Anthropic’s articles: Claude Code tutorials and Claude Code: Best practices for agentic coding.
Solution overview: Try Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
This section provides step-by-step instructions for setting up and configuring Claude Code to work with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), including prerequisites, installation commands, environment configuration, and verification steps.
Prerequisites
Before you get started, make sure that you have the following in place:
- An AWS GovCloud (US) account with access to Amazon Bedrock.
- Appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and permissions for Amazon Bedrock. At minimum, your IAM policy should include: 
         
  - For bedrock-runtime: bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles, and bedrock:GetInferenceProfile.
  - For bedrock-mantle (if using the Mantle endpoint): bedrock-mantle:CreateInference, bedrock-mantle:GetProject, bedrock-mantle:ListProjects, and bedrock-mantle:ListModels.
  - Alternatively, attach the AmazonBedrockMantleInferenceAccess managed policy.
- Amazon Bedrock model access to Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5 enabled in your AWS GovCloud (US) account.
- AWS CLI configured with valid AWS session credentials using short-term API keys or AWS SSO login.
Set up Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
After configuring AWS CLI with your credentials, install Claude Code using one of the following methods:
macOS, Linux, WSL:
Windows PowerShell:
Windows CMD:
Homebrew (macOS/Linux):
For additional installation methods, see Claude Code installation docs.
Option A: Interactive setup wizard (recommended)
- Navigate to your project:
- Launch Claude Code:
- Run through the login wizard:
At the login prompt, select 3rd-party platform, then Amazon Bedrock. Follow the wizard prompts to choose your authentication method, region (us-gov-west-1), and pin your models. The wizard saves configuration to your settings file automatically.
If you have previously configured Claude Code, run /setup-bedrock to reopen the wizard and update your credentials, region, or model pins.
Option B: Manual environment variable configuration
For scripted or enterprise deployments, set the following environment variables:
To use Claude Opus 5.5 as the primary model instead:
To pin specific model versions for consistent team deployments:
Then navigate to your project and launch Claude Code:
Option C: Using the Bedrock Mantle endpoint
Bedrock Mantle supports the Anthropic Messages API natively and is available in AWS GovCloud (US-West). To route Claude Code through Mantle:
