Today, Amazon SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference introduces the aws-ai-ml skill, available through the Agent Toolkit for AWS. This skill gives coding agents like Kiro, Claude Code, and Codex deep expertise in inference optimization and benchmarking. Install the skill, and your existing agent can benchmark endpoints, recommend deployment configurations, compare performance runs, and generate executable SageMaker Python SDK v3 code on your behalf. The aws-ai-ml skill is a toolkit that plugs into any coding agent that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP), turning it into a SageMaker AI inference optimization expert.
In this post, we walk through what the skill enables, how to set it up, and how it helps you move faster from model to production.
The challenge: Bridging intent and infrastructure
Amazon SageMaker AI supports serverful hosting across real-time, batch, and asynchronous modes. It offers on-demand and reserved capacity, heterogeneous instances, virtual private cloud (VPC) isolation, automatic scaling, and integration with every SageMaker AI training path. The surface area is broad and deep, but most engineers do not arrive knowing which instance family or serving container will best serve their needs. They arrive with a use case: a performance target they want to hit, a cost envelope they need to stay within, or a model they need to evaluate before committing to production.
The agentic experience for SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference closes this gap. You tell the agent what you want to accomplish, and it produces executable SageMaker Python SDK v3 code that you can review, modify, and run in your own environment. The agent asks targeted clarifying questions, generates code grounded in real benchmarks and measured performance data, and adapts to your business constraints the way a solutions architect would.
Throughout, you stay in control. Every step is visible in real time and expressed as code you can read and question. Nothing happens behind an opaque UI.
Getting started
You can install the aws-ai-ml skill through the Agent Toolkit for AWS on your local machine, or use it within an Amazon SageMaker Studio JupyterLab space. Either way, you can go from zero to a working conversation in 10 minutes.
Option A: Use with any coding agent (Kiro, Claude Code, Codex, or any MCP-compatible agent)
Step 1: Install the Agent Toolkit for AWS. If you haven’t already, set up the Agent Toolkit. This requires AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) 2.35+ and uv installed.
This auto-detects your agents, installs skills, and configures the AWS MCP Server. For agent-specific setup (plugin install commands, MCP config), see the Agent Toolkit for AWS getting started guide.
Step 2: Install the aws-ai-ml skill. Add the SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference skill to your agent:
Step 3: Confirm and begin. Open your coding agent’s chat panel and ask: “What skills are available?” You should see aws-ai-ml listed. After you confirm, describe your intent in natural language. Your coding agent now has SageMaker AI inference optimization expertise built in.
Prerequisites: Your AWS credentials must have permissions to call SageMaker AI APIs (creating endpoints, running benchmark and recommendation jobs). The skill generates code that runs under your credentials. No additional AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) configuration is needed for the skill itself.
Note: For Kiro and Claude Code, agents can discover skills at runtime. They can search for and load skills on demand through the AWS MCP Server, without any local installation. Ask your agent: “Search for AWS skills related to databases.” Refer to the readme for discovering skills at runtime.
Option B: Use within Amazon SageMaker Studio
If you prefer to work inside a managed JupyterLab environment, you can use the skill in Amazon SageMaker Studio with a pre-configured image.
Step 1: Open Amazon SageMaker Studio. Navigate to Amazon SageMaker Studio in your target AWS account and AWS Region. Select your Studio domain and launch the Studio IDE from your user profile.
Step 2: Create a JupyterLab space. From the Studio landing page, choose JupyterLab, then choose Create JupyterLab space. Name the space (for example, my-inference-opt) and keep the sharing setting Private (skills only sync on private spaces). Under the Image menu, select the image that includes the SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference skill. This image ships pre-configured with the aws-ai-ml agent skill and all necessary dependencies. Choose Run space and wait for it to boot (5–10 minutes the first time).
Note: Use a fresh space. A reused space with a locally modified skill version may not pick up the pre-configured image.
Step 3: Open JupyterLab and launch a terminal. After the space boots, open JupyterLab and choose Terminal.
Step 4: Authorize your coding agent. In the terminal, authenticate with your coding agent using your identity provider. For example, with Kiro:
Step 5: Confirm and begin. Open your coding agent’s chat panel and ask: “What skills are available?” You should see aws-ai-ml listed. Once confirmed, describe your intent in natural language.
        Troubleshooting:
If the agent reports no skills are available, verify that your space is set to Private. You can also check from the terminal:
        If that directory is empty but /etc/sagemaker/skills/ contains the skill files, run restart-jupyter-server, refresh the page, and retry.
What you can do
The agentic experience covers the following capabilities across the inference optimization lifecycle. You don’t need to know which capability to invoke. Describe what you want, and your agent figures out the next step or asks clarifying questions if anything is unclear.
Benchmark an existing endpoint
If you already have a model deployed on a SageMaker AI endpoint, you can ask the agent to benchmark it. Tell the agent which endpoint you want to test, and it generates a Python notebook that runs a load test using the Workload.synthetic() and start_benchmark() APIs from the SageMaker Python SDK.
Before running any benchmark, the agent confirms that your endpoint is safe to load-test, because benchmarking drives real traffic to a live endpoint.
When the benchmark completes, you get a quantitative performance report with:
- Throughput: requests per second, output tokens per second.
- Latency: p50, p99, time-to-first-token, inter-token latency.
- Concurrency: number of simultaneous requests supported.
These are measured values from real load on real infrastructure, not estimates. The agent also recommends improvement mechanisms (such as prefill decoding) to boost performance.
Example prompt: “Benchmark my Llama endpoint on SageMaker AI.”
Find the right instance type for your model
If you have a model and need to find the right instance type to deploy it on SageMaker AI, tell your agent. It doesn’t matter where your model lives or how you obtained it:
- Fine-tuned or custom model in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3): You trained or downloaded a model and stored it in S3. Provide the S3 URI and your optimization goal. Example prompt: “I want to find the cheapest instance type to deploy my fine-tuned model on SageMaker.”
- Publicly available foundation model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: You want to deploy a foundation model (FM) from the JumpStart catalog then provide the model ID. Example prompt: “Find the best instance for model huggingface-reasoning-qwen3-8b on SageMaker AI.”
- Model on the Hugging Face Hub: You want to use a model hosted on Hugging Face. Provide the model name. For gated models (such as Llama variants), your agent surfaces the license terms and asks you to accept them and provide your Hugging Face token. Example prompt: “I want to deploy a Llama model from Hugging Face Hub. What’s the cheapest option?”
In every case, your agent generates code that evaluates your model against candidate instances and configurations, then presents ranked deployment options with concrete performance metrics: throughput, latency percentiles, time-to-first-token, and concurrency. You choose based on your cost and performance requirements.
Compare benchmark runs
If you ran multiple benchmarks (for example, before and after a configuration change, or across two instance types), you can ask the agent to compare them. Provide the two benchmark job names, and the agent generates a comparison that computes deltas across key metrics: throughput, latency percentiles, and time-to-first-token.
The results show percentage changes where positive means better, giving you a single, interpretable summary of whether your change improved performance, degraded it, or had no meaningful effect.
If one of the benchmark runs doesn’t exist, the agent offers to run it first before proceeding with the comparison.
Example prompt: “I have two benchmark runs and I want to compare them. Which one is faster?”
Benchmark results
This table compares two deployed models on the same benchmark workload (512/256 tokens, concurrency 4). The Δ% column shows how much faster Model B (Qwen3-8B) is than Model A (Qwen3-1.7B) on each metric. A positive value means Model B is better.
| Metric | Qwen3-1.7B (Model A) | Qwen3-8B (Model B) | Δ% | 
| Output token throughput | 188.2 tokens/s | 271.2 tokens/s | +44.1% ✅ | 
| Per-user throughput | 47.5 tokens/s | 69.4 tokens/s | +45.9% ✅ | 
| Request throughput | 0.736 req/s | 1.08 req/s | +46.7% ✅ | 
| Inter-token latency | 20.9 ms | 14 ms | +33.0% ✅ | 
| Request latency | 5,382 ms | 3,658 ms | +32.0% ✅ | 
| Time to first token | 67.5 ms | 166.3 ms | −146.5% ❌ | 
The two models run on different hardware. Qwen3-8B uses a 4-GPU ml.g5.12xlarge (4x A10G), while Qwen3-1.7B uses a single L4 GPU (ml.g6.4xlarge). The deltas reflect approximately 4x the compute, not just the models themselves.
The takeaway: Qwen3-8B delivers approximately 44–47 percent higher throughput and lower end-to-end latency, largely thanks to the additional GPU compute. Qwen3-1.7B wins only on time-to-first-token, the expected advantage of a smaller model on a single GPU.
Putting it all together
You don’t need to memorize capability names or know which workflow to request. The following table shows how common requests map to outcomes.
| You say | What you get | 
| “I already deployed a model and want to know how fast it is.” | Quantitative performance report: throughput, latency percentiles, concurrency metrics from real load. | 
| “I have a model in S3 and I don’t know what instance to deploy on.” | Ranked deployment options with cost, throughput, and latency for each candidate configuration. | 
| “I want to deploy a JumpStart model and find the cheapest instance. I only have the model ID.” | Ranked deployment options, no S3 staging required. Gated-model alternative surfaced if needed. | 
| “I ran a benchmark before and after a change. Which one is faster?” | Percentage change across all metrics indicating improvement or regression. | 
| “I want to optimize a Llama model from Hugging Face Hub.” | License surfaced, model staged to S3, then standard recommendation output. | 
If your request spans multiple capabilities (for example, staging a Hugging Face model and then getting deployment recommendations), the agent chains them naturally within the same conversation.
What to expect from the agent
Your agent, equipped with the aws-ai-ml skill, follows a few behaviors that make the experience predictable and safe:
- It asks for what it needs. If information is missing (such as an endpoint name or S3 URI), the agent asks you to provide it rather than guessing.
- It confirms before impactful actions. Before running a benchmark that drives real traffic to a live endpoint, the agent warns you about the impact and asks for explicit confirmation.
- It tells you when something is out of scope. If you ask for something the agent can’t do (such as deploying a model), it explains what it can offer instead, such as generating the deployment configuration that you need.
- It generates SageMaker Python SDK v3 code. Every output is executable code you can inspect, modify, and run in your own environment.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:
- Delete SageMaker AI endpoints created during benchmarking or recommendations.
- Stop or delete your JupyterLab space if you used SageMaker Studio.
- Remove S3 objects stored by benchmark and recommendation jobs in your SageMaker AI default bucket.
Conclusion
The aws-ai-ml skill for Amazon SageMaker AI optimized generative AI inference turns your existing coding agent into a SageMaker AI inference optimization expert. Whether you need to benchmark a live endpoint, find the cheapest instance for your model, compare configurations, or stage a Hugging Face model for evaluation, you describe what you want and your agent delivers measurable results.
To get started, install the skill through the Agent Toolkit for AWS and add it to the coding agent you already use, or launch a pre-configured JupyterLab space in Amazon SageMaker Studio. For more information, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

articles.title: Humanoid robots pummel YouTuber in cage matches, California tells startup to stop the fights
articles.text:
WTF?! You might think there are plenty of reasons why a real person shouldn't fight a humanoid robot in a cage match, but it happened anyway. The state of California wasn't pleased about this and has now sent a cease-and-desist letter to the robotics startup behind the event, telling it to stop holding these unsanctioned matches.
Last month, YouTuber Frankie LaPenna fought three different robots from REK, including a distinctly Terminator-like machine. At one point, the robot gave LaPenna a brutal kick to the face that sent him into the side of the cage, while another kick to the stomach sent the influencer flying onto his back. A different robot also put LaPenna on the ground with a fast series of punches to the face. It's all a bit concerning, really, though the child-like robot didn't put up much of a fight.
The California State Athletic Commission was also concerned about the event. It sent a cease-and-desist letter on September 30, demanding that REK stop hosting, promoting or sponsoring these fights.
REK CEO Cix Liv proudly shared the letter on X, writing that "we made it boys."
 – CIX 🦾 (@cixliv) September 30, 2026
The letter notes that any boxing or mixed martial arts contest, match, or exhibition, involving any human in the state of California, must first have approval from the California State Athletic Commission.
The letter adds that Business and Professions Codes section 18870 and 18878 make it a misdemeanor to promote or participate in a boxing or martial arts contest, match, or exhibition involving any human without a license.
Liv's unlikely to be too worried about the letter: don't be surprised if the fights simply move to another state or country. The free promotion will probably help, too.
Away from the legal ramifications, the fights illustrate just how quickly humanoid robots are advancing. It wasn't too long ago when a slight push from a human would have sent one of these machines sprawling to the floor and flopping around like a fish out of water. Video of the robots pounding the crap out of LaPenna looks like one of those pre-apocalypse news reports you'd find in an RPG about an AI that destroys the world.
There have been several reports recently about the military investigating use cases for humanoid robots. The US Army just named five companies as winners of the xTechHumanoid competition, which looks at ways these machines can be utilized in future military operations. One of the robots developed by a winner looks like it should be carrying a laser rifle and already has ballistic protection.
More recently, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of a new military command designed to expand the use of autonomous and robotic capabilities across the US armed forces.
It's not just the US, either. China is preparing humanoid robots for combat as it moves them from labs to military training grounds.

articles.title: Hyundai CEO says only a ‘level playing field’ can minimize damage from China
articles.text:
There’s been a lot of doom and gloom from the auto industry lately when the subject of China comes up. Automaker CEOs, in particular, warn that allowing low-cost, high-tech Chinese electric vehicles to be sold in the US would effectively spell the end of their businesses.
Hyundai CEO says only a ‘level playing field’ can minimize damage from China
Hyundai CEO José Muñoz says the US could be overrun like Europe without protections in place.
Hyundai CEO José Muñoz is not as pessimistic as some of his counterparts. He says he’s confident the right mix of protectionist policies and improvements on the product side can keep China at bay. Even though his company is feeling the squeeze from China, Muñoz isn’t ready to throw in the towel. But he also acknowledges that China could flood the US with affordable imports without established protections in place.
“As long as there is a level playing field for everybody,” Muñoz said at the reveal of the new 2027 Hyundai Tucson in New York City last week. “That’s all we ask, right? We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.”
Chinese automakers have expanded rapidly in Europe, gobbling up market share and damaging domestic brands like Volkswagen, Volvo, and Mercedes by offering vehicles at much lower prices. US automakers warn the same could be true for them if China were allowed to import its vehicles here.
“We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.”
— José Muñoz
Steep tariffs and laws that prohibit the sale of cars with software from China have basically made it impossible to sell Chinese vehicles in the US. But in recent months, the dam appears to be weakening. President Donald Trump has said several times that he would be open to Chinese automakers building manufacturing plants in the US if they hire American workers. And experts across the board believe it’s only a matter of time before China finds a way to sell its cars in the US.
But if Chinese brands eventually set up manufacturing inside North America or enter via partner channels, it’s not clear whether Hyundai has a defensive strategy ready. I asked Muñoz whether his company had begun to plan for the eventuality of Chinese imports available in the US market. He said it had not.
“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors,” he said. “We are always trying to do better.”
If Hyundai has any strategy, Muñoz added, it’s vertical integration: bringing down costs by making its tech and components. “This allows us to be more competitive,” he said. “Better quality over cost.”
“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors.”
Muñoz cited Hyundai’s $5.8 billion investment in Louisiana to produce green steel as an example of the company’s efforts to vertically integrate in the US. Hyundai expects the investment to provide better, more competitive, and more environmentally friendly steel. He says the same philosophy applies to software and other technologies that Hyundai wants to develop internally.
“So there is always room to do better,” he continued. “So if the Chinese competitor were to enter in the market, we would see what would happen, but I don’t know, I don’t have a crystal ball. I just look around, for example, Europe, and see what has happened, and then you may expect similar type of behaviors.”
Chinese vehicles sold in Europe are on average about 30 percent cheaper than comparable European-made rival models, even when factoring in EU import tariffs. The US has already fallen behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption, after Trump and Republicans in Congress eliminated federal subsidies. In Europe, EVs account for over 20 percent of sales; in China, it’s over 60 percent. In the US, it’s less than 6 percent.
Political polarization certainly plays a role in depressing sales, as does inadequate charging infrastructure. But the lack of affordable electric models is regularly cited as the biggest barrier to adoption in the US. On that front, Muñoz thinks the US can still catch up.
“I think the American market is the most competitive in the world,” he said, noting that Hyundai still records robust EV sales here. That may be true, but the company’s hybrids are what’s keeping its EV business afloat. Hyundai has added hybrids to a wide range of vehicles, including its top-selling Tucson.
Unlike other automakers, Hyundai hasn’t retreated from EVs. It continues to sell its Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 here in the US, as well as a growing number of hybrids. In fact, the Hyundai Group recently surpassed Honda to claim second place in US hybrid sales behind Toyota.
Muñoz acknowledged that the US was still catching up to China’s dominance in EV batteries. Hyundai operates a battery manufacturing joint venture with SK On in Georgia near its massive Metaplant, where it builds all of its EVs and hybrids.
“Obviously if you don’t have the critical mass, the volume, it’s very difficult to be competitive,” he said. “One of the biggest pieces of cost is the battery. That is the key element, right? But there is a lot of production of batteries in the United States with some of the best global manufacturers. So I’m not concerned.”

articles.title: Anthropic reports Florida woman’s Claude ‘diary’ threat to shoot up sheriff’s office, felony charge follows — it’s at least the third such conversation to reach police since August
articles.text:
Anthropic reports Florida woman’s Claude ‘diary’ threat to shoot up sheriff’s office, felony charge follows — it’s at least the third such conversation to reach police since August
Investigators say a message the following day mentioned a new gun.
A Lee County, Florida, woman was arrested on a felony charge after a threat linked to an Anthropic Claude AI chatbot conversation, or “diary,” by her account was reported to law enforcement via Anthropic’s human review team, according to WINK News. The arrest report includes a Sept. 26 statement from a user identified as “Carli” saying she would “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff’s Office (LCSO), and allegedly a message the next day mentioned a new gun. The conversation was at least the third of its type to reach police since August.
Anthropic monitors chats for key phrases and content that could be deemed threatening, the arrest report says, and depending on severity, they can be elevated for human review. In this case, the team decided to report its findings to law enforcement. The Bonita Springs woman was detained at home without incident, and an LCSO intelligence detective took over the case from there. The arrest report is not yet in the court file, but our own check shows court records listing the Sept. 30 felony charge under Florida Statute 836.10: written or electronic threat of a mass shooting or act of terrorism.
No comment from Anthropic on the case is currently on record. Anthropic’s public privacy policy, effective Sept. 10, says that disclosure to law enforcement may occur where it has a good-faith belief “that disclosure is reasonably necessary to … prevent serious harm to any person or to property.” Its government requests report for the latter half of 2025 uses a narrower standard for emergency disclosures, the “danger of death or serious physical injury to a person,” and lists zero emergency requests from law enforcement in that period, though it doesn’t count referrals Anthropic makes on its own.
As booked, the charge is listed as “THREAT-TERRORISTIC-STATE OFFENSES-WRITTEN/ELEC THREAT MASS SHOOTING/TERRORISM ACT,” which covers the mass-shooting/terrorism half of the statute. The conversation with the chatbot may fall under the law as a threat sent, posted, or transmitted “in any manner in which it may be viewed by another person.” The messages found by Anthropic’s human review, including the next-day gun mention, are likely the supporting evidence for the arrest and charge. No attorney is named on the docket, and a public defender was appointed at the time of the charge.
The incident follows a string of recent cases tied to the use of chatbots from Anthropic and rival OpenAI. One incident, in San Antonio, involves Aug. 11 queries in “an Anthropic AI chat” about shooting at a nearby elementary school. The police, alerted by the FBI, arrested a 22-year-old man on a felony terroristic threat charge. Days later, in San Francisco, a user threatened Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in an Aug. 14 Claude chat, saying he had bought an AR-15. Anthropic notified police, but the user ended up not being arrested or charged. Both cases were detailed in regional news reports.
OpenAI has faced similar challenges in Florida over a message in March to its AI chatbot platform, ChatGPT, where user Darren Zhou spoke about killing his ex-girlfriend, and OpenAI reported him to the FBI, according to the Palm Beach Post. Zhou pleaded guilty in August to charges including written threats to kill, under the same statute, 836.10, and was sentenced to eight years’ probation.
The Florida attorney general also filed a lawsuit against the company in June, citing the 2025 Florida State University shooting, and last month asked a judge for a temporary injunction. OpenAI was also sued by British Columbia last month for not warning police about the Tumbler Ridge shooter, whose ChatGPT account, the lawsuit says, it had identified eight months before the attack. These incidents, and more, show a pattern where AI companies are expected to respect privacy while simultaneously being held responsible when they don’t report threats to law enforcement.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The increasing scrutiny on both privacy and security concerns related to AI products has led to calls for caution from experts such as Florida Gulf Coast University’s Chrissann Ruehle, who spoke to WINK News. This comes alongside demands for stricter, independently approved guidelines, such as those requested by Florida’s attorney general.
For users, it’s a reminder that what you share with your favorite AI companion is “never truly anonymous,” as Lee County Sheriff Carmine Marceno told WINK News. A marked conversation can act as a “diary” to human reviewers, and that can get you in trouble, as the woman identified as “Carli” discovered. More details about the case should be available after the arraignment on Nov. 2.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Buscando entre las ofertas del Prime Day, encontré un mini PC con Windows 11 por menos de 400 euros
articles.text:
Los miniPCs se convirtieron en una gran alternativa para todas aquellas personas que no tienen mucho espacio en su escritorio. Pero en los últimos años, no es esa la única razón. Ocupan poco pero están de sobra preparados para rendir al máximo. Entre todas las marcas para comprar un mini PC, NIPOGI es una de las que mejor lo está haciendo, con equipos muy potentes y con precios bastante bajo.
De hecho, en cualquier modelo podemos encontrar componentes top tanto en procesadores como en gráficas. Y todos ellos cargados con sistema operativo, algo cada vez más difícil de ver en equipos de bajo precio.
Con la llegada del Prime Day de Amazon, que se celebra los días 6 y 7 de Octubre, NIPOGI ha bajado todavía más el precio a alguno de sus productos más vendidos. En este caso ellos han alargado la promoción hasta finales del 11 de octubre pero date prisa porque con estos precios, vuelan. Te los ordenamos según el precio, de mayor a menor.
NIPOGI ACEMAGIC K1 Mini PC, de 419 euros a 389 euros
Es el equipo más simple de los tres propuestos, pero es perfecto para la mayoría de personas. Para empezar, es súper compacto y se puede colocar en cualquier lugar. En cuanto a configuración, es el más sencillo pero te garantizamos que el procesador AMD Ryzen 5 no te va a dar ningún problema para tareas de ofimática o tareas sencillas. Tiene una memoria RAM de 16GB LPDDR4X y viene con 512GB de almacenamiento.
Pese a su bajo precio, una cosa que no sufrirás son calentamientos excesivos. Se mantiene siempre fresco gracias a su sistema de refrigeración de doble salida. También tiene puertos de sobra, tanto de USB como HDMI así que podrás conectar lo que necesites a tu miniPC. Viene con Windows 11 Pro preinstalado.
Para conseguirlo por menos de 400 euros tienes que usar el código 26JY7530 para que pase de 419 euros a 389 euros. Date prisa porque la oferta acaba el 11 de octubre.
NIPOGI ACEMAGIC W1 Mini PC, de 549 euros a 479 euros
Este miniPC es de lo más completo que vas a encontrar. Procesador AMD Ryzen 7 H255, 16GB de RAM y 512GB de almacenamiento SSD. Es un equipo perfecto tanto para uso empresarial, como doméstico e incluso te permite jugar a bastantes juegos. Tiene una gráfica AMD Radeon así que es un equipo perfectamente equilibrado para cualquier tipo de uso. Viene con Windows 11 Pro preinstalado.
Ahora viene la parte interesante. Este equipo tiene un precio habitual de 549,99 euros pero usando el código 26JYH255 hasta el 11 de octubre, tienes un descuento del 13% quedando un precio final de 479 euros.
NIPOGI ACEMAGICIAN, de 549 euros a 479 euros
Otro gran equipo que cambia un poco con respecto al modelo anterior. Tanto el precio oficial como el descuento son similares, pero hay pequeñas diferencias. La primera es estética, este modelo es mucho menos tradicional pero llama la atención de todo el mundo por el lado gaming donde destaca el uso de luces.
En cuanto a datos técnicos, tiene un procesador AMD Ryzen 7 H255, 16GB de RAM LPDDR5, 512GB de almacenamiento SSD conectado por NVMe PCI 4.0, Windows 11 Pro preinstalado y un sistema de refrigeración de 54W para que el equipo no se sobrecaliente ni lo más mínimo.
Es complicado ver este tipo de configuración, no sólo en un equipo de este rango de precio tan bajo, sino también en uno tan compacto que cabe en cualquier lugar.
En cuanto a precio y códigos, debes utilizar el código 26VJ3FQ3 antes de que finalice el 11 de octubre para que el precio pase de 549 euros a 479 euros. 
Si llevas tiempo dándole vueltas a tener un miniPC por espacio, pero te echaba para atrás que pudiera ser caro o muy limitado en especificaciones, échale un vistazo a todo lo que tiene NIPOGI porque seguro que hay algo que te encaja y se convierte en una decisión sin margen de error.

articles.title: Hackers steal 8 million citizens' records from Danish government database | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Danish government has confirmed that its central database of citizens’ data was breached and most of its contents were stolen. The data breach affects some 8 million citizens and residents of Denmark, including people living abroad and the deceased.
In a statement, Danish minister Christina Egelund said the breach of the country’s Central Person Register (CPR) was a “serious incident,” which allowed hackers to steal names, addresses, Danish social security numbers, and other information.
The CPR is a government database of Danish citizens’ information, including their government-issued identity number for paying taxes and accessing other services. Denmark’s current population is about 6 million people, but the database includes records for about 11 million people, with some of the data going back decades.
The Danish government would not say who is behind the breach, which happened in September but was discovered on October 2. However, it said the unauthorized access was obtained by “abusing a Danish company’s lawful access to search for information in the CPR system.” (Some companies in Denmark have access to the CPR for verifying people’s information with the government.)
The data breach is thought to be the biggest in the country’s history. It follows similar cyberattacks targeting government national identity databases, including a 2016 breach affecting millions of Turkish citizens and several exposures of national ID cards and data spilled from India’s national Aadhaar database of citizens.

articles.title: Google risque de devoir payer 1,2 milliard de livres pour les commissions du Play Store
articles.text:
Liz Coll réclame à Google 1,2 milliard de livres sterling, soit près de 1,4 milliard d’euros, au nom de quelque 20 millions d’utilisateurs britanniques d’Android. Devant un tribunal londonien, cette spécialiste des droits des consommateurs accuse le groupe d’avoir gonflé le prix des applications pendant plus de dix ans, avec ses commissions sur le Play Store.
Octobre 2025, les juges du Tribunal d’appel de la concurrence (CAT) donnent raison à l’universitaire Rachael Kent contre Apple, reconnu coupable d’avoir imposé des commissions abusives sur l'App Store. Ils évaluent à environ 1,5 milliard de livres la somme due aux consommateurs, et Apple fait appel d’un jugement que la Cour d'appel devra examiner l’an prochain.
Sauf accord de dernière minute, c’est au tour de Google de comparaître devant le CAT à partir de ce lundi 5 octobre, pour un procès de sept semaines. Après six ans de bataille judiciaire avec Epic Games, le groupe se présente à l’audience avec un Play Store remanié. Il a accepté en juillet d'héberger des boutiques concurrentes dans sa vitrine aux États-Unis, quatre mois après avoir ramené sa commission standard à 20 %. Les juges devront dire si les commissions prélevées depuis 2015 ont alourdi la facture des utilisateurs d’Android, et dans quelle proportion.
Des commissions jusqu’à 30 % répercutées sur les prix, selon les plaignants
Ancienne responsable du numérique chez Consumers International, Liz Coll porte la plainte en tant que représentante du groupe. Elle reproche à Google d’avoir prélevé jusqu’à 30 % sur les achats intégrés et les abonnements souscrits depuis la boutique, et d'avoir protégé ce modèle en freinant les boutiques concurrentes et en obligeant les fabricants de smartphones à préinstaller le Play Store. Les développeurs ont, d’après elle, répercuté ce surcoût sur leurs clients avec des prix plus élevés. Beaucoup d’utilisateurs ignorent que l’éditeur d’une application de rencontre ou de streaming musical reverse à Google une part de chaque achat, a-t-elle expliqué au Financial Times.
Les achats concernés sont ceux réalisés entre le 1er octobre 2015 et le 31 juillet 2026. En cas de victoire, chaque utilisateur pourrait toucher en moyenne 60 livres, soit environ 69 euros. Liz Coll a chiffré sa demande en reprenant en partie les conclusions du tribunal dans l’affaire Apple. Pour fixer le montant final, il faudra toutefois aux juges estimer quelle part du surcoût les développeurs ont réellement répercutée sur leurs clients. Le cabinet Hausfeld défend les plaignants, et Fortress Investment Group finance la procédure. Ce fonds est soutenu par Mubadala, qui investit pour le compte d’Abu Dhabi.
Du côté des développeurs, Google a préféré payer. Professeur de droit de la concurrence à l’université de Strathclyde, Barry Rodger menait en leur nom une action parallèle, qui devait être jugée en même temps que celle des consommateurs. Le 22 août, le groupe a accepté de verser 260 millions de livres à environ 67 000 développeurs, sans reconnaître la moindre responsabilité, et le CAT a validé cet accord le 16 septembre. Google n’a en revanche trouvé aucun terrain d’entente avec Liz Coll, si bien qu’il doit défendre ses commissions sur le fond.
Google défend l’ouverture d’Android et la sécurité du Play Store
Google conteste toute pratique anticoncurrentielle et rappelle, dans sa défense écrite, que la grande majorité des applications du Play Store sont gratuites. D’après l’entreprise, seuls les plus gros développeurs, soit environ 3 % d’entre eux, paient une commission, dont le taux a baissé au fil des années. En novembre 2025, Google a d’ailleurs étendu au monde entier, jusqu’en 2032, les concessions négociées avec Epic Games. Les utilisateurs d’Android peuvent en outre installer des applications hors du Play Store, ou passer par des boutiques concurrentes, dont le Galaxy Store de Samsung.
Pour Google, les clients seraient davantage exposés aux arnaques et aux fraudes si des boutiques et des moyens de paiement non vérifiés étaient plus nombreux sur Android. En octobre 2024, le groupe a mis en avant les risques pour plus de 100 millions d’utilisateurs américains afin de bloquer l’ouverture du Play Store, imposée par la justice américaine après sa défaite contre Epic Games. « Android offre aux utilisateurs plus de choix que toute autre plateforme mobile quant aux applications et aux boutiques d’applications qu’ils souhaitent utiliser, Play proposant des tarifs parmi les plus bas du marché », a fait savoir Google, qui promet de défendre ses services « avec vigueur ».
Liz Coll a conscience du poids modeste de cette somme pour Alphabet, maison mère de Google. « Bien sûr, on peut dire que c’est une goutte d’eau dans l’océan pour l'entreprise, mais il est vraiment important que les gens sachent que ces entreprises ne peuvent pas faire tout ce qu’elles veulent, et qu’il existe un recours », a-t-elle confié au quotidien britannique. « Je pense qu’on peut ébranler certaines parties de l’empire », a-t-elle ajouté.

Researchers at Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, University of California, Santa Barbara, and National University of Singapore published a technical paper titled “Low contact resistance and high current density in ballistic p-type transistors based on oxygen-doped WSe2 monolayers.”
Abstract Excerpt:
“The development of high-performance p-type monolayer transistors is critical for extending two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors beyond silicon in sub 1-nm technology nodes for complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) circuits. However, insufficient doping and metal-induced gap states (MIGS) during metal deposition lead to high contact resistance, greatly limiting p-type on-state currents. Here, we demonstrate high-performance ballistic p-type monolayer tungsten diselenide (WSe2) transistors by oxygen p-doping. ”

articles.title: Electric Car Makers Need to Appeal to the ‘Other 90%’ - EE Times
articles.text:
Declining EV sales in the U.S. are triggering fear in the electric car community and panic in the media. The New York Times earlier this year declared that “the American EV has been crushed,” and ABC News suggested that the electric vehicle is rapidly becoming “a niche” product with a dwindling chance for broad appeal.
Much of the blame, of course, is aimed at the loss of electric car tax credits and the repeal of the Biden administration’s EV targets. There’s also a share of blame for U.S. automakers, which have backed away from earlier commitments to EVs.
But the unspoken solution to this sales dilemma is innovation. This should be obvious. In the U.S., less than 10% of new vehicle sales are electric. There’s a huge swath of the market that still won’t consider an electric car, largely for reasons of initial cost and practicality. Yet the pundits seldom cite innovation as a way of attracting the other 90% of the market.
That’s strange, because innovation is what brought us to this moment in history. Forty years ago, the electric car was a joke. Detroit engineers liked to say that no one quoted their 0-to-60 times because they couldn’t go 60 mph. Even Martin Eberhard, who later co-founded Tesla, referred to electric cars of the 1980s as “punishment cars.” They were for people, he said, “who needed to be punished because they weren’t riding bicycles.”
Then came two Caltech-educated engineers named Wally Rippel and Alan Cocconi, who in 1992 started a company called AC Propulsion. Using power electronics, Rippel and Cocconi built a mobile inverter. Their inverter enabled them to use a brushless AC motor, which in turn endowed their electric car with speed—lots of it. Instead of struggling to reach 60 mph, their tZero electric car could go 160 mph. It zipped from 0 to 60 in less than four seconds, making it faster than a Ferrari, Corvette, or any other gasoline-burning vehicle.
When Eberhard drove the tZero, he was so impressed that he decided to launch Tesla Motors. Three years afterward, employing the basics of AC Propulsion’s powertrain, Eberhard and his co-founder, Elon Musk, showed off their first Roadster at a star-studded event at the Santa Monica Airport in California. The Roadster buzzed around the airport’s runways to the delight of celebrities, including Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger and Disney’s Michael Eisner. Within two weeks, Tesla had gathered 127 checks for $100,000 each, in expectation of Roadster production. No one would ever have believed an electric car could have such appeal, but here it was. Wealthy celebrities couldn’t wait to park one in their driveways.
It was a story of innovation in its purest form. At the time, there were no tax credits or EV mandates. There was only a non-existent electric car market and a nation full of skeptics. Yet Rippel and Cocconi, in a flash of genius, appealed to people who never dreamed they’d want an electric car. As Tesla co-founder Marc Tarpenning later said, some of those consumers didn’t care what fuel this high-performance vehicle burned. “If it burned baby harp seals, they would have been totally fine with that, as long as it accelerated like crazy,” he said.
The situation is not so different today. Yes, more than a million EVs are sold in the U.S. every year. But to appeal to the 90% who don’t buy electric cars, automakers will have to keep innovating. They’ll need that flash of genius. There are plenty of targets for it: faster charging, better infrastructure, and cheaper batteries. Getting there might take years; it might take decades. But short of an out-and-out ban on gasoline vehicles, it may be the only way to bring broader appeal to the electric car.
Recent history teaches us that consumers buy new tech products if they’re priced reasonably. Such was the case with the internet and the cellphone. Both came after the electric car. Both now serve billions of people, while the EV still attempts to struggle to its feet. The internet and the cellphone showed that consumers won’t reject a new technology if it meets a personal need.
That’s the challenge facing the electric car community right now. It can’t keep preaching to the choir. It can’t keep complaining about tax credits. It needs to appeal to the consumers who don’t yet know they want an electric car. There are plenty of them out there, just waiting to be wowed.
To succeed, the electric car community will need to innovate, just as Rippel and Cocconi did.
Charles J. Murray is the author of “The EV Guys: How Caltech Engineers Reinvented the Electric Car,” published by Purdue University Press.

Points forts
- Conception soignée.
- Affichage lumineux.
- Autonomie confortable.
Points faibles
- Fiche technique en partie recyclée.
- Quantité de RAM et stockage discutable.
- Téléobjectif décevant.
Le Samsung Galaxy S26 FE est un smartphone très solide : design soigné, bon écran Oled, performances élevées, autonomie confortable, expérience logicielle riche et durable. Mais l’augmentation tarifaire causée par la crise actuelle des composants rend ses concessions difficiles à accepter. La photo évolue peu, le téléobjectif accuse son âge, l’affichage n’est pas LTPO, les 8 Go de mémoire vive paraissent justes et l’autonomie régresse légèrement. Face à un S26 désormais plus abordable, cette Fan Edition manque surtout d’audace et d’un positionnement cohérent.

articles.title: Galaxy S27 Ultra pode corrigir problema da Tela de Privacidade • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy S27 Ultra pode corrigir problema da Tela de Privacidade
Rumor indica que a Samsung trabalha para deixar tela mais nítida e definida com o recurso ativado.
A Samsung pode mudar a Tela de Privacidade do Galaxy S27 Ultra para reduzir problemas relatados no atual S26 Ultra. O recurso limita o ângulo de visão da tela para dificultar que pessoas ao redor enxerguem o conteúdo exibido, mas alguns consumidores têm relatado perda de brilho e qualidade de imagem.
Segundo o site PhoneArena, a Samsung trabalha para aprimorar a tecnologia na próxima geração e deixar a tela mais nítida e definida mesmo quando o recurso estiver ativado.
A Tela de Privacidade estreou no Galaxy S26 Ultra como uma das grandes novidades do aparelho. A tecnologia controla o ângulo de emissão de luz do painel para dificultar a visualização pelas laterais, funcionando como uma espécie de película de privacidade integrada ao display.
No entanto, a Samsung reconheceu que a tela pode ficar um pouco mais escura quando o recurso está ativado. Como noticiamos aqui no Tecnoblog, alguns consumidores relataram problemas de tonalidade no display do Galaxy S26 Ultra.
A possível melhoria seria interessante porque a Samsung estaria pensando em expandir a presença da Tela de Privacidade na próxima geração. Rumores indicam que o recurso pode chegar a toda a linha Galaxy S27, incluindo os modelos básico, Plus e o possível S27 Pro.
Além da tela, outros vazamentos apontam mudanças maiores no Galaxy S27 Ultra. O aparelho pode adotar um novo módulo horizontal para as câmeras e suporte nativo a acessórios magnéticos, além de possíveis atualizações no sensor principal, nas câmeras auxiliares, bateria maior e memória e armazenamento mais rápidos.
O lançamento da família Galaxy S27 é esperado para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. Até lá, os detalhes sobre a nova Tela de Privacidade, o conjunto de lentes e outras especificações ainda podem mudar.

articles.title: Microsoft Teams pourra bientôt détecter les deepfake
articles.text:
Les vidéos truquées et les voix bidonnées utilisées par certains malfrats pour tromper leur interlocuteur pourront bientôt être détectées dans Microsoft Teams. Microsoft est en effet en train de plancher sur la possibilité d’intégrer un outil tiers capable de détecter les vidéos et voix synthétisées grâce à l’intelligence artificielle.
Un plugin tiers contre les deepfake dans Teams
Devant la menace grandissante des deepfake alimentés par l’IA, Microsoft prépare sa riposte. La firme de Redmond est en train de préparer une nouvelle fonction de sécurité pour son logiciel collaboratif Teams. Microsoft entend protéger les utilisateurs de sa solution en leur permettant des outils pour démasquer d’éventuels cybercriminels qui tenteraient de se faire passer pour quelqu’un d’autre en utilisant des vidéos et des voix hyper réalistes générées par l’IA, ou pour éviter qu’un candidat à un entretien à l’embauche utilise l’IA et les deepfake pour gonfler ses chances de réussite.
Pour éviter ces fraudes, Microsoft va permettre aux entreprises d’intégrer des outils spécialisés dans la détection des deepfake et des voix synthétiques développés par des fournisseurs tiers certifiés. C’est en tout cas ce que l’entreprise a indiqué dans sa Roadmap Microsoft 365.
Ces outils, qui s’intégreront directement dans les réunions, pourront analyser les flux audio et vidéo en temps réel pour repérer les contenus générés ou manipulés par l’IA, avant d’afficher une alerte directement dans Teams.
La firme de Redmond ne prévoit toutefois pas de développer elle-même ce type de solution. Elle indique vouloir s’appuyer sur des fournisseurs tiers de confiance auxquels elle fournira l’intégration dans Teams ainsi que les fonctionnalités permettant d’afficher les signaux de détection et les mesures à prendre.
Si la disponibilité de cette nouvelle fonction n’est pour l’heure pas détaillée, et que Microsoft n’a pour l’instant donné aucune précision quant à la liste des éditeurs certifiés qui seront choisis, l’entreprise envisage un déploiement susceptible de démarrer dans le courant du mois de novembre, sur Windows, macOS, Android et iOS.

articles.title: Making Amazon Quick enterprise-ready: Automated, auditable cross-account resource promotion | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Making Amazon Quick enterprise-ready: Automated, auditable cross-account resource promotion
Amazon Quick is Amazon’s agentic AI companion built for work. You build agents that reason over your data, call action connectors, and carry multi-step tasks to completion. Promoting those resources (chat agents, action connectors, knowledge bases, flows, and spaces) from a development to a production AWS account, the way you would any other application, has been a manual and error-prone chore. This post shows how to automate it with an idempotent, auditable Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
The building blocks of an agentic solution are its agents, action connectors, knowledge bases, and spaces: chat agents configured with custom instructions, connectors for Slack, Jira, and other integrations, knowledge bases grounded in your own documents, and the Space that binds them together. Teams assemble and iterate on them quickly in a development account.
Most enterprises run separate AWS accounts for development and production, sometimes with quality assurance (QA) in between. When agents, action connectors, and knowledge bases are validated in a development account, there is no native, one-click way to promote them into the next account. Teams rebuild each resource by hand: recreate each agent with the same instructions and starter prompts, re-attach each agent’s action connectors, re-grant resource permissions, and reprovision the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, bucket policy, and data source behind each knowledge base. The work is slow, difficult to audit, and easy to get subtly wrong, which undermines the governance story enterprises need.
Manage Amazon Quick resources through an API
Amazon Quick resources are programmable. Spaces, agents, action connectors, knowledge bases, and flows are managed through the Amazon Quick API (part of the Amazon Quick Sight API surface), which provides the full resource lifecycle, create, read, update, delete, and list. Anything a business user configures in Amazon Quick, an agent with its instructions and starter prompts, a connector, a knowledge base, or a flow, we can inspect, recreate, update, and govern programmatically, permissions included.
This programmable surface is what makes governed promotion possible. Instead of recreating each resource by hand, we read a resource and its permissions through the API and reapply them in another account exactly as they were. The migrator in this post composes the create, read, update, and list operations into one repeatable workflow, and it never issues a delete against the target, so a run only adds or updates.
In this post, we walk through the Quick Resource Migrator, a sample MCP server hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that automates cross-account promotion of Amazon Quick resources in a single tool call. It’s resource-driven: you pick a resource type (agent, connector, knowledge base, flow, or space) and select by id, by name, or all. It’s idempotent (safe to re-run), and it copies permissions faithfully by describing the source and replaying the same actions in the target. The full source code is available in the aws-samples repository.
Solution overview
The migrator promotes a chosen set of resources in a single call. It is an upsert: a resource that does not yet exist in the target is created, and one that already exists is updated in place. Every update is protected by a versioned backup written to Amazon S3 before the change, so each resource keeps a full history you can review and roll back to. A read-only preview reports exactly what a run would create or update before you commit, and the migration itself runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so it can be driven from Amazon Quick or any MCP-compatible client.
What gets migrated
- Selection model: Pick a resource type (agent, connector, knowledge base, flow, or space) and choose resources by id, by name, or all. Selection is resource-driven. Migrate a resource type directly, or migrate a space to bring its linked resources across with it.
- Chat agents: Recreated with their custom instructions, identity, tone, starter prompts, and welcome message, with their action connectors re-attached (remapped to the target account). When a space is migrated, its agents are re-linked to it automatically.
- Action connectors: Recreated with their configuration. Secret values are never read from the source. Connectors are created with placeholder credentials and re-authenticated in the target.
- Knowledge bases: The knowledge base is registered in the target account, its data source is recreated, and its permissions are copied. For S3-backed knowledge bases the migrator also provisions the target bucket and its bucket policy (a distinct output of the migration). The documents (S3 objects) themselves are not copied.
- Flows: Recreated in the target account from their definition. Because flow IDs differ across accounts, flows are matched by name: a same-named target flow is updated, otherwise a new one is created. Flow permissions are copied.
- Spaces: Recreated in the target account and re-linked to their agents, connectors, and knowledge bases (with resource Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) remapped to the target). Migrate the linked resources first so the target ARNs resolve. Space permissions are copied.
Key design principles
- Resource-driven selection. You migrate one resource type at a time (agent, connector, knowledge base, flow, or space), selecting by id, by name, or all. Agents are recreated with their action connectors re-attached. Spaces are recreated and re-linked to their agents, connectors, and knowledge bases, with ARNs remapped to the target account.
- Permission fidelity. Permissions aren’t hard-coded. The server calls the relevant Describe*Permissions API on each source resource and replays the identical action list in the target, remapping principals to registered users in the target account.
- Idempotency. Every resource is created-or-updated. The server describes the target first and decides whether to create or update, so re-running a migration converges on the same state instead of producing duplicates or failing.
- Least privilege and isolation. The source role is read-only. The target role holds only the actions the migration needs. The runtime authenticates callers with a Cognito JSON Web Token (JWT) and can run in virtual private cloud (VPC) network mode.
- Safe, reversible updates. Before the migrator updates any existing target resource, it writes a versioned snapshot of that resource, and its dependencies, to a dedicated backup bucket. If that backup can’t be written, the update is aborted. Every created or updated resource is also snapshotted, and a restore tool can roll any resource back to an earlier version.
Architecture
The solution uses a three-account model. A central runner account hosts the MCP server on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The server assumes a read-only role in the source account and a read-write role in the target account using AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS), so no long-lived credentials are stored anywhere.
Component responsibilities
| Component | Responsibility | 
| AgentCore runtime (runner account) | Hosts the MCP server ( server.py). Assumes roles into the source and target accounts and orchestrates the migration. Runs in VPC network mode with a Cognito JWT authorizer. | 
| Amazon Cognito (runner account) | User pool, resource server, and a machine-to-machine app client. Issues the JWT (client-credentials grant, scope invoke) that callers present to AgentCore. | 
| Runner execution role | The AgentCore execution role: Amazon CloudWatch Logs, telemetry, and sts:AssumeRole into the source and target roles. | 
| Migrator role (source account) | Read-only Quick Sight describe/list permissions plus knowledge base read. | 
| Migrator role (target account) | Read-write Quick Sight create/update permissions, knowledge base and S3 write, and ListUsers for principal resolution. | 
| Backup bucket (runner account) | Encrypted S3 bucket that stores versioned pre-update and post-migration snapshots of target resources. The runtime writes to it directly. Restore reads from it. Optional (disabled when unset). | 
Table 1: Architectural components
Migration flow
- Resolve resources: from the resource type and selector (id, name, or all), resolve the concrete resource IDs in the source account.
- Describe the source: describe each selected resource to capture its configuration and permissions.
- Connectors: recreate each connector. The authentication config is sanitized to the create (write) model with placeholder secrets, then re-authenticated in the target. Copy permissions.
- Knowledge bases: create the target bucket (knowledge-base-<env>-<account>), bucket policy, data source, and knowledge base, then copy knowledge base permissions. S3 objects are not copied.
- Agents: recreate each agent with its action connectors attached (remapped to the target account), then copy agent permissions. Agent-to-space linkage is restored when the space itself is migrated (see the space step).
- Flows: recreate each flow from its definition, matched by name (flow IDs differ across accounts): update a same-named target flow or create a new one, then copy flow permissions.
- Spaces: recreate each space and re-link its agents, connectors, and knowledge bases with ARNs remapped to the target account (migrate those resources first), then copy space permissions.
- Report: return a JSON report of the created or updated resources, buckets, backups, skipped permissions, and any errors.
Tools exposed by the MCP server
The server exposes five tools, all defined in server.py.
preview_migration (read-only)
preview_migration takes a source account ID, a resource type (agent, connector, knowledge base, flow, space, or all), a selector (id, name, or all), and an AWS Region. It returns an inventory of the agents, action connectors, knowledge bases, and flows that would be migrated, with names and types, without making any change. Use it as a dry run to confirm scope and to support a change-management approval step before promotion. When you also pass a target account ID, the response adds a source-to-target mapping that marks each resource CREATE or UPDATE, so you can see exactly what a migration would change before running it.
migrate_resources (full migration)
migrate_resources takes source and target account IDs, a resource type (agent, connector, knowledge base, flow, or space), a selector (id, name, or all), a region, source and target environment names (used in the knowledge base bucket name), and the Quick Sight service role name. It performs the full create-or-update migration described above and returns a structured report of everything it created, updated, and granted, along with any errors. Because it’s idempotent, you can run it repeatedly, for example on every release, and it converges on the same target state.
list_backups (read-only)
list_backups searches the backup catalog and lists the available versions for each asset. Backups are the pre-update snapshots the migrator writes to the backup bucket, one versioned object per update, so you can see the full history for any migrated resource.
get_backup (read-only)
get_backup returns the full stored backup for a given asset and version (the latest by default), including the captured resource configuration and its dependencies.
restore_backup
restore_backup re-applies a stored backup version onto the target resource, updating it in place, or recreating it if it no longer exists. It first takes a fresh pre-restore backup, so the revert is itself reversible.
Deploy the solution
The full source and step-by-step deployment instructions live in the aws-samples repository README. At a high level you deploy three AWS CloudFormation stacks, the cross-account AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, the VPC network, and the Cognito-authenticated AgentCore runtime that hosts the MCP server, then register that runtime as an action connector in Amazon Quick.
Use the migrator through a Quick App
By registering the runtime as an action connector, you can drive the migrator from Amazon Quick in natural language, and you can also build a Quick App: a point-and-click web experience layered on the same MCP tools. You don’t build that UI by hand. The repository includes a ready-to-use app-builder prompt that you paste into the Amazon Quick app builder, replacing the placeholder connector and action IDs with your own to generate the app. The app turns the workflow into a guided flow: choose a source and target account and the resources to promote, preview what will be created or updated, run the migration, and review a history of every past migration, each backed by the versioned S3 snapshots the server writes. The following screens show that experience.
An example Quick App
- Because the app is generated from a prompt, each build differs. The following screens show one such example. In it, the landing page prompts for the Source Account ID, Target Account ID, resource type (agent, connector, knowledge base, flow, or space), and selector (id, name, or all), with additional options available as needed.
- After you choose Confirm & migrate, you see a response like the following:
- After you confirm and migrate, you should see the response from the MCP server returning the resources that were created/updated.
- Open the History tab to see every past migration. Each entry is backed by the versioned snapshot the migrator wrote to Amazon S3, so you get a full, auditable record of what was promoted and when, with the option to inspect any earlier version.
- To roll back, select a resource’s backup version and choose Restore. The app re-applies that saved version to the target. Because it first captures a fresh backup before restoring, the revert is itself reversible.
Conclusion
Cross-account promotion is a baseline expectation for enterprise software, and until now it has been the missing piece for Amazon Quick. The Quick Resource Migrator turns a slow, manual, hard-to-audit task into a fast, repeatable, and governed one: a single tool call recreates agents, connectors, and knowledge bases in a target account and copies permissions faithfully, all idempotently, so you can run it on every release.
Clone the sample repository, deploy it into a runner account, and try promoting an agent or knowledge base from development to production. Then adapt the pattern to your own governance and hardening requirements.

articles.title: Décès suspect en Sibérie : pourquoi la peste est-elle encore étudiée en 2026 ?
articles.text:
Une technicienne d’un laboratoire russe spécialisé dans la peste est morte le 1er octobre 2026, peut-être après avoir contracté la maladie qu’elle étudiait. Selon le média indépendant en exil Lioudi Baïkala, cité par l’AFP, Daria Chipilova était une technicienne de laboratoire de 28 ans, travaillant pour l’Institut anti-peste d’Irkoutsk. Elle avait été hospitalisée le 29 septembre avec des symptômes de pneumonie sévère, et son décès est survenu deux jours plus tard.
Daria Chipilova aurait brisé par accident un tube à essai contenant la bactérie de la peste, et aurait ainsi pu contracter la forme pulmonaire de la maladie. Près de 200 personnes ayant pu être en contact avec elle ont été placées sous surveillance médicale, dont plus d’une centaine à l’hôpital.
Cette suspicion autour d’une fuite de peste en laboratoire peut paraître inquiétante. Elle ne doit pas pour autant faire oublier ce qu’est réellement la peste. Contrairement à une croyance répandue, la peste n’a jamais disparu. Ce cas ne signifie donc pas que la maladie ferait son retour.
La peste, une zoonose qui a décimé l’Europe au Moyen Âge
La peste est une zoonose, qui se transmet principalement par la puce infectée par la bactérie Yersinia pestis. La puce peut être véhiculée par de petits animaux, notamment des rongeurs : s’ils sont au contact d’humains, ils peuvent les exposer à cette puce, et donc à la maladie en cas de piqure. En l’absence de traitement, la peste tue de 30 à 100 % des malades, selon la forme de la maladie.
La maladie est connue pour les ravages qu’elle a provoqués au Moyen Âge, avec la « mort noire » qui a sévi au milieu du 14e siècle, tuant entre 30 et 60 % de la population européenne. Après ce choc démographique, d’autres vagues épidémiques se sont produites pendant les siècles suivants, contribuant à donner à la peste cette image d’une maladie moyen-âgeuse dévastratrice, avant que l’on comprenne mieux son fonctionnement au gré des progrès de la médecine.
Aujourd’hui, la peste n’est pas éradiquée
La peste a pourtant survécu au Moyen Âge. « Quoique la peste ne soit plus de nos jours le fléau qu’elle a été par le passé, grâce en particulier à la découverte de l’agent causal, du cycle de transmission, et surtout grâce à l’utilisation de traitements antibiotiques efficaces, elle est loin d’avoir été éradiquée », expliquaient ainsi en 2008 les chercheuses Françoise Guinet et Elisabeth Carniel de l’Institut Pasteur.
Entre 1990 et 2020, près de 50 000 cas de peste ont été déclarés à l’OMS par 26 pays, selon l’Institut Pasteur. La maladie sévit principalement en Afrique, en Asie et en Amérique (en France, les derniers cas remontent à 1945, en Corse) et « fait partie des maladies actuellement ré-émergentes dans le monde ». Grâce à l’usage des antibiotiques (efficaces s’ils sont administrés rapidement) et aux mesures de santé publique, la mortalité a fortement baissé au cours du 20e siècle.
D’ailleurs, « une des caractéristiques des épidémies de peste est leur capacité à ‘s’éteindre’ pendant plusieurs années avant de réapparaître brutalement sous forme épidémique », souligne l’Institut Pasteur. Ainsi, en 1994, l’Inde a connu une épidémie de peste pulmonaire, alors que l’on pensait la maladie éradiquée depuis presque 30 ans. La Russie elle-même a vu réapparaître des cas humains en 2013, après 34 ans d’absence. Il est donc nécessaire de continuer à étudier de près cette maladie, et de ne pas la considérer comme appartenant au passé.
Aucun vaccin efficace et sûr contre la peste
Il n’existe à ce jour aucun vaccin sûr et efficace contre la peste, et les traitements utilisés ont parfois leurs limites. Françoise Guinet et Elisabeth Carniel ont ainsi relevé que le bacille pesteux, Yersinia pestis, peut développer dans certains cas une résistance aux antibiotiques utilisés pour le traitement de la peste. Ces antibiotiques restent une solution pour guérir la maladie, mais la possibilité d’une émergence de souches du bacille résistantes doit être surveillée, car elle constituerait « une menace majeure en santé publique ».
Françoise Guinet et Elisabeth Carniel résument ainsi : « La peste ne se présente plus aujourd’hui sous la forme des épidémies massives et dévastatrices qui ont marqué l’histoire et la mémoire collective des hommes. Cependant, cette maladie pose encore au monde actuel d’importants défis. » Sa gravité et sa contagiosité obligent encore aujourd’hui à réagir vite au moindre début d’épidémie. La panique que provoque la maladie pose aussi problème, car elle peut pousser des populations à fuir et propager ainsi la peste. La peste peut aussi se manifester de nouveau là où on ne l’observait plus, si bien que « l’éradication d’un foyer de peste établi ne peut jamais être tenue pour acquise ».
Des foyers naturels restent actifs sur plusieurs continents, et des établissements comme l’Institut anti-peste d’Irkoutsk servent justement à étudier les agents pathogènes dangereux de Sibérie et d’Extrême-Orient. Pour la jeune technicienne d’Irkoutsk, aucun diagnostic de peste n’a été confirmé publiquement. L’agence sanitaire russe Rospotrebnadzor affirme même n’avoir retrouvé dans ses prélèvements aucun des agents pathogènes de son laboratoire, sans dire pour autant de quoi elle est morte.

articles.title: Germany's Aleph Alpha releases Kolibri, a sovereign AI model for mission-critical government and industry applications | EU-Startups
articles.text:
German AI company Aleph Alpha has launched Kolibri, a specialised large language model (LLM) built for mission-critical applications in public administration and industry.
Referred to as sovereign AI made in Germany and released on 3 October 2026, Aleph Alpha says Kolibri is designed for organisations that require data control, documented compliance, and a model trained to operate natively in German.
“Kolibri demonstrates that we have the talent and expertise in Germany to develop competitive AI models. For us, AI sovereignty means freedom of choice by retaining the ability to build and advance this technology, and giving customers control over how they use it. Our ambition is to bring that capability into everyday operations in industry and public administration,” said Ilhan Scheer, CEO of Aleph Alpha.
Founded in 2019, Aleph Alpha is on a mission to build sovereign, human-centric AI. Along with Mistral, the company has become one of the two European champions challenging frontier labs in the US and China. It employs around 200 people across four locations in Germany, and says its specialised LLMs are used by enterprises and government institutions looking to maintain data sovereignty and build trustworthy AI applications.
Kolibri is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model combining 78 billion total parameters with approximately 3 billion active per token. The model is designed in such a way that instead of activating the entire model during inference, its architecture selectively engages only the relevant parts, a design approach that improves efficiency without compromising on capability. Aleph Alpha says German-language text makes up around 23% of its pre-training data, and it has developed a German-optimised tokeniser that represents German text using fewer tokens to enable faster and more efficient processing of German content.
The model supports agentic workflows, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and native tool calling. In RAG applications, Kolibri is trained to answer questions based on supplied documents and abstain from responding when those documents don’t contain sufficient evidence. In other words, Aleph Alpha claims to have reduced hallucinations in high-stakes settings. It also allows users to adjust the balance between reasoning depth and response speed through built-in reasoning controls.
To meet the compliance and provenance demands of regulated industries and government institutions, Aleph Alpha has screened Kolibri against a blocklist of more than 4.5 million URLs, drawing on sources including the European Commission’s Piracy Watch List. It has also accessed every third-party dataset individually for licence terms, lawful sourcing and adherence to opt-outs. In a technical report, Aleph Alpha has detailed how Kolibri addresses copyright, data protection and EU AI Act requirements, while its licence terms and supporting documents are available on Hugging Face.
Samuel Weinbach, co-founder and co-Chief Research Officer, Aleph Alpha said, “We designed Kolibri around the needs of German-language applications, from a tokeniser optimised for German to training the model to reason in German. For our customers, this is an important step of making AI useful in everyday workflows.”
The new sovereign AI model, Kolibri, follows the company’s April announcement of an agreement with Canadian AI firm Cohere to build a joint transatlantic sovereign AI company. While the merger is subject to regulatory approval, the two companies officially signed a definitive business agreement last month, announcing that the combined entity will operate globally as Cohere with headquarters, R&D centres, and leadership roles in Canada and Germany.
With Kolibri now available and a merger in the pipeline, Aleph Alpha is not only showing that Europe can build its own large language models but do so without compromising on sovereignty.

articles.title: Windows 11: Dieser Shortcut bringt dich bald schneller in den Profilordner
articles.text:
Bei Windows-11-Updates konzentriert sich Microsoft meist auf die Einführung neuer KI-Funktionen. Mit einem kommenden Update für die aktuelle Version des Microsoft-Betriebssystems könnte bald ein kleiner, aber umso praktischerer Shortcut kommen, der Nutzer:innen den Zugang zu ihrem Profil- oder Benutzerordner erleichtern soll.
Wie Neowin berichtet, soll es sich bei der neuen Navigationshilfe für den Datei-Explorer um das aus Linux- und Unix-Umgebungen bekannte Tilde-Symbol (~) handeln. Die Eingabe der Tilde in der Adressleiste des Datei-Explorers bringt die Nutzer:innen künftig direkt in den Benutzerordner ihres Profils.
Ebenfalls vereinfachen lässt sich damit der direkte Zugriff auf Profilordner wie Appdata. Bisher bietet Windows 11 die Möglichkeit, den Ordner über die Eingabe von %USERPROFILE%\AppData zu erreichen. Künftig soll dann ~\AppData ausreichen.
Windows 11: Tilde-Symbol als Shortcut
Der Shortcut ist nicht zuletzt für all jene eine Erleichterung, die das Tilde-Symbol schon jetzt in anderen Umgebungen als Abkürzung verwenden. Darüber hinaus müssen sich Nutzer:innen damit nicht mehr ihren Profilnamen merken. Der Shortcut funktioniert ganz unabhängig davon, über welches Konto Nutzer:innen angemeldet sind.
Noch ist allerdings nicht vollständig sicher, dass der Tilde-Shortcut auch wirklich ausgerollt wird. Denn aktuell befindet sich die Funktion im experimentellen Teststatus des Windows-11-Insider-Programms. Hier kann Microsoft theoretisch noch die Reißleine ziehen, wenn sich der Shortcut doch als unpraktisch herausstellen sollte.
So lässt sich das Tilde-Zeichen erzeugen
Das Tilde-Zeichen selbst ist wiederum auf einer deutschen Windows-Tastatur etwas versteckt. Um es zu erzeugen, kann man etwa die Alt-Gr-Taste gedrückt halten und dazu die Taste + (neben dem Buchstaben Ü) drücken.
Eine weitere kleinere Änderung könnte künftig in Windows 11 die Privatsphäre der Nutzer:innen verbessern. Mit der neuen Funktion, die aktuell ebenfalls im Testmodus ist, soll sich besser einstellen lassen, welche Apps und Dienste Zugriff auf Mikrofon und Webcam bekommen.

articles.title: Senate Passes Bipartisan Bill to Strengthen Healthcare Cybersecurity
articles.text:
The US Senate has passed the bipartisan Health Care Cybersecurity and Resilience Act, introduced by Senators Bill Cassidy, Maggie Hassan, Jon Cornyn, and Mark Warner.
The bill was first introduced in 2024, but failed to pass before the end of that congressional term. It was reintroduced in December 2025.
Having passed the Senate by unanimous consent, the Health Care Cybersecurity and Resilience Act now heads to the US House of Representatives for consideration.
“Cyberattacks on our healthcare sector not only put patients’ sensitive health data at risk but can delay life-saving care. This bipartisan legislation ensures health institutions can safeguard Americans’ health data against increasing cyber threats,” claims Cassidy. Its purpose is to assist the sector in reducing the number of future successful criminal attacks.
Healthcare is a primary target for cybercriminals. More than 730 cyber breaches affected over 270 million Americans last year – costing an average of $10 million per breach.
Major incidents include the historic Anthem breach of 2015 (compromising the PI and health records of 78.8 million customers, and costing more than $115 million); the ransomware attack against Ascension in 2024 (which disrupted clinical operations and electronic health records across 11 US states), and the Change Healthcare attack in 2024 that is believed to have exposed the data of over 190 million people while causing significant delays in care and electronic prescribing.
The definitive criminal weapon of choice in this war against healthcare is ransomware coupled with double-extortion (and increasingly, pure data-extortion). Ransomware is devastating to healthcare. The sector is caught between government advice not to pay ransoms and its own requirement to protect its patients. Criminals expect it to pay a ransom rather than risk the health of patients. The new Act aims to help the sector improve its resilience against these attacks.
“Patients deserve absolute confidence that their sensitive medical data stored online is protected and shielded from cybersecurity breaches or ransomware attacks,” said Cornyn. “This legislation would strengthen interagency coordination and improve security practices for rural providers, ensuring Texans’ health care is not delayed or compromised by cyberattacks.”
Hopefully, the intention is to protect patients beyond the borders of Texas.
Key elements of the Act include the provision of grants to improve cyberattack prevention and response, and training in best cybersecurity practices; improved support for rural health clinics; better coordination between HHS and CISA (to improve response to cyberattacks); updates to current regulations to ensure use of the best cybersecurity practices; and a requirement for the HHS Secretary to develop and implement a cybersecurity incident response plan.
The Act attempts to provide central cybersecurity guidance across the various existing frameworks. Of particular relevance is the formalized inter-agency coordination establishing the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR) as the clear Sector Risk Management Agency, and building a direct pipeline for CISA to provide tailored, actionable threat intelligence.
The Act is generally welcomed by the healthcare sector, but the security industry cautions that success will depend on how consistently it is enforced. There are concerns about the financial strain of compliance if federal funding or technical assistance fails to keep pace with the regulatory requirements.
The reality is that this is fundamentally a new compliance requirement on healthcare. The concept of regulation is good in theory but difficult to fulfill in practice. This regulation requires full compliance from two parties – both the government and the healthcare sector.
